10099-towards-the-goal:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1917 book, with an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt and dedicated to André Chevrillon, true son of France and true friend of England, reports England's effort in the Great War. It follows her earlier England's Effort, tracing the rapid march of events.

Ward visits munition areas, watching enormous and rapid work, and writes of the navy, an aerodrome, and the task of aviators, with Herr Zimmermann and national training among her themes. She writes as a convinced supporter of the Allied cause. Readers get a wartime report from a famous novelist turned observer.
10140-rhetoric-and-poetry-in-the-renaiss:
Donald Lemen Clark, assistant professor of English at Columbia University, published this 1922 study of rhetorical terms in English Renaissance literary criticism. Part first sets out the general theory of rhetoric and of poetry, with an introduction on the distinction between the two arts.

Classical poetic theory follows, through Aristotle and Longinus, the ancient critics Renaissance writers read. Clark writes for students of literature, with care for terms and their history. Readers get a scholarly guide to how Renaissance England talked about poetry, and why its words still matter. His examples come from the critics themselves.
10361-the-creative-process-in-the-indivi:
T. Troward published this metaphysical study in 1915, on how the mind creates its own life. Troward, a writer on New Thought, opens with the old saying that order is heaven's first law. He argues that progress comes not from new laws of nature, but from arranging known things in a better order.

Chapters treat the starting point, self-contemplation of spirit, the divine ideal, the personal factor, race thought, and the divine offering. A Whitman motto frames the book's hope for human grandeur. Readers get a calm, idealist philosophy of creation, aimed at readers seeking spiritual self-command.
10603-with-kelly-to-chitral:
Lieutenant W. G. L. Beynon, staff officer to Colonel Kelly's relief force, wrote this frontier memoir in 1896, as a letter to his mother from Gilgit in October 1895. Beynon warns that his short history holds no heroic deeds, only daily life of British officers and Indian troops on a frontier expedition. Marches, food, jokes, and trials fill the days.

Chapters follow the march, the Shandur Pass, Laspur to Gasht, a reconnaissance from Mastuj, a fight at Nisa Gol, and the goal at Chitral. Snow, rain, hot valleys, and pleasant fields mark the route. Readers get a vivid, soldier's-eye account of a famous relief march on India's northwest frontier.
10985-the-infant-system-for-developing-t:
Samuel Wilderspin, inventor of the infant school system, set out his method in this book, revised in an eighth edition in 1852. Wilderspin had taught more than twenty-five thousand children under six and organised scores of schools across Britain. He argues that children from one to seven should learn through play, objects, and short lessons, not long hours of rote work.

Gallery lessons, Wilderspin insists, should last no more than an hour or two, with mornings for teaching, afternoons for object lessons, spelling, and outdoor moral and physical training. Robbing children of play to show off precocity, he warns, harms health and defeats learning. The book remains a landmark in early childhood education, shaping how infant schools were built and run.
10988-the-devil-s-admiral:
Frederick Ferdinand Moore set this 1913 sea adventure aboard the cargo steamer Kut Sang in the China Sea. The narrator, Trenholm, joins Captain Riggs and his crew for a night and a day of fighting, spying, and piracy. A missionary, a red-headed beggar, a dead boatswain, and a spy called Thirkle drive a plot of gold, thieves, and a battle on the bridge.

Riggs at first refuses to have the story told, fearing he will look beaten, though the narrator insists he was the bravest man aboard. Mouldy biscuit, warm water, and a forecastle mess show the rough side of cargo-boat life. Moore writes a fast yarn of the old China trade, full of fights in the dark and councils of war.
10999-tales-of-bengal:
S. B. Banerjea wrote these seventeen tales of Bengal, edited by Francis Henry Skrine. Stories include the Pride of Kadampur, rival markets, a foul conspiracy, an outrageous swindle, a peacemaker, a Brahman's curse, and a rift in the lute. Village life, joint family estates, markets, and magistrates supply the plots, with morals such as patience and economy stated plainly.

The introduction argues against the idea that East and West can never meet, noting Bengal's fertile, silt-rich soil, its ancient civilisation, and its vulnerability to malaria and invaders. Banerjea writes for English readers, explaining Bengali customs from inside. The tales give a vivid, humane picture of rural Bengal under British rule, told with humour and local knowledge.
11432-the-youth-s-coronal:
Hannah Flagg Gould's 1851 Youth's Coronal, addressed to the youth of her country, aims to entertain and instruct at once. pleasant as spring blossoms in reading and fruitful as ripened fruit in afterlife influence. Gould borrows her title from Proverbs, instruction as an ornament of grace, and promises no moral a good and judicious parent would not wish a child to imbibe. Her coronal is woven of little flowers of poesy, scented and thornless, offered for the giver's sake.

Gould, author of Poems, writes verse and short pieces for young readers in a didactic, affectionate voice. The book belongs to the gift-book tradition for children, where poetry served character formation. Readers of nineteenth-century children's literature will find its preface a clear statement of its method.
11632-woman-man-s-equal:
Thomas Webster's 1873 book, with an introduction by Bishop Simpson, argues for woman as man's equal from nature, history, and the Word of God. Publishers call it a discussion of one of the most important topics of the day, presented in a manner at once attractive and convincing.

Webster sets out abuses suffered by women in heathen nations and brute ages, and says Christianity enlarged woman's area and multiplied her duties. America, he claims, stands ahead of all nations in opportunity. A later passage notes that men who preach female inferiority are often led and duped by frivolous women.
11722-first-lessons-in-geography-or-intr:
James Monteith's First Lessons in Geography, dated 1856, is number one in the National Geographical Series. It serves as an introduction to his Youth's Manual for beginners in schools. Later numbers in the series cover junior, intermediate, and advanced classes, by Monteith and McNally.

Lessons run in question and answer form throughout the book, with the pupil learning states, rivers, and divisions of land by heart. The southern states are counted at ten in one lesson, with Texas named as the largest and Florida as the furthest south. Florida is called a peninsula, and Cuba is named as the island south of it. The book is a school primer meant for recitation aloud.
11754-forty-years-in-south-china-the-lif:
John Gerardus Fagg, missionary of the American Reformed Church at Amoy, wrote Forty Years in South China as a life of Rev. John Van Nest Talmage, published in 1894. An introduction by T. De Witt Talmage says his brother, called the hero of the family, turned down a Brooklyn call with a large salary to go to China.

Chapters run from the ancestral home and a call to China, through the city of the elegant gate, to market towns and country churches. One passage praises babes in Christ whose knowledge of Scripture is remarkable, and recalls W. C. Burns, first English Presbyterian missionary to China in 1847. The book is a missionary biography of steady labour.
12041-the-shadow-of-the-cathedral:
Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's Shadow of the Cathedral, translated from Spanish by Mrs. W. A. Gillespie with a critical introduction by W. D. Howells, appeared in 1919. Its first chapter opens at dawn, as Gabriel Luna arrives in front of the cathedral, though in the narrow street of Toledo it is still night.

Silvery morning light scarcely touches the eaves and roofs, spreading slowly over the old city, while Luna enters the shadow of the great church that will dominate his story. Blasco Ibáñez, a Spanish novelist of passion and politics, uses Toledo's cathedral as both setting and symbol: faith, history, and human desire contending in a single, ancient place.
12896-essays-sthetical:
George H. Calvert's Essays Æsthetical, published in 1875, meditates on beauty, poetry, style, Dante, Sainte-Beuve, Carlyle, national drama, and the usefulness of art. The opening essay calls beauty an immortal theme, born on the same day as the sun, easy in its riches and hard in its demands. Calvert writes as a thoughtful American man of letters.

A passage on style, quoting Buffon, stresses sequence and close dependence of thought and word, detesting a chopped, jerky manner. Composition, Calvert says, begins when separate threads are woven into a continuous whole. The essays suit readers who enjoy nineteenth-century reflection on art and letters.
13248-mckinlay-s-journal-of-exploration-:
John McKinlay's Journal of Exploration in the Interior of Australia records the Burke Relief Expedition, published at Melbourne by Bailliere with three maps. McKinlay, leader of the relief party, writes to the Chief Commissioner of Crown Lands from Depot Camp at Cudye-cudyena in October 1861. His journal runs day by day, with chart and detail.

Entries note horses, bullocks, camels, and sheep all right, save a lame ewe heavy in lamb lost overnight. McKinlay crosses creeks, marks trees MK, names Marchant Creek for William Marchant of Mananarie, and passes quartz reefs and spinifex. The journal is a plain, daily record of search in harsh country, made by a man seeking lost explorers.
13554-aftermath-part-second-of-a-kentuck:
James Lane Allen's Aftermath, part second of A Kentucky Cardinal, was published in 1899. It returns to a Kentucky garden where the narrator works butterbeans, a vegetable of solid merit, while Georgiana watches from her window. She teases him for loving vines, and asks if he expects her to be a vine when they are married.

Congressmen seeking a military asylum for disabled soldiers wander to Lower Blue Lick Springs, Louisville, Frankfort, Maysville, Paris, and Lexington. Georgiana warns that everybody is sensitive in an extraordinary time, while the narrator replies that men must choose liberty for mind and prison for body, or the reverse. Allen writes a Kentucky love story in garden talk and aphorism.
13979-for-the-admiral:
W. J. Marx wrote For the Admiral in 1906, a Huguenot adventure novel set in sixteenth-century France. A perilous ride, a fight by the way, and keeping a ford open the chapters. A traitor to the king, an unknown cavalier, and a commission for the admiral follow. The tragedy of Jarnac and a glorious victory test the heroes.

Marx dedicates the book to his wife, without whose encouragement it would never have been written. A heroine sets aside fear, for the admiral's safety is at stake, and Huguenots gladly sacrifice for their leader. The novel follows Coligny's party through war and faith. It suits young readers of historical adventure. Marx writes with brisk, loyal enthusiasm.
13989-the-duty-of-disobedience-to-the-fu:
Lydia Maria Child addressed this 1860 appeal to the legislators of Massachusetts. Published as Anti-Slavery Tract number nine, it urges disobedience to the Fugitive Slave Act. Child opens with Deuteronomy: thou shalt not deliver an escaped servant to his master. She apologises not for speaking as a woman, citing Scott on truth's right to a tongue.

Child pictures children torn from tender arms by slave traders, and Bibles sealed from people of black, brown, or yellow skin. She argues that unjust law deserves resistance, not obedience. Her prose is earnest, biblical, and political at once. The tract shows women shaping abolitionist argument. It remains a strong statement of higher-law doctrine.
14625-military-instructors-manual:
Captain James P. Cole and Major Oliver Schoonmaker wrote this Military Instructors Manual for the Plattsburg training camps, under Colonel Wolf's supervision, with help from candidates Alcott, Farrar, Elwell, and Prouse. The manual trained officers for the Great War.

It covers rifle grenades, including the Newton Improved with a range of 250 yards and the Hale No. 3, and insists that dummy grenades precede live ones, since carelessness with weapons cannot be tolerated. Drill, throwing, and safety fill the pages. The book is a practical wartime handbook, direct and technical. Plattsburg trained thousands of new officers for France.
14628-the-sweet-and-touching-tale-of-fle:
Mrs. Leighton translated this medieval legend of Fleur and Blanchefleur from the French, with thirty-seven colored illustrations by Eleanor Fortescue Brickdale, published in London in 1922. The tale begins in the year 624.

A heathen king of Spain ravages Christendom, and two children, Fleur and Blanchefleur, grow up together, are parted, and seek each other across ports and courts. A hostess at Nicaea recalls a sighing maiden sold for a great price. The legend is a tender romance of faithful love, retold here in graceful modern English for new readers. Brickdale's illustrations add color to the old tale.
15067-the-cathedral:
J. K. Huysmans's novel, first published in France in 1898 and translated by Clara Bell, follows Durtal, a writer drawn to the cathedral at Chartres. Each morning he crosses a windswept square to enter the vast, dim church, where nuns and bent women hurry through the cold. The building itself becomes the book's true subject.

Durtal studies stone, glass, sculpture, and liturgy, and weighs his own faith against the art around him. Huysmans writes in dense, sensory prose, lingering on scent, light, and detail. Readers who love cathedrals, medieval art, or slow, meditative fiction will find the novel rich, strange, and deeply felt.
15092-the-aldine-vol-5-no-1-january-1872:
Issued in New York in 1872, this art journal mixes essays, poems, and travel notes with fine engraved plates. Its pages range from Alpine scenery and American home life to notes on books, music, and the work of painters. The whole volume was meant to show off both good writing and good printing.

Contributors include well-known names of the day, alongside unsigned editorial pieces on art and taste. Short poems sit beside longer talks on architecture, nature, and foreign lands. Taken together, the number gives a clear sense of what a cultured American reader in the 1870s prized in art, letters, and the wider world.
15180-the-honorable-percival:
Alice Hegan Rice's 1914 novel follows Percival, a blighted being in need of a counter-irritant, through convalescence, counter-currents, and a stranding by the sea. Chapters move from a wind-shelter and a day that never was to a crow's-nest, a gymkhana, and a siren's song. Percival procrastinates, then rises to an occasion.

Rice, known for Mrs. Wiggs, writes with humor about a man adrift who finds purpose, love, and a port at last. Surf boats, wharves, and seaside talk fill the scenes. Readers who enjoy light, character-led romance will find Percival charming, funny, and gently moral.
15352-venereal-diseases-in-new-zealand-1:
This 1922 New Zealand report, from a Board of Health committee chaired by W. H. Triggs, studies venereal diseases and their control. Members include doctors, a hospital board representative, and Lady Luke, with Sir Donald McGavin as medical services director. The report went to both houses of the General Assembly.

Sections cover inquiry scope, ignorance, sex education for the young, syphilis and gonorrhoea, diagnosis, and early, completed treatment. The tone is official, medical, and frank for its day. Public health historians will find the report a revealing record of how a dominion faced a sensitive subject.
15483-rambles-and-recollections-of-an-in:
Major-General Sir W. H. Sleeman wrote these rambles and recollections of India, revised and annotated by Vincent A. Smith for Oxford University Press in 1915. Sleeman dedicates the book to his sister, recalling how letters from home cheered Englishmen in India. Notes moved to chapter ends in this edition, and spelling follows the printed original.

Chapters range widely: fairs on sacred rivers, Hindu religion, the legend of the Nerbudda, a suttee, Hindu marriages, castes, witchcraft, and the peasantry and land settlement. Sleeman writes as an official who traveled, talked, and watched, mixing anecdote with observation. The volume gives a long, detailed view of early nineteenth-century India, valuable for its firsthand scenes even where its judgments belong to its age.
1651-the-mystery-of-orcival:
Émile Gaboriau's detective novel begins on a July morning at Orcival, where poachers find signs of violence near the Seine and a young countess is missing from her home. A local magistrate, a doctor, and the sharp-eyed M. Plantat piece together footprints, a broken window, and a household full of people with reasons to lie.

The investigation turns on money, marriage, and an old scandal, and Gaboriau lets the reader watch the case build clue by clue rather than by sudden confession. As one of the early French crime novels, it shows the police procedural taking shape. Careful inquiry and false leads lead toward a solution that reorders everything the village thought it knew.
16531-old-st-paul-s-cathedral:
William Benham, rector of St. Edmund the King and canon of Canterbury, tells the story of old St. Paul's Cathedral in this 1902 volume. Pictures drawn from old prints show the cathedral by Three Cranes Wharf, bishops placing relics, funeral processions, and pontifical masses. Wenceslaus Hollar's engravings supply much of the visual record.

Benham writes as a churchman and historian, tracing the great church that burned in 1666 and lives on in prints and memory. The book mixes architecture, ritual, and London life. For lovers of old London, it is a rich, well-illustrated guide to a vanished landmark.
16906-discourse-of-the-life-and-characte:
Hugh Blair Grigsby delivered this discourse on the life and character of the Hon. Littleton Waller Tazewell before the bar of Norfolk, Virginia, and citizens generally, in the Freemason Street Baptist Church on June 29, 1860, issued at Norfolk by J. D. Ghiselin. Grigsby opens by recalling how the bar met in mourning, then bore their friend's remains to a steamer over the noble bay Tazewell loved and called the Mediterranean of the Commonwealth.

Grigsby praises Tazewell as lawyer, statesman, and Virginian, in formal, funeral prose. The discourse gives a full, period portrait of a Virginia public man. Readers of Virginia history will find a rich, if admiring, life sketch, useful for its detail and its view of how Norfolk honored its great men.
16998-the-betrayal:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this 1904 novel of betrayal, in forty chapters. Contents run from a face at the window and good Samaritans into a cry in the night and Miss Moyat's promise. The graciousness of a duke, Lady Angela's advice, and Colonel Ray's ring follow. A wonderful offer, treachery, a bribe, and a reluctant apology appear. Two fair callers, Lord Blenavon's surrender, a secret, and the traitor at last close the tale.

Oppenheim builds a society thriller around a duke, a colonel, a lady, and a man who loses his post and must speak out. The plot turns on rings, bribes, and confessions, with brisk, popular pace. Readers who like Edwardian intrigue will find a long, plot-rich novel of loyalty, treachery, and love under pressure.
17087-ancient-art-and-ritual:
Jane Ellen Harrison's 1913 study argues that art grew out of ritual, not apart from it. Greek drama is her main case: a great art form rose from early communal rites, dances, and spring feasts. She traces the path from pantomime dance and dithyramb to the stage, then tests the same link in sculpture, from the Parthenon frieze to the Apollo Belvedere.

The point is not a survey of old art or old rites, and Harrison says so at the start. She wants to show how art, faith, and moral life join and part, and what art can do for the spirit today. Short, bold, and full of Greek examples, the book still shapes how readers think about where art begins.
17174-the-makers-of-canada-bishop-laval:
A. Leblond de Brumath's life of Bishop Laval, in the Makers of Canada set, follows Francois de Laval from early years to the founding of the Catholic Church in Canada. Chapters cover the sovereign council, the seminary and its smaller school, settlement of the colony, and Laval's troubled rule with Frontenac. A third voyage to France, resignation, last labors, and death close the tale.

The book opens with a look back from the twentieth century to apostles, doctors, and martyrs of the faith. Its tone is warm and Catholic, proud of Laval's work in Quebec. Readers new to New France will find a solid first life of its first bishop and school founder.
17455-the-poison-tree-a-tale-of-hindu-li:
Bankim Chandra Chatterjee wrote this Bengali novel of Hindu life, translated by Miriam S. Knight with a preface by Edwin Arnold and printed in London in 1884. It opens with Nagendra's boat trip and moves through his household, where Surja Mukhi, Kunda, and the servant Hira all play their parts. Chapter titles trace envy, a caged bird, a dark house, and a poison tree that buds, blossoms, and bears fruit.

The poison tree gives the book its moral image: a small wrong, nursed in secret, grows until it ruins happiness. A glossary of Hindu terms helps English readers follow the customs of the household. Readers get a classic of Bengali fiction, domestic in scale and tragic in shape, still valued for its portrait of family duty and desire.
1747-the-red-seal:
A New York police court hears a banker named Benjamin Clymer testify about his late housemate Judge Hildebrand and a clerk called John Sylvester. A red seal on a document soon refuses to fit any easy story. A death soon follows, and a red seal on a document becomes the clue that will not fit any easy story.

The novel follows the inquiry through apartments, offices, and society rooms, with Barbara and her circle adding comedy to the suspense. Lincoln writes in the brisk manner of the 1920s detective story. The puzzle turns on character as much as on evidence: who had reason to lie, and who stood to gain from a dead man's papers.
17855-hemp-hurds-as-paper-making-materia:
Lyster H. Dewey and Jason L. Merrill wrote this 1916 bulletin on hemp hurds as paper-making material, printed by the United States Department of Agriculture. Dewey led fiber-plant work, and Merrill served as paper-plant chemist, so the paper joins farm facts with mill tests.

Dewey covers what hurds are, how retting shapes them, yields per acre, and baling costs. Merrill then tests hurd paper for strength and quality, and weighs it against trade practice. The bulletin is short, plain, and practical, and it shows an early push to find farm waste a new, useful life in the paper mill.
18031-a-dweller-in-mesopotamia-being-the:
Donald Maxwell wrote A Dweller in Mesopotamia as the tale of an official artist in the Garden of Eden, printed in London by John Lane. Maxwell went to Iraq with brush and sketchbook after the Great War, and he drew what he saw in color, monochrome, and line.

Chapters run from the fiery furnace to the Venice of the East, Sinbad the soldier, wise men from the West, old Baghdad, and paradise lost. Maxwell writes with an artist's eye for light, river, and bazaar. The book gives a vivid, British view of Mesopotamia in 1919, best read now as both travel art and period witness.
181-the-project-gutenberg-rst-manual:
Project Gutenberg's RST Manual teaches volunteers to build ebooks from plain-text sources. The manual centers on EpubMaker, the project's converter from PG-RST to HTML, EPUB, PDF, and plain text. Opening sections cover installing Python and setup tools on Windows.

Later guidance walks through markup, tables, figures, and contents for a finished ebook. The manual's own structure models the format it teaches, with title pages and lists. Volunteers use it to turn raw texts into readable editions. It documents the workflow behind thousands of Gutenberg books. The manual remains useful for anyone converting plain text into polished ebooks.
1839-other-things-being-equal:
A humming-bird dips to a palm below an open window on a hazy California morning. The novel that follows is a romance of mixed marriage and divided loyalty. What follows, set among San Francisco Jews and Gentiles, is a tale of mixed marriage and divided loyalty. It takes its title from the condition that never quite holds.

A man shorn of his two loves through the same medium that robbed him of his birthright turns to vengeance. The novel follows the cost of that turn. Wolf writes with sympathy for both sides of her divided world. The book is notable as an early American novel to treat Jewish life from within, without apology or caricature.
18673-astrophel-and-other-poems-taken-fr:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Astrophel and Other Poems appears here from volume six of his collected poetical works, published at London by Heinemann in 1917, first printed by Chatto in 1904. The title poem, dedicated to William Morris, follows reading Sidney's Arcadia in an old manor garden. Other poems include A Nympholept, Grace Darling, Loch Torridon, and odes to England and Eton.

Later pieces add sonnets on Robert Browning's death, a threnody, the Ballad of Dead Men's Bay, and memorial verses for William Bell Scott. Swinburne's music runs rich and rolling throughout, with classical and English themes side by side. The book gives a full late sample of his verse.
1929-the-school-for-scandal:
R. B. Sheridan's School for Scandal, a comedy, remains the classic English comedy of manners, built around the Surface brothers: Joseph, the hypocrite, and Charles, the spendthrift with a heart. The scandal school itself is a circle of gossips — Lady Sneerwell, Crabtree, and Sir Benjamin Backbite — who invent reputations for fun.

In one scene, Lady Teazle swears her color is natural, having seen it come and go. Crabtree answers that it goes at night and comes again in the morning, and the exchange shows Sheridan's wit at its sharpest. The play's plot turns on a screen, a portrait, and a test of character. It has held the stage for over two centuries because its jokes about gossip never date.
19445-omnilingual:
H. Beam Piper wrote this science fiction tale of Mars, first printed in a science fiction magazine in the late nineteen fifties. Martha Dane, a linguist with an Earth dig team, studies the ruins of a dead Martian city under a copper sky. The team finds tools, machines, and writings no living mind can read.

The puzzle turns on a bold idea: science itself can serve as a shared tongue, since the laws of matter do not change from world to world. By matching Martian signs to known facts of nature, Dane cracks the code. The story is a tribute to patient scholarship, set on a cold and dusty Mars.
19587-the-christmas-kalends-of-provence-:
Thomas A. Janvier wrote this book of Provencal festivals, published in New York and London in the early nineteen hundreds with pictures. The title piece covers the Christmas kalends of Provence, from planting Saint Barbara's grain to toasts to the count's health.

Two more pieces follow: a feast day on the Rhone, part of a pilgrimage of southern exiles in Paris, and the Comedie Francaise at Orange. Janvier, a member of the Felibrige society, writes with affection for the songs, rites, and summer heat of the south of France. The feast table runs from sweet Mouscat wine and fizzy clairette to old Châteauneuf-du-Pape as its climax.
19723-the-cliff-ruins-of-canyon-de-chell:
Cosmos Mindeleff wrote this report on the cliff ruins of Canyon de Chelly, Arizona, printed in the Smithsonian's annual report for the mid eighteen nineties. It surveys dwellings built into canyon walls, room by room, with notes on masonry, plaster, and doorways.

One ruin shows large flat slabs set in dry mud mortar below, and finer selected stone above, finished with thin plaster and a small tapering door. Mindeleff's report remains a base record of Ancestral Pueblo building in a great southwestern canyon. A tower room coated inside with whitewash counts as a singular feature the surveyor finds hard to explain.
19745-something-of-men-i-have-known-with:
Adlai E. Stevenson served as Vice President under Grover Cleveland. Something of Men I Have Known gathers his recollections of public life. The contents promise chapters like Cleveland As I Knew Him. Others include A Camp-Meeting Orator and The Sage of the Bar. A piece called The Gentleman from Mississippi recalls Senate figures. The tone is that of an insider telling stories after dinner.

Political memoirs of this kind trade in portraits, not policy. Stevenson had practiced law and politics in Illinois for decades. He knew the men who ran the post-Civil War republic. His sketches preserve their talk, humor, and habits. Historians mine such books for color. Readers get a front-row seat at a vanished Washington.
19961-aboriginal-remains-in-verde-valley:
Cosmos Mindeleff surveyed aboriginal remains in Arizona's Verde Valley. His report appeared in the Bureau of Ethnology's Thirteenth Annual Report. Written history of the region extends back only a few years, he notes. Since the aboriginal inhabitants abandoned it, Apache and Walapai roamed there unhindered. Cliff houses and pueblos stood empty above the river. Mindeleff mapped and described them for science.

The Verde Valley holds some of the Southwest's richest ruins. Mindeleff, brother of Victor, worked the same federal survey tradition. His plans recorded sites before looting thinned them. Montezuma Castle country is his terrain here. The report joins description to careful measurement. It remains a baseline for Verde Valley archaeology.
20120-the-priest-the-woman-and-the-confe:
Father Chiniquy wrote The Priest, the Woman, and the Confessional, a fierce attack on Catholic confession. Chiniquy had been a Catholic priest before he left that church. He then spent years preaching and writing against its teachings. Scripture fills his pages, quoted to back each charge he makes.

One passage cites Ezekiel on sins that fill a land with violence. Chiniquy reads such texts as proof against the confessional itself. The book stirred strong feeling on both sides when it appeared. It remains a stark record of religious conflict in the nineteenth century.
20209-history-of-steam-on-the-erie-canal:
History of Steam on the Erie Canal traces steam power on New York's great waterway. From 1858 to 1862, a first series of steamers proved the idea. Their success sparked wide enthusiasm for steam transport on the canal. That fall, the governor and Canal Board toured by chartered steam-tug.

Public receptions and speeches greeted them at cities along the route. Steam promised faster, cheaper freight than horse-drawn canal boats could give. Yet locks, size, and cost all limited steam's canal future in fact. Readers get a close record of a key shift in American transport.
20307-kate-s-ordeal:
Emma Leslie wrote Kate's Ordeal, a tale for girls of school and sudden change. Kate races to catch her friends before they reach the school gates. She fans herself with her handkerchief and brings great news breathlessly. She is going to London, she tells them with a triumphant glance.

That glance is aimed at Esther Odell, who called her proud and stuck-up. London, to a country schoolgirl, means wonder, risk, and a test of character. Leslie wrote many tales where faith steadies girls in new trials. Young readers get excitement with a clear moral thread running through.
20924-ely-cathedral:
Cardinal de Luxemburg's tomb, built into the north wall, marks one stop in Ely Cathedral. The retro-choir holds Dr. Mill, a Hebrew scholar from Cambridge, who died in 1853. Faint wall paintings with no known tale mark the east wall's close.

Guidebooks in the Bell's Cathedrals set walk readers stone by stone through great churches. Ely's vast nave, lady chapel, and lantern tower star in this volume. Dates, tombs, and carved work unfold in calm, exact order. The book serves walkers in the church and armchair readers alike, keeping Ely's long past in one handy, trusted guide.
20959-mexico-its-ancient-and-modern-civi:
Thanks for photos crowd the front of Mexico, a survey of its ancient and modern civilisation. The Mexican Financial Agency, rail firms, and banks all aided the plates. C. Reginald Enock built his book with help from men on the ground.

Aztec ruins, mines, farms, railways, and politics fill Enock's wide account. He treats Mexico's past glory and its modern push for growth as one tale. British readers then weighed Mexico for trade and travel in its pages. The book stands as a full, dated portrait of the country on the eve of its great revolution.
21097-tom-finch-s-monkey-and-how-he-dine:
John C. Hutcheson gathers five short late Victorian yarns in this volume, opening with a monkey dressed as an officer aboard ship. The pet is presented to a visiting admiral, who invites all the officers to dinner and asks especially for the quiet one. The tale plays the joke out at sea off Callao.

Other pieces explain icebergs and follow a yachting cruise among the Greek islands. There the party saves a Greek's life and meets bandits. A third reports the sea serpent sighted by HMS Daedalus in 1848. A curious cricket match closes the set. Sea humour ties the five together.
21900-the-principles-of-breeding-or-glim:
Better farm animals through science is S. L. Goodale's aim in The Principles of Breeding, published at Boston in 1861. Goodale, secretary of the Maine Board of Agriculture, says farmers lacked a handy book of the principles behind improvement. His subtitle promises glimpses at the physical laws of reproduction in domestic animals. A transcriber's note warns modern readers that neat cattle are cattle of the bovine kind, not tidy dressers.

Goodale writes for working breeders, not scholars, and keeps the book compact. Heredity, selection, and crossing are handled in plain terms for the farm. The volume shows American agriculture reaching for science just before the Civil War. Its ideas, some since refined away, shaped the breeding sheds of its day.
22035-dramatized-rhythm-plays-mother-goo:
John N. Richards published Dramatized Rhythm Plays in 1922 for teachers of young children. The book turns Mother Goose rhymes and old singing games into small plays acted in rhythm. Little Jack Horner, Humpty Dumpty, and Sing a Song of Sixpence all appear. So do See Saw Marjory Daw and Dickory Dickory Dock.

Louise Westwood, who directed music in the Newark public schools, helped with the musical side. Words and tunes came, with permission, from J. Elliott's nursery rhyme settings. The aim was exercise, music, and play in one lesson. Such rhythm work was a proud feature of progressive classrooms in the 1920s.
22040-prairie-farmer-vol-56-no-3-january:
The Prairie Farmer had served farm families from Chicago since 1841. This weekly issue, volume 56 number 3, is dated January 19, 1884. Its motto covers the farm, the orchard, and the fireside. Two dollars a year bought news, advice, and letters from working farmers across the Midwest.

One writer tells how he raised his corn yield past ninety bushels an acre by small experiments. Other pages carry market reports, household hints, and questions answered in print. Such weeklies were the internet of their day for country readers. A single surviving issue shows what prairie families worried about, planted, and hoped for in midwinter 1884.
2285-ridgway-of-montana-a-story-of-to-da:
William MacLeod Raine's western hero Ridgway comes to Montana as a modern man in a raw land, facing cattle barons, gunmen, and a woman whose trust he must earn. Ridgway of Montana mixes range warfare with romance, as its hero uses brains as well as a gun to survive. The title's boast about its hero signals Raine's confident, pulpy style.

The novel moves fast through stampedes, ambushes, and courtroom showdowns. Raine knew the West's stories from the inside and wrote dozens of such tales. Fans of classic westerns will find this one energetic and unpretentious.
22897-the-ideal:
Two talkers argue about time in The Ideal, a dialogue in an old-fashioned vein. The Friar looks up and echoes his companion. Time is, indeed, he says. Uttering the word time, the Friar argues, must mean asserting something beyond its bare existence. That existence itself he treats as beyond doubt, since without time nothing could be at all.

From that playful knot the talk ranges over what an ideal is and whether it can exist outside minds. The piece belongs to a tradition of philosophical dialogue written for general readers, more fencing match than lecture. Its pleasure lies in watching an abstract word get chased around a room. Readers who enjoy talk-driven pieces will find a curious, mannered performance preserved here.
23157-other-people-s-business-the-romant:
Harriet Lummis Smith inspects a chair in Other People's Business, the romantic career of the practical Miss Dale, published in 1916. Persis has just rescued her furniture, tactfully, from a heavy guest. Her appraising glance at the vacated chair confirms the damage. Front rung sprung, exactly as expected, and Etta West ought to know better.

Persis Dale's practicality is her fortune and her comedy. She runs a boarding world of other people's business while her own romance assembles itself under her nose. Smith keeps the observation at chair-rung level, where character actually shows. The novel offers small-town American comedy of the sunniest kind, with a heroine whose competence the plot must teach her to set down, briefly, for love.
23344-the-magic-fishbone-a-holiday-roman:
Charles Dickens framed this holiday tale as the work of Miss Alice Rainbird, aged seven, and gave it the full warmth of a fairy story. A king and a queen rule a house full of children who keep outgrowing their clothes, while funds run short and tempers run high.

Help comes in the shape of a magic fishbone, which grants wishes to the child who holds it. Dickens follows the wishes as they tumble out, one after another, with comic mishaps and kind turns along the way. Pictures by S. Beatrice Pearse add to the fun. The tale suits reading aloud, with its child's logic, its royal fuss, and its belief that a small wish, well used, can set a house right.
23497-through-forest-and-stream-the-ques:
George Manville Fenn wrote this South American adventure, a sequel of sorts to Nat the Naturalist. It appears on no list of his books and seems rare enough to lack a firm publication date or a British Library record. Published in one cover with The New Forest Spy, it reads aloud in about three hours.

An expedition pushes through forest and stream in search of the quetzal, a beautiful bird with a long tail and bright colours, aiming to shoot, skin, and mount specimens. Jungle travel, river work, and naturalist lore fill the pages, with Fenn's usual brisk incident. Readers who love Victorian natural history adventure will enjoy the quest, while noting its period view of collecting, which prized a mounted bird above a living one.
2438-daphne-an-autumn-pastoral:
Margaret Sherwood's Daphne: An Autumn Pastoral is a romance of the Italian countryside, where an American woman and an Italian shepherd find love among olive groves and ruins. The novella takes its mood from the season: golden light, ripe harvests, and a sense of time passing. Sherwood writes the landscape with a poet's care.

The story's charm lies in its atmosphere rather than its plot, and its gentle romance suits quiet reading. Readers who love Italy in fiction will enjoy its warmth. It is a small, lovely book. Sherwood taught at Wellesley and wrote several Italian romances.
24715-the-western-world-picturesque-sket:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote this long, picturesque survey of American plants, animals, and peoples, seen from a late nineteenth-century view. It is not a novel, but a book to read through, covering quadrupeds, birds, plants, trees, and the indigenous races, in an interesting and readable style.

Almost two hundred engravings, many excellent, by a variety of artists illustrate the text. Kingston warns that the book cannot serve as a full guide to American natural history, but it can give a reader a general picture. Nature lovers will enjoy its breadth, its pictures, and its Victorian enthusiasm.
25341-the-28th-a-record-of-war-service-i:
Colonel H. B. Collett's 28th, volume one, records the Australian Imperial Force battalion's war service from 1915 to 1919 in Egypt, Gallipoli, Lemnos, and Sinai. Collett, the battalion's first commanding officer, writes with a foreword by the Archbishop of Perth.

Entries follow companies in and out of the line, shells that killed Western Australians, and Sir Ian Hamilton's visit to the Apex. Hamilton's diary, quoted in the text, calls the Australians fine fellows in tangled country where Turks and Australians puzzled over each other's lines. The volume is a unit history written close to events.
26038-drawings-and-pharmacy-in-al-zahraw:
Sami Hamarneh studies drawings and pharmacy in al-Zahrawi's tenth century surgical treatise, paper twenty two in the Smithsonian's Museum of History and Technology bulletin of 1961. Al-Zahrawi, known in the West as Abulcasis, wrote al-Tasrif, an encyclopedia of thirty treatises and probably the earliest independent Arabic work in Spain to cover all medical knowledge of its time. Hamarneh treats only the last treatise, on surgery.

Its many drawings of surgical tools, meant to teach apprentices, join formulas, drug preparations, and lucid notes on operations. One wound powder mixes frankincense and dragon's blood, two parts each, with three parts lime, pounded, sieved, and laid on the wound. Al-Zahrawi tied arteries by ligature, a pioneer practice, and set out four ways to suture intestines. The paper is a clear window on medieval surgery.
26152-characteristics-of-women-moral-poe:
Mrs. Jameson's Characteristics of Women, here in an 1889 Boston and New York printing from the last London edition, studies Shakespeare's heroines as moral types. Its introduction frames the book as a talk between Alda and Medon, who debate whether women deserve praise or blame. From there, chapters group the heroines by cast of mind.

Characters of intellect include Portia, Isabella, Beatrice, and Rosalind. Passion and imagination bring Juliet, Helena, Perdita, Viola, Ophelia, and Miranda. Affection gives Hermione, Desdemona, Imogen, and Cordelia, while historical chapters treat Cleopatra, Volumnia, Constance, and Lady Macbeth. The book argues that Shakespeare drew women with a depth and truth few writers matched.
26158-seed-dispersal:
W. J. Beal, professor of botany and forestry at Michigan Agricultural College, wrote this 1898 book to help young botanists and teachers. Its preface says most claims rest on his own watching in the field, not on books alone. Drawings by B. O. Longyear show the structures he describes.

Chapters move from animals that carry seeds, to plants that spread by roots, stems, and runners. Water transport, wind-borne fruits, and seeds that float or cling all get their turn. A willow-herb fruit, for one, holds seeds out on silky hairs so the wind can lift them. The book makes plant travel feel like a lively chase, and it invites readers to watch it happen outdoors.
26184-simple-sabotage-field-manual:
The Office of Strategic Services issued this field manual, number 3 in its series, at Washington on January 17, 1944. It defines simple sabotage as small acts an ordinary citizen can carry out with everyday materials, without special tools or ties to an organized group. Its aim is to slow an enemy's work while keeping danger, detection, and reprisal to a minimum.

Chapters cover the effects such acts can have, how to stir a saboteur to act, and how to pick tools, targets, and timing. Specific suggestions follow for workshops, offices, transport, and stores. Once marked for careful control, the manual now reads as a plain record of wartime doctrine, and as a window onto how the OSS thought about resistance behind enemy lines.
26278-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
The Christian Foundation, a scientific and religious journal, opens its first volume in January 1880 with an essay called The Conflict. It argues that ancient minds built Thebes, the Vedas, the Parthenon, and the Apollo Belvedere, and it denies that modern science holds all wisdom. Greek thinkers, it says, aired ideas of species change six centuries before Christ, while Buddhists and Brahmins taught systems of materialism long ago.

Later pages turn to the grave, asking what message, if any, reaches humanity from beyond it. The journal defends faith against modern materialist schools, praising Plato and Cicero over boastful sciolists. It reads as a Victorian effort to hold science and religion together, with ancient learning called as witness for both.
26726-pascal:
Principal Tulloch published this life of Blaise Pascal with William Blackwood and Sons at Edinburgh and London in 1878, reprinted in 1882. Tulloch calls Pascal one of the few names most classical in modern literature, at once famous in literature, science, and religion. Gone at thirty-nine, that fatal age for genius, Pascal had already won his distinction as a geometer and discoverer of physical science.

His Provincial Letters and Pensées spread his fame far and wide, admired by Encyclopedist and Romanticist, Catholic and Protestant alike, from Voltaire and Sainte-Beuve to Bossuet and Neander. Chapters cover Pascal's family and youth, his scientific discoveries, Pascal in the world, Port Royal and his later years, the Provincial Letters, and the Pensées. Tulloch notes that Pascal's sister Jacqueline, severe and holy, shaped his spiritual anxieties and his withdrawal from worldly engagements.
26747-reminiscences-of-two-years-with-th:
J. M. Addeman, late captain of the Fourteenth Rhode Island Heavy Artillery, Colored, published these reminiscences at Providence with N. Bangs Williams and Company in 1880. They form number seven, second series, of Personal Narratives of Events in the War of the Rebellion, papers read before the Rhode Island Soldiers and Sailors Historical Society.

By summer 1863, eager white enlistment had dried up, and a draft was impending. Governor Smith won permission to raise a company, then a battalion, then a full twelve-company regiment of colored men for heavy artillery duty. Addeman, at first doubtful, accepted a second lieutenancy and organized companies at Camp Smith before commanding Company H. The regiment wintered on Dutch Island, sailed on the transport Daniel Webster in January 1864, and later relieved the Forty-Second Ohio amid guerilla bands and hostile spectators.
27385-the-conspirators-or-the-chevalier-:
Alexandre Dumas wrote this historical romance of conspiracy, published in volume six of Collier's nine-volume edition of his works in New York in 1893. It was copiously illustrated with pen and ink and wood engravings. The translator is unknown, and the text keeps the original's varied spellings of names.

Chapters follow Captain Roquefinette, the Chevalier d'Harmental, a masked ball, the arsenal, and the Prince de Cellamare. They go on to Alberoni, a garret, an agreement, the Denis family, Jean Buvat, Bathilde, and first love, building toward the conspiracy itself. Dumas tells a Regency intrigue of plots, lovers, and daring with his usual speed. It is a lively entry point to his romantic histories.
27649-church-work-among-the-negroes-in-t:
Delivered in Chicago in 1907, this sermon by Robert Strange, Bishop of East Carolina, addresses the Episcopal Church's work among Black Southerners. It was preached on the fifth Sunday in Lent at Grace Episcopal Church as the second Hale Memorial Sermon, under the Western Theological Seminary.

The sermon opens with extracts from the will of Charles Reuben Hale, whose bequest funded its preaching and printing. Strange then sets out the church's duty to sustain congregations, clergy, and schools for Black communities in the South, framing that work as a lasting obligation rather than a passing effort.
27778-outlines-of-dairy-bacteriology-8th:
H. L. Russell, dean of the College of Agriculture at the University of Wisconsin, wrote this concise manual for students in dairying, revised into its eighth edition in 1907. It explains dairy bacteriology, the science of microbes in milk and its products.

Russell argues that future progress in dairying depends on bacteriological research, replacing guesswork with knowledge of causes. The manual covers the principles students needed as dairy schools adopted laboratory methods, and it shows a practical science coming of age. Russell quotes the German dairy scientist Fleischmann on abolishing uncertainty in dairy manufacture.
27832-zenith-television-receiver-operati:
Zenith Radio Corporation issued this operating manual for its black-and-white television receivers, headed The Royalty of Radio and Television. The booklet also carries the customer's warranty registration card and serial number, with a warning to dealers not to remove it.

The warranty covers parts, transistors, and tubes, with picture tubes covered for one year and other parts for ninety days from purchase. As a document, the manual captures early television ownership: a new appliance, a careful warranty, and a company teaching customers how to run a set. Zenith disclaims labor and transport costs for repaired parts, and limits its duty for failures beyond its control.
28066-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
The Christian Foundation for February 1880, volume one, number two, is a journal of science and religion. Its lead essay argues that the Bible shaped civil and religious liberty, defining civil liberty as freedom bounded by the rights of others. Other articles treat liberty of conscience, ancient cosmogonies, and the writings of India and China.

Further pieces weigh Darwinism, ask whether God can author falsehood, and test the claims of atheism and Ingersoll. The writers defend a Christian view of law, morals, and nature against new scientific ideas. The number offers a clear sample of American religious argument in 1880.
28075-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
The Christian Foundation for March 1880, volume one, number three, continues the journal of science and religion. Its lead essays trace the Bible's influence on moral and social institutions, arguing that pagan thought lacked a settled standard of right and wrong. Other pieces treat law, cause, and agent, and the claims of materialism about person and personality.

Further articles ask whether the race rose from barbarism, view the Flood from science and Scripture, and trace Mosaic law in Greece, Rome, and English common law. The tone is confident and combative. The number shows American Christians answering Darwin and unbelief in their own journal.
28126-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
The Christian Foundation for April 1880, volume one, number four, continues the journal of science and religion. Its lead lesson asks whether a counterfeit can exist without a genuine, arguing that myths point back to real truths, and that Bible stories cannot be mere myths of myths. Other pieces treat design in nature and Draper's conflict of religion and science.

Further articles ask if atheists err, whether humans are merely animals, and what Christians owe to ancient law and prophets. A report on the National Liberal League's funeral services adds a sharp, topical note. The number shows the journal's combative defence of faith against new unbelief.
28297-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
The Christian Foundation for May 1880, volume one, number five, continues the journal of science and religion. Its lead essay treats the old covenant, the Sabbath, the law, and the commonwealth of Israel in Christ, defining testament and covenant from Greenfield's lexicon. The term, it notes, occurs thirty-three times in the New Testament, in senses of will, promise, and law.

Other pieces attack infidelity, link Paine to French and American revolutions, ask whether to unchain the tiger, and test Ingersoll as philosopher. A life of Elder E. Goodwin closes the number. The journal's tone is combative and confident, defending faith against unbelief.
28570-astronomy-of-to-day-a-popular-intr:
Cecil G. Dolmage's Astronomy of To-Day, in its third edition of 1910, promises a popular introduction in non-technical language, with a colour frontispiece and forty-five illustrations. Dolmage, a fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society, writes for readers with no scientific training.

Chapters move from the ancient view and the modern view through the solar system, celestial mechanism, distances, and measurement. They go on to eclipses, famous eclipses of the sun and moon, and the growth of observation. Later chapters cover spectrum analysis, the sun, the planets, comets, meteors, the stars, and the stellar universe, closing with the beginning and end of things.
28601-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
The June 1880 number of The Christian Foundation, Or, Scientific and Religious Journal, volume 1, number 6, opens with the work of the Holy Spirit. Its first essay asks what that work is, and what its relations and uses are in creation, providence, and redemption. The writer argues against an immediate, direct operation on sinners' hearts as the common account of conversion.

Other pieces weigh the evidence for the resurrection of Christ, broad-gauge religion, papal authority in the bygone, and the religion of the future. A bill of indictments against Protestants, a summary of truth, and a piece on Ethan Allen the infidel and his daughter complete the number. Readers get a window on American religious debate in 1880.
28615-the-flaw-in-the-crystal:
May Sinclair's The Flaw in the Crystal, published by E. P. Dutton and Company of New York in 1912, opens on a Friday. Friday is the day Rodney Lanyon always comes, if he comes at all, since the week-end alone lets him slip away unremarked. His wife Bella, a mass of furious and malignant nerves, has worn his own nerves thin across ten years.

Agatha Verrall's house is his refuge and place of peace, with a room ready at the village inn or nearby farm. Agatha holds a secret gift: she can make him come, without his knowledge, across separation, and she guards herself against using it. She fears what the power might come to mean. Readers get a psychological novel of love, will, and restraint.
28668-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
Volume one, number seven of The Christian Foundation, a scientific and religious journal, is dated July 1880. Its opening essay, The Fountain of Happiness, argues that knowledge and enjoyment of God are the source of all created good. It pictures a person cut off from God as a ship's crew lost at sea or a child without a father.

The issue speaks in the earnest devotional voice of late nineteenth-century American Protestant writing, mixing sermon-like reflection with appeals to scripture and poetry. Readers interested in the period's religious press will find here a plain example of how such journals taught faith as both feeling and reason. The number stands alone as a single monthly installment of a longer run.
28669-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
August 1880 turns The Christian Foundation, volume 1, number 8, to the importance and nature of reformation from sin. Its text comes from 2 Timothy, chapter 3, verses 1 to 5, on perilous times when men love pleasure more than God. The writer questions infant vows taken by sponsors, who pledged to forsake the devil and the world's pomp.

Such sponsors, he argues, often serve profit, honor, and pleasure more devoutly than Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Baptism that saves, he says, is not the putting away of bodily filth but the answer of a good conscience toward God. Readers get a plain-spoken sermon against a mere form of godliness.
28672-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
Volume one, number nine of The Christian Foundation, a scientific and religious journal, is dated September 1880. Its leading essay argues for the divinity of the Christian religion from concessions by its enemies, quoting Voltaire on how even ancient writers acknowledged one supreme God. It then turns to old Hindu scripture, the Shastah, for a lofty statement of God's unity and power.

The issue shows the journal's method: gather testimony from hostile or distant sources and press it into service for Christian belief. Its language is formal and argumentative, typical of nineteenth-century religious periodicals aimed at educated believers. As a single monthly number, it offers a clear sample of how that press defended faith with history, quotation, and reason.
28673-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
Law and atonement fill the October 1880 number of The Christian Foundation, volume 1, number 10. Its opening text pairs two claims: the soul that sinneth, it shall die, and it shall not die. The writer rejects the scholastic idea of God's law as inexorable, absolute, and unmoved by reformation or petition.

He argues that punishing an innocent person cannot satisfy a law aimed at the soul that sinned, and faults the theory of vicarious punishment laid on Christ. Sabbatarian claims about the ten commandments fare no better, since the tables in Deuteronomy run from verse 6 to verse 21. Readers get a close doctrinal argument, verse by verse.
28677-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
November 1880 asks what character the Christian religion requires, in volume 1, number 11 of The Christian Foundation. The gospel's character, the writer says, is made of all that is lovely, formed on the highest model, not of anger, pride, egotism, or worldliness. Cold indifference, rank scepticism, and intellectual rashness have left the heart more miserable, not less.

Emmanuel, God with us, gathers wisdom, authority, and goodness into one person, the writer argues. The world's spirit is pride, selfishness, and self-will, while the Savior imparts humility, a modest estimate of self, and a sense of unworthiness. Before honor is humility, the piece insists. Readers get a devotional portrait of Christian character.
28678-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
Volume one, number twelve of The Christian Foundation, a scientific and religious journal, is dated December 1880. Its leading question asks whether the sinner is a moral agent in his own conversion, and it opens by noting how many rival theories of conversion exist. Mormons, Roman Catholics, and Protestants each point to their own experience, the essay says, yet their accounts contradict one another.

The writer warns against taking personal experience as an infallible rule, since people can be deceived and still act in good conscience, as Saul did before his change. The issue thus argues for testing religious claims by scripture and reason rather than feeling alone. It is a plain sample of the journal's doctrinal debating style, aimed at readers wrestling with questions of faith and free will.
28681-the-cook-s-oracle-and-housekeeper-:
William Kitchiner's The Cook's Oracle and Housekeeper's Manual, in Harper's stereotype edition printed by J. and J. Harper of New York in 1830, promises receipts tested by experiment. Kitchiner, a doctor, states every quantity by weight and measure, from results in his own kitchen. A medical gentleman adapted the last London edition for the American public.

Contents cover cookery receipts, directions for carving, and the art of broths, gravies, soups, sauces, and flavouring essences. Pastry, preserves, puddings, pickles, and a complete system of cookery for Catholic families follow. Readers get a practical kitchen authority, exact where older books guessed.
28710-the-christian-foundation-or-scient:
The 1880 volume index of The Christian Foundation, by Aaron Walker of Kokomo, Indiana, maps a journal devoted to civilization, literature, and Christianity. Walker's motto holds that science properly understood and the Bible rightly interpreted harmonize. Carlon and Hollenbeck of Indianapolis printed the volume, from Walker's office on Main and Mulberry Streets.

Index entries run from the conflict between Christianity and unbelief through the Bible as background and picture, the motive for adopting Darwinism, and blind force or intelligence. Man and the chimpanzee, spontaneous generation, stone implements, Huxley on the soul, and the flood viewed scientifically and biblically follow. Readers get a whole year of argument, indexed for reference.
28835-the-tale-of-brynild-and-king-valde:
George Borrow wrote these two ballads, printed for private circulation in London in 1913 from a Thomas J. Wise pamphlet. The Tale of Brynild tells how Sivard, on the swiftest colt beneath the sun, wins proud Brynild from the Hill of Glass, where her father set her beyond any knight's climb. He bears her away and gives her to Sir Nielus, setting off a quarrel over a bright gold ring.

The second ballad, King Valdemar and His Sister, pairs with it in the same small volume. Borrow's verse keeps the stark, singing manner of old northern ballads, with maids washing silken robes by a river and gold rings passing between lovers. Readers get a rare Borrow curiosity: a poet-translator trying his hand at the ballad form he loved.
28961-cuore-heart-an-italian-schoolboy-s:
Edmondo De Amicis wrote Cuore, Heart, an Italian schoolboy's journal, translated by Isabel F. Hapgood from the thirty-ninth Italian edition. The book is dedicated to boys of the elementary schools between nine and thirteen. It tells a school year as written by a third-class pupil in an Italian municipal school. The boy noted each day what he saw, felt, and thought, and his father later wrote the pages from those notes.

Four years later the boy, then in the lyceum, read the manuscript and added memories of persons and things. Chapters follow the first day of school, the master, an accident, the Calabrian boy, and a generous deed. Readers get a beloved Italian classic of school life, warm, moral, and humane, in a translation that kept it popular in English for decades.
29248-the-young-lady-s-equestrian-manual:
This manual, published in London in 1838 by Whitehead and Company, teaches ladies the art of riding on horseback. It first appeared inside the publishers' Young Lady's Book, a manual of elegant feminine recreations, and was then issued separately with additions and new illustrations. Royal patronage had favored the parent work.

Chapters move from an introduction and equestrian technical terms through the lady's horse, personal equipment, and accoutrements, to rules of the road and the mode of mounting. Later sections teach management of the reins, seat and balance, aids and defenses, and the paces: walk, trot, canter, and gallop. Readers get a complete Victorian riding guide for women, practical and polite, from an age when sidesaddle skill was a social art.
29345-mountain-interval:
Robert Frost published this book of poems in New York with Henry Holt and Company, copyrighted in 1916 and 1921. The dedication speaks of intervals. There is the South Branch interval under black mountains. There is the Upper interval at Plymouth, walked in spring beyond the covered bridge. The earliest interval of all belonged to the old farm brook.

Contents include The Road Not Taken, Christmas Trees, An Old Man's Winter Night, A Patch of Old Snow, and In the Home Stretch. Later poems include The Telephone, Hyla Brook, The Oven Bird, Birches, and Putting in the Seed. Readers get Frost at his early height, in poems of New England farms, woods, and choices, plain in speech and deep in implication.
29383-the-hawaiian-islands-their-resourc:
The Department of Foreign Affairs of Hawaii issued this illustrated survey of the Hawaiian Islands, printed by the Hawaiian Gazette Company. Its subject is the islands' resources: agricultural, commercial, and financial. Eight chapters lay out the land and its economy, followed by an official directory.

Illustrations show Sanford B. Dole, president of the Republic of Hawaii. They show the executive and judiciary buildings. They show the working islands: Ewa Mill and rice fields at Pauoa Valley and Pearl City. Pineapple and coffee plantations at Hamakua and Puna appear too. Waikiki Beach, the Kohala Railroad, Kamehameha School, and Oahu College also appear. Readers get a promotional yet detailed portrait of Hawaii's economy in the republic years.
29437-the-martian-cabal:
R. F. Starzl's complete novelette, printed in Astounding Stories in May 1932, follows Sime Hemingway of the I. F. P. as he strikes at a secret Martian plot. Twelve chapters run from a strange intruder and Scar Balta, through the price of monarchy, torture, and the wrath of Tolto. A fight in the fort, the flight of a princess, desert peril, and plot against counter-plot follow. The close pits giant against giant, at odds of one thousand to one.

Starzl writes at pulp speed, with thrones, torture, and desert chases driving a tale of conspiracy on Mars. Hemingway must prove himself a man of Earth in a court of aliens. Fans of early planetary romance will enjoy a brisk, colorful yarn of intrigue, valor, and escape.
29524-the-masked-bridal:
Mrs. Georgie Sheldon's Masked Bridal, copyrighted in 1894, 1895, and 1900 and printed by A. L. Burt Company of New York, opens with a prologue and two unexpected visitors. A staunch friend makes a vain appeal, a young lawyer meets two extraordinary surprises, and a mystery unfolds through a mother's last request and a heritage of shame. Later chapters turn on jealousy, parted ways, and a heroine's bold stand.

Sheldon, author of Edrie's Legacy, Max, and Faithful Shirley, writes the popular melodrama of her day: secrets, wrongs, and strong feeling, all resolved in the end. The masked bridal of the title hides a past that must come to light. Readers of Victorian sensational fiction will find a fast, emotional tale in the classic dime-novel vein.
29665-prairie-farmer-vol-56-no-4-january:
Volume fifty-six, number four of The Prairie Farmer is dated Chicago, Saturday, January 26, 1884. It served as a weekly journal for the farm, orchard, and fireside, established in 1841 at two dollars a year in advance. Its contents list agriculture, live stock, the dairy, and veterinary notes, with raising onions, an Illinois tile-makers' convention, and better management needed among the farm items.

Live stock pages treat herd books, sweepstake prizes, and raising young mules, while Wisconsin dairymen get a page of their own. A note on crops warns that weeds and poor care make harvests uncertain. Readers of farm history will find a full week of practical advice from the prairie's own paper.
29842-histology-of-the-blood-normal-and-:
P. Ehrlich and A. Lazarus wrote this histology of the blood, normal and pathological, edited and translated by W. Myers. G. Sims Woodhead, professor of pathology at Cambridge, wrote the preface. Cambridge University Press printed the book in 1900. Woodhead notes that in no branch of pathology has advance been so fitful as in blood changes in disease, though none promises so rich a return for the time spent.

Early chapters treat normal histology and classification, the places of origin of the white blood corpuscles, and the demonstration of cell granules. Leucocytosis and leukopenia follow, with the blood pictures of disease set beside the normal. Observations by Wharton Jones and others frame the work. The book is a classic of early hematology, dense, technical, and foundational for later blood science.
31087-a-rebel-war-clerk-s-diary-at-the-c:
J. B. Jones, clerk in the War Department of the Confederate States government and author of Wild Western Scenes, wrote this diary at the Confederate States capital, published in two volumes by J. B. Lippincott in Philadelphia in 1866. His preface says the diary was written with the knowledge of the President and the Secretary of War, whom he informed of it by note.

They did not deprecate criticism of their official conduct, since they allowed him to keep executing the functions of a very important position until the end of the government's career. Jones notes that he accepted the poor title of a clerkship after declining the Chargéship to Naples, tendered by Mr. Calhoun during President Polk's administration. The diary opens with his flight from the North and escape into Virginia, and the Union Convention passing the Ordinance of Secession. It is a first-hand Civil War diary.
31220-a-new-subspecies-of-bat-myotis-vel:
Terry A. Vaughan's 1954 paper names a new subspecies of cave bat, Myotis velifer brevis, from southeastern California and Arizona. The first California specimens had been taken in 1909 by C. L. Camp at Needles in San Bernardino County, with later records down the lower Colorado River Valley. The species was known west of the Rockies across southern Arizona and into New Mexico and Utah.

Comparisons made possible by recent Kansas museum collections from Mexico showed that the California and Arizona animals formed an unnamed subspecies of their own. Published as volume 7, number 8 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series, the paper is the formal record for this western bat.
31231-under-padlock-and-seal:
Harold Avery's children's mystery, published by Thomas Nelson in London, Edinburgh, Dublin, and New York, opens at night in the rambling old house called The Pines. Elsie, awake beside her sleeping elder sister Ida, hears a grindstone hissing below and creeps to the window to find the tool-house faintly lit. She wonders who sharpens anything at such an hour.

Twelve chapters follow a lost carving-knife, Uncle Roger's box, its opening, a naval disaster, more mystery, sad news, a fright, a fresh discovery, Elsie's confession, Uncle Roger's legacy, and the riddle solved. With an illustration of children peering into the wonderful box, the book is a tidy Edwardian mystery for young readers.
31282-mars-confidential:
Jack Lait and Lee Mortimer's Mars Confidential, printed in Amazing Stories in April and May 1953, applies the reporters' famous exposé manner to the Red Planet. The magazine's blurb promises the lowdown on Mars, from its canals, caves, satellites, and catacombs to the vice, violence, and Mafia said to be undoing it, told in vivid, jet-speed style.

The narrators boast that they turned New York inside out and Chicago upside down. Mars was their toughest task, since cab drivers spoke another language and bell-hops could not read their currency. Satirical and pulp-swift, the piece treats Mars as another seamy city to be X-rayed, beside which Earth looks white as the Moon.
31299-the-ultimate-criminal:
Archibald H. Grimké's 1915 annual address to the American Negro Academy, number seventeen in its Occasional Papers, asks who the ultimate criminal really is. Grimké protests a national habit: treating offenses, proven or merely alleged, by single Black men as proof condemning every Black person's moral character. He calls that judgment monstrously unjust and wicked.

He does not deny that Black men commit crimes, too many for their own good, but he asks who inquires into their origin. He traces in outline the hostile and unequal social, industrial, and political conditions of the last fifty years from which Black crime emerged. The address is a fierce early argument against collective blame.
31595-the-return-of-the-prodigal:
May Sinclair's novel The Return of the Prodigal was published by the Macmillan Company in 1914, with copyright the same year. It opens in conversation. One man tells a clergyman about another man who was given nine distinct starts in life, shipped off to capital waiting on the other side, and drank that capital away. The talk turns on sin, and on how many sins such a life amounts to.

Sinclair's novel follows the prodigal's return in two parts, and it asks what homecoming means when the welcome has been spent many times over. The opening talk sets the terms: fresh starts, squandered chances, and a family that must decide what forgiveness costs.
31608-the-lords-of-the-ghostland-a-histo:
Edgar Saltus's The Lords of the Ghostland, a history of the ideal, was published in New York by Mitchell Kennerley in 1907, the year given as MCMVII, with copyright by Saltus. Saltus, author of Historia Amoris and Mary Magdalen, traces the history of an idea: the ideal as it has appeared in religion, philosophy, and art, from ancient gods to modern dreamers. The book's epigraph, in French, speaks of wandering with fingers joined in the Alhambra of dream, a fitting motto for its subject.

Saltus writes with the jeweled prose of the decadent movement, treating ideas as lords ruling a ghostly kingdom. His history is impressionistic rather than systematic, preferring vivid portraits to argument. Readers of Saltus will find a characteristic work: erudite, beautiful, and willfully unorthodox, on the ideals that haunt human thought.
31886-pretty-michal:
Pretty Michal, a free translation by R. N. Bain of Maurus Jókai's romance A Szép Mikhál, was published in New York by Cassell in 1892. Its first chapter shows how sagely the Reverend Master Fröhlich brought up his motherless daughter, pretty Michal, and its second shows how an evil dragon brought all his sage devices to naught.

Later chapters follow robbers and dangers from which the righteous are wondrously delivered, and a stern father chastising a lost son and granting forgiveness to a repentant prodigal. They also follow the perils that befall women who do not obey their lords and masters. Readers get a Hungarian romance in Victorian dress, full of fairy-tale trials, family quarrels, and reconciliations.
32164-in-the-oregon-country-out-doors-in:
George Palmer Putnam's In the Oregon Country was published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in New York and London in 1915. It is an outdoor book on Oregon, Washington, and California, with legendary lore and glimpses of the modern West in the making. Putnam, author of The Southland of North America, adds an introduction by James Withycombe, governor of Oregon. The book has fifty-two illustrations, and is dedicated to the Emblem Club.

Its chapters run from Out West and The Valley of Content through The Land of Legends and The Land of Many Leagues. They continue to How the Railroads Came, The Home Makers, On Oregon Trails, and Uncle Sam's Forests. Readers get a 1915 portrait of the Pacific Northwest at the moment of change. Legend and trail lore stand beside railroads, home makers, and national forests, written by a traveller who loves the outdoors.
32367-outlines-of-dairy-bacteriology-10t:
H. L. Russell and E. G. Hastings present dairy bacteriology in a concise manual for students in dairying, in a tenth edition published in Madison, Wisconsin, in 1914. Russell, dean of agriculture at the University of Wisconsin, and Hastings, professor of agricultural bacteriology there, grew the book from lectures to practical students in the winter dairy course. By 1914, they note, no dairy student counted training complete without the basic principles of the subject.

The volume aims not at an exhaustive treatise but at an outline with enough detail to show how bacteria affect milk and other dairy products, even without laboratory practice. Where possible, students are urged to gain laboratory knowledge, but the general reader can still gain a survey of the field. The tenth edition adds recent developments in dairy science.
32373-the-golden-treasury-selected-from-:
Francis T. Palgrave's Golden Treasury, in a revised and enlarged edition published in London in 1902, selects the best songs and lyrical poems in the English language, arranged with notes. Palgrave, late professor of poetry at Oxford, dedicated the book to Alfred Tennyson, poet laureate. He had wished to dedicate a true national anthology of three centuries to Henry Hallam. Tennyson's encouragement, given while walking the wild scenery of Treryn Dinas, led Palgrave to begin the work.

The anthology gathers short lyric poems that reward reading aloud and memory, chosen for judgment, feeling, and craft. Its notes help readers place poems and poets without breaking the pleasure of the verse. The Golden Treasury remains a classic introduction to English lyric poetry for students and general readers alike.
32542-dave-dawson-on-guadalcanal:
R. Sidney Bowen's Dave Dawson on Guadalcanal follows Dave Dawson and Freddy Farmer through wartime flying and planning for attack. Aboard a Flying Fortress over the Indian Ocean, Dave jokes with Freddy, an English-born air ace, while the crew keeps watch for enemy aircraft on a long hop from India toward Australia.

Later chapters turn to the Guadalcanal and Tulagi attack, with orders, blind eyes, steel sharks, missing airmen, and flights that end in luck or loss. The war adventure entry keeps its action close to pilots, orders, and danger, where courage must hold when plans go wrong.
33012-carnival:
Compton Mackenzie's Carnival, published in New York in 1912, follows a girl born to the stage. The chapters run from the birth of Columbine through fairies at her christening, dawn shadows, and the ancient mischief of childhood, to ambition waking and looking in the glass. Later chapters take her through life, art, and love, Drury Lane and Covent Garden, the Orient Palace of Varieties, and growing old. They end with the ballet of Cupid, rain on the roof, and love's halcyon.

Mackenzie traces a dancer's life from pretty apples in Eden to the gift of opals and a fête galante, closing with an epilogue, an unfinished statue, and two letters. The novel is a portrait of the theater world and of a woman shaped by it. It remains a vivid, if dated, story of ambition, applause, and the price of a life lived in public.
33021-the-carlovingian-coins-or-the-daug:
Eugène Sue's Carlovingian Coins, or The Daughters of Charlemagne, is one volume in the vast series The Mysteries of the People. The series is a history of a proletarian family across the ages. The series runs from The Gold Sickle and The Brass Bell through The Iron Collar, The Silver Cross, and The Basque's Lark. It goes on to The Poniard's Hilt, The Branding Needle, and The Abbatial Crosier, before reaching this volume on Charlemagne's daughters. It continues on through iron arrows, skulls, shells, pincers, trevets, and knives.

Sue's design is bold: one family, traced through centuries of French history, carries the story of ordinary people against kings, priests, and lords. The Carlovingian volume places that family in the age of Charlemagne, when empire, church, and kinship shaped Europe. For readers interested in the popular historical novel, it is a striking example of fiction written as a people's history.
33201-the-complete-club-book-for-women-i:
Caroline French Benton's Complete Club Book for Women, a companion to her Woman's Club Work and Programs, gathers everything a women's club needed to organize and run its programs. It includes subjects, material, and references for study programs, together with a constitution and by-laws, rules of order, and instructions for making a year book. It adds suggestions for community work and a resume of what some clubs are doing. Benton's other books included Fairs and Fetes, Living on a Little, and Easy Meals.
