The volume belongs to the club movement that gave American women a public, organized life in the early twentieth century. Study clubs, civic work, and social reform met in parlors and halls. Benton writes as a guide, not a theorist, giving forms and programs a club could use at once. For historians of women's organizations, it remains a manual of how clubs actually worked.
34768-the-outlook-uncle-sam-s-place-and-:
Newton Macmillan read a paper on America's place in world affairs. The paper went to the Fortnightly Club of Oswego on May 2, 1899. The club then had it put in print that year. One year and a day had passed since Oswego sent men to war. That war with Spain frames his whole theme in the talk.

Young men of peace bore the flag off to fight, he recalls. The town did not grasp the scene's full weight at the time. Now the land holds new isles and new tasks past its shores. Macmillan asks what rank and role the land should take. His hearers were town men in a time of change. The talk stays grave and proud.
35152-algic-researches-comprising-inquir:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft wrote Algic Researches, inquiries into the mental traits of the North American Indians, here a first series of Indian tales and legends in two volumes. Harper and Brothers in New York issued the set in eighteen thirty nine. The hosted text is volume one. Schoolcraft gave the work to Lieutenant Colonel Henry Whiting of the United States Army. Whiting had backed the literary gifts of the Indian character in poetic fiction.

Few have studied the intellectual traits of these scattered branches of the human family without deep interest, Schoolcraft says. An age of many excitements pours topics and inventions on us, he notes. His collection of oral fictions comes from years among the tribes as agent and traveller. Tales and legends fill the volume, told in the Indian own manner. Readers get early, firsthand records of Ojibwe and kindred lore, with notes on custom and belief.
35175-algic-researches-comprising-inquir:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft gathered Indian tales and legends in Algic Researches, Volume Two. Harper and Brothers issued the set in New York in 1839. Schoolcraft had traveled to the sources of the Mississippi and to Itasca Lake. The tales aim to show the mind and fancy of North American Indians.

The Red Swan leads, telling of three brothers left alone by their parents' death. The eldest hunts to keep the boys alive in a lone forest home. More tales treat the Red Head, the Lost Daughter, strong Kwasind, and the Whitefish's source. Readers gain early records of oral tales set down in print.
35334-folk-lore-and-legends-oriental:
Folk-Lore and Legends: Oriental is a set of Eastern tales for readers. Gibbings published it in London in the year 1889. A prefatory note says the East is rich in folklore for collectors. The lorist's trouble is not to find material, but to choose the best. Conditions of life there favour the keeping of ancient legends in speech.

Practice in narration fits the Oriental to polish his stories well. Readers will note likenesses between these tales and Western folk fiction. Thought and incident match across the world, the note argues in warmth. That oneness of folk fiction speaks the brotherhood of man most eloquently. Gorgeous extravagance of imagination lights the Eastern tales throughout each page.
35503-the-girl-at-central:
Geraldine Bonner builds a murder tale around a telephone operator in a novel issued in New York in 1915. Molly Morganthau, the day operator at the exchange in Longwood, New Jersey, tells the story herself. She sets out the Hesketh mystery, which baffled police and public across the state.

Sylvia Hesketh, rich and without an enemy, took tea with her mother at Mapleshade at five o'clock. That same night she was found dead by a lonely road, one hundred and eighteen miles away. Molly, who supported herself from age sixteen and works the switchboard at the center of local talk, is placed to hear what others miss. Readers get a brisk mystery told in a working girl's plain voice.
35990-the-story-of-lewis-carroll-told-fo:
The Story of Lewis Carroll is a biography for young people by Isa Bowman, who calls herself on the title page the real Alice in Wonderland. Dutton published it in New York in 1900. Bowman had played Alice on the stage and knew Carroll as a friend. The book holds a diary, facsimile letters written to her and others, and sketches and photographs by Carroll himself.

The illustrations list shows the intimacy of the record. Carroll's room in Oxford and his house at Eastbourne appear. Bowman is shown as Alice, as the Duke of York, and with Bessie Hatton as the little princes in the tower. A facsimile of a charade fills three pages. A Chinaman, beggar children, and Saint George and the dragon stand among Carroll's photographs. No other life of Carroll was written by a child friend; hers preserves the shy don as his young visitors knew him.
36200-history-of-the-dewitt-guard-compan:
The DeWitt Guard published its own history at Ithaca, New York, in 1866: Company A of the 50th Regiment, National Guard of the State of New York. The preface gives the tally: total membership from the organization in December 1851 to 1866 was two hundred and two. Eighty-two served in the army or navy during the late rebellion, eighty-eight did not, twenty-nine are unknown either way, and nine died before the war. Members had contributed two thousand seven hundred and twenty dollars and fifty-six cents, the company being self-supporting.

The book prints every member's name, enlistment date, and trade, with a short personal history, before the collective story. It opens with Arch McNeil, the merchant elected second lieutenant at the first election, who organized the company and died in 1855. The company issued the volume to show as honorable a record as any similar organization could produce.
36373-h-p-blavatsky-a-great-betrayal:
Blavatsky: A Great Betrayal is a polemic by Alice Leighton Cleather, one of Blavatsky's pupils. Thacker, Spink and Company published it at Calcutta in 1922. It sold for a rupee, or fifty cents, or a shilling and sixpence. Cleather also wrote a life of Blavatsky as her life and work for humanity.

The title page motto calls for a clean life, an open mind, and a pure heart. Cleather charges that the Theosophical Society after Blavatsky's death betrayed her teaching. Her book attacks the leaders who, in her view, traded the founder's message for wonders and power. It is a document of the bitter splits inside theosophy.
36432-the-coming-of-coal:
The Coming of Coal is a social study by Robert Bruere of the Bureau of Industrial Research, published in New York by the Association Press in 1922. Bruere prepared it for the educational committee of the Federal Council of Churches' commission on the church and social service. A map of the coal fields of the world fronts the book.

Ten chapters trace coal's place in modern life. After the challenge of power and the drama of civilization, the book turns to coal in America. The awakening of the miners, the struggle for organization, and the rise of democracy follow. Rivals of coal and a technical revolution fill the late chapters. The study ends at a strait gate, asking what power will do to men's will. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
3652-history-of-the-mackenzies-with-gene:
Alexander Mackenzie writes a history of the Mackenzies, a great Highland clan, with genealogies of its principal families. The book traces the clan from its early chiefs through centuries of war, landholding, and loyalty in Ross-shire and beyond. Mackenzie, a historian of the Highlands, gathers charters, traditions, and family trees into one record.

Readers meet chiefs, cadet branches, and the septs that served them, with the feuds and marriages that shaped the north. The genealogies make the volume useful for descendants tracing Mackenzie lines. The book suits readers interested in Scottish clan history and in the Highlands before and after the Jacobite risings.
36710-the-black-opal:
Katharine Susannah Prichard's The Black Opal, published by William Heinemann in London in 1921, opens with a funeral crossing the plains below Fallen Star Ridge. A string of buggies moves slowly out of the New Town, and men walk two abreast behind. In the back of Newton's buggy lies a long box covered with wreaths and paper daisies. Little Sophie, in a black dress cut down for her, rides beside the driver, Michael Brady.

Nearly the whole township has turned out: miners from the Three Mile and the Punti rush, storekeepers, and riders from Warria. Prichard, who wrote The Pioneers, sets her story in this opal country of the Ridge, the Old Town, and the New Town. The child's clear eye over the procession is the reader's way into that world.
36896-benjamin-franklin-self-revealed-vo:
William Cabell Bruce wrote a life of Benjamin Franklin from Franklin's own words. His study fills two books, this being the first of them. The book came out in New York and London in 1917. First words lead, then Franklin's moral stand and scheme. His faith views take the next long part of book one.

Franklin as good doer and town man fills the third part. His home ties and kin take a long, full part in the list. His American friends and his British friends stand in two parts. His French friends close the first book's roll of names. False takes of Franklin's bent were rife till late, Bruce holds. His own pen is the cure, Bruce argues in his scheme.
36897-benjamin-franklin-self-revealed-vo:
William Cabell Bruce wrote Benjamin Franklin Self-Revealed, a study based mainly on Franklin's own writings. Putnam put out volume two at New York and London in 1917. The contents treat Franklin's personal traits, his life in business, and his work as a statesman. Later parts treat Franklin as a man of science and as a writer, with an index to close. The statesman part runs the longest, by far, in this half of the work.

Bruce opens with the crowd of friends Franklin drew at each stage of his long life. A robust, honorable character and fine mental gifts explain that draw, he holds. As a youth Franklin swam from near Chelsea to Blackfriars, half on and half under water.
36948-the-gamekeeper-at-home-sketches-of:
Richard Jefferies's The Gamekeeper at Home, sketches of natural history and rural life, was published by Smith, Elder of London in an edition dated 1878. Jefferies says in his preface that anyone who has roamed the fields or stayed at a country house has met the keeper. The man is so marked a figure in rural life, he holds, as almost to demand a record.

One keeper's house and habits form the core, but the facts, Jefferies insists, all come from his own watching. From the man the book moves to his ground: meadows, woods, and streams, and their furred and feathered folk. His foes come with the ground: vermin, poachers, and trespassers, against whom he wages a war that never ends.
3709-love-eternal:
H Rider Haggard builds this novel around two souls who meet as children and keep finding each other through a lifetime of partings. Isobel and Godfrey grow up side by side, sharing a garden and a chapel. Then years apart pull them in opposite ways, with India, France, and the church claiming Godfrey while marriage and duty claim Isobel. Haggard frames their bond as a love that outlasts single lives, with dreams, spirit rappings, and ghostly hands testing what the pair believe.

The later chapters turn earnest, as Godfrey takes orders and the lovers weigh faith against feeling. Readers who know Haggard for adventure tales will find a slower, more inward book here, though ghosts and foreign scenes still crowd the pages. It is a romance about constancy, and it asks whether love can hold its shape across time, distance, and death itself.
37228-index-to-university-of-kansas-publ:
Index to University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume one, is a reference volume. The Museum of Natural History at Lawrence, Kansas issued it in 1950. Raymond Hall heads the list of editors on the title page. The volume covers the museum's publications from 1946 to 1950. Its contents list each paper with author, pages, and date. The pocket gophers of Utah, by Durrant, lead the list. That paper runs to eighty two pages with a figure.

Hobart Smith wrote several of the early papers listed. They treat skinks, tadpoles, and garter snake hybrids from Kansas and Oklahoma. Records of reptiles and amphibians recur through the list. Soft shelled turtle variation is another listed study. The volume lets readers trace four years of museum research output. It is a finding aid for a university science series.
3735-the-inspector-general:
Nikolay Gogol wrote this five act comedy about a small Russian town that mistakes a penniless young traveler for a government inspector sent in secret from Saint Petersburg. The mayor and his officials, each with his own petty corruption to hide, rush to bribe and flatter the supposed great man, who accepts their money with cheerful ease. Dobchinsky's gossip, Anna's questions about the stranger's age, and the tour of charitable institutions all feed the panic.

The play is a national classic in Russia, where its name alone calls up a whole world of bribery and fear. Thomas Seltzer's translation keeps the talk brisk and the jokes pointed. Readers who like satire will enjoy watching a town condemn itself out of its own mouth, while the true inspector is still on the road.
37448-comet-s-burial:
Comet's Burial is a science fiction story by Raymond Z Gallun. Outside Tycho Station on the Moon, Jess Brinker shows Arne Copeland the odd footprints made in the dust by explorers from Mars, fifty million years ago. A man-made cover of clear plastic now keeps them from being trampled. Copeland growls that everyone has heard about such prints.

There is no air or weather on the Moon to rub them out, even in eternity. Copeland is nineteen, tough and wary, with a girl named Frances back in Iowa. Love had to wait, for he needed the Moon the way Peary once needed the North Pole. Earth needed it too, for minerals, for observatories, and as a jump-off point to the planets. The heading warns that a man may be a scoundrel and a confidence man, and still work toward a great dream.
37508-the-cochineal:
The Cochineal is a small church tract for the young on a small bug of that name. It was put out at New York by a church school guild. The tract is cast as a talk past a father and his son of ten years. The boy finds the bug crawl on a sheet of white in the study room.

The father sets the bug past two panes of glass and brings his glass of sight. To the bare eye the back is dull brown with spots. Past the glass it shows rank past rank of fine scales in white, black, and blue, set in more neat rows than tiles on a roof. Both cry out at the craft of God in so small and scorned a thing. The tract turns that sight to praise.
37538-southern-war-songs-camp-fire-patri:
Southern War Songs, collected and arranged by Fagan, gathers the camp-fire, patriotic, and sentimental songs of the South. Richardson printed the book in New York in 1890, from a copyright of 1889. Plates give the Southern Cross battle flag and the Stars and Bars.

The preface, dated at Havana, Alabama, in December 1889, makes the case plain. The songs, Fagan argues, are part of the history of the Lost Cause. A historian needs them to judge the temper of the Southern people. Song, as feeling in print, indexes the passion. No poetic merit is claimed for all of them, but each holds a fact or a principle. Some read harsh and vindictive, written when minds were aroused. Eight million people read and sang them, which alone warrants their keeping. Most came from Southern newspapers.
37887-mexico-aztec-spanish-and-republica:
Volume one of Brantz Mayer's Mexico, Aztec, Spanish and Republican was published at Hartford by Drake in 1852, entered for copyright in 1850. Mayer had been secretary of legation to Mexico. The book promises a historical, geographical, political, statistical, and social account of the country from the Spanish invasion to the present time. With it go a view of the ancient Aztec empire, a sketch of the late war, and notices of New Mexico and California.

Mayer inscribes the volumes to Henry Clay, from Baltimore in July 1850, in gratitude for kindness to men in the quieter walks of literature. His preface argues America's deep interest in Mexico. It was not commerce alone: while Spain's exclusive policy shut her colonies away, the ancient history of Peru and Mexico drew American students, eager to solve the enigma of a strange civilization.
37944-southern-spain-painted-by-trevor-h:
Southern Spain is a travel volume in words and pictures: painted by Trevor Haddon and described by Calvert. Black of London published it in 1908. Eight chapters tour Andalusia and the old kingdoms beyond it, from Cadiz round to Valencia.

Seville, the pearl of Andalusia, takes the longest chapter, and the plates return to it again and again. They show the Giralda, the cathedral inside and out, the gardens of the Alcazar, the Casa de Pilatos, and the market place. Cordova, Granada, Malaga and Murcia follow. The text opens at Cadiz, which Byron thought the prettiest of all the towns of Spain. Calvert would rather call her the most beautiful. She rises out of the sea, he writes, the boundless salt ocean that stretches from pole to pole. The Black colour books were armchair tours in watercolour.
38014-government-in-the-united-states-na:
James W Garner wrote Government in the United States, a school book on rule at all levels of the land. Garner taught the science of rule at the University of Illinois. The work held rights from 1911, with fresh rights through 1922. A view of the Capitol at Washington fronts the book.

The book starts close to home, with towns, townships, and counties. It then takes up towns and small places as ruled things in their own right. State rule comes next, with its law house, its chief, and its courts. Votes, polls, and the way men are put up for posts get a full part. The rise of the Union and its two houses close the first span. Garner notes that most folk live under at least four kinds of rule at once.
38488-folk-tales-of-bengal:
Folk Tales of Bengal, by Lal Behari Day, was published in London in 1912. Warwick Goble drew thirty two pictures in colour. Day had written Bengal Peasant Life before. He gives the book to Richard Carnac Temple, who first urged him to gather the tales. Twenty two tales fill the contents. Life's Secret opens the set, and Phakir Chand follows. The Indigent Brahman and the Story of the Rakshasas come next.

Later tales tell of Prince Sobur, the origin of opium, and a ghost Brahman. A match making jackal and a boy with the moon on his forehead appear. The Field of Bones and The Bald Wife close the book. Plates show queens, demons, and princes in bright scenes. The set preserves tales told by mouth in Bengal homes.
38579-recitations-for-the-social-circle-:
Recitations for the Social Circle is a book of pieces for reading aloud, gathered by James Clarence Harvey. The Christian Herald published it in New York in 1896. Its subtitle says the pieces are selected and original. An introductory note gives advice on the art of recitation. In reading and recitation the tendency is to overdo, it warns. Quiet reserve force in the voice will reach the heart, it holds. Gesture and ranting fail where that force succeeds, it says. Be bold, be not too bold, should be the reciter's watchwords.

Self possession is the keynote to success, the note adds. Never gesticulate if you can help it, it advises. Only he who feels the force of what he utters can hope to sway others. The book supplies parlour pieces for that art. Its selections served home and church entertainments of the day.
39133-the-dramas-of-victor-hugo-mary-tud:
The Dramas of Victor Hugo in volume twenty one gathers three plays in English dress. Mary Tudor, Marion de Lorme, and Esmeralda make up the contents of the volume. Peter Fenelon Collier published the set at New York with many wood engravings. A front plate called The Rendezvous opens the book in style.

Mary Tudor comes first, set in London in 1553 under Queen Mary. Its cast lists Jane, Gilbert, Fabiano Fabiani, and Simon Renard among the chief roles. The first day of that play opens on a deserted strand by the Thames. Hugo wrote for the French stage of the romantic era in these works. English readers met his queens, lovers, and plotters in this illustrated library edition.
39152-a-biographical-sketch-of-some-of-t:
Robert Williams wrote A Biographical Sketch of Some of the Most Eminent Individuals Which the Principality of Wales Has Produced Since the Reformation, issued at London in 1836. Williams had writ a history of Conway Castle. The Cymmvodorion gave him a silver medal in 1831. An added part holds lives of Doctor William Owen Pughe and Richard Llwyd.

A note to the public states the aim in one line. Williams wants English readers to see that Wales has bred much talent. More names could be added, but living men are left out, he says. Names sent in will go in a future edition. William Baxter leads the lives. Baxter was born in Wales in 1650 and went to Harrow at eighteen with no tongue but Welsh. He soon won English and beat all bar, the tale says.
39267-the-power-of-the-popes-an-historic:
Daunou, a French scholar, wrote a history of the temporal power of the popes, here in English in two volumes bound as one in 1838. The work grew out of the clash between Pope Pius the Seventh and the French Emperor over the return of the Catholic faith in France. Its aim was to show the vast claims of the Roman court to the world.

Chapters trace papal power century by century, from its first rise through the contests of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Later parts weigh papal policy in the 1500s and tries in the 1600s, with a summing up and a time table at the end. The translator gave the work to a cleric friend who had urged the task.
39349-wyndham-s-pal:
Wyndham's Pal, by Harold Bindloss, copyright 1919, was published in England as Wyndham's Partner and issued in New York by the Burt company. Three parts carry the lure of ambition, Wyndham claiming his reward, and reparation. The tale opens in a yacht race, the fifty mile Commodore's Cup.

Wyndham sails the Red Rose through haze, watching for a rival's canvas and meaning to leave nothing to chance. From racing the book moves to lagoons, revolts, and lost explorers in warmer seas. Bindloss wrote sea and frontier tales of duty and grit, and his hero's ambition here costs more than a cup.
39494-poetry-of-the-supernatural:
Poetry of the Supernatural is a reading list compiled by Earle Walbridge and printed by the New York Public Library in 1919. It was reprinted from the Branch Library News of May that year. Walbridge's list is not a bibliography or a reading list in the usual sense, the introduction says. It is an intelligent selection of cases where poets, major and minor, turned to ghostly themes.

The introduction quotes Lafcadio Hearn's Interpretations of Literature at length. Hearn warns that it would be a mistake to think stories of the supernatural have had their day in fine literature. Wherever fine literature is made, he says, the supernatural element stays very much alive. Scarcely any great European author, old or new, has not distinguished himself in treating it. English literature, he believes, has no exception at all. The list then points readers to the poems themselves.
39509-the-black-man-the-father-of-civili:
James Morris Webb, an evangelist of the Church of God, wrote The Black Man, the Father of Civilization, proven by biblical history. A portrait of Webb fronts the book, with pictures of Lincoln, Frederick Douglas, and Booker Washington named as three of the greatest men in American history. The preface sets out Webb's objects plainly. First, he writes, he loves his race in spite of prejudice against her.

Webb presents the book as a defense against writers and lecturers, ancient and modern, who misread his race and took from her the deeds and honors justly hers. He joins a body of race defenders, hoping to count as one little finger of it, in the spirit of the widow's mite. His proofs rest wholly on the Bible, he says, which he calls the real and only authority on ancient history. Readers should keep a Bible at hand and test his references.
39783-canzoni-ripostes-whereto-are-appen:
Ezra Pound gathered his early verse in Canzoni and Ripostes, printed by Elkin Mathews in London in 1913. Bound with it are the complete poems of Hulme, a short, prized body of work. Pound gave the Canzoni to Olivia and Dorothy Shakespear.

Song forms of old Provence rule the book: canzon, ballata, madrigal, and sestina. Pound sings to Guido Cavalcanti, the great Italian of the sweet new style. He turns Propertius, Du Bellay, Leopardi, and Heine into English. Paracelsus speaks in one piece, Egypt in another. Victorian eclogues and sharp short epigrams vary the feast. Young readers of 1913 met a poet drunk on old song and bent on making it new.
39973-how-to-produce-amateur-plays-a-pra:
How to Produce Amateur Plays, a practical manual by Barrett Clark, appears here in a new and revised edition from Little, Brown in 1923, copyrighted in 1917 and 1922. Clark orders the work as a producer meets it: choosing the play, organization, choosing the cast, and three chapters of rehearsing. The stage, lighting, and scenery and costumes follow, with selective lists of amateur plays behind.

Chapter one warns that the first question, what play, is too often answered in a haphazard way, and that publishers' lists bewilder. Every play considered, Clark insists, should be read by the director or the whole club after the conditions are weighed. The first condition is the size of the cast: a cast of ten cannot play Shakespeare. The second, harder one, is the cast's ability. Appendices treat copyright and royalty, and make up.
4031-the-london-prodigal:
A comedy of London life follows a young prodigal whose waste and swagger trouble his family and tempt his friends. In the sampled scenes, a Devonshire lad boasts of his purse and person, while Lucy whispers aside that it is Arthur she loves, not the rich suitor pressed on her.

Lovers, fathers, and sharp-tongued servants trade verse and prose in the manner of the early English stage. The play mixes farce, romance, and moral warning, as the prodigal learns the cost of his pleasures. Readers who enjoy Shakespeare-era comedy will find a lively, old-fashioned piece about money, love, and coming home.
40348-the-crime-and-the-criminal:
Richard Marsh, author of The Beetle, wrote The Crime and the Criminal for the New Amsterdam Book Company at New York in 1899. Harold Piffard drew two full-page plates. A front plate shows a woman fallen backwards through an open carriage door. Four books divide the tale: the crime, the club, the woman, and the criminal.

Book one opens with an open door, a man with a silk handkerchief, and a name on a scrap of paper. Blackmail and a confession follow. Book two enters a club where lots are drawn and a little game is played. Book three follows Louise O'Donel and a man named Townsend with a double. A trial fills the late chapters, with Mrs Carruth removing her veil in court.
4046-the-garden-of-survival:
Algernon Blackwood's novel opens with a letter about talent raised beyond its own height by a guiding hand. The writer and his sibling, puzzled and happy, ask whose unerring hand shaped the result, and promise another curious item in the tale to come.

The garden of the title stands for a place where art, love, and a strange power meet. Blackwood writes in his usual mode of quiet wonder, where the unseen presses close on daily life. Readers who enjoy supernatural fiction without shock will find a gentle, thoughtful story of growth and mystery.
40875-adventurings-in-the-psychical:
Addington Bruce published Adventurings in the Psychical in Boston in 1914. Bruce had already written Historic Ghosts and Ghost Hunters and The Riddle of Personality, and here he gathers his case for taking strange mental powers in earnest. The first chapter opens with a Frenchwoman who said she did not believe in ghosts but was terribly afraid of them.

Bruce argues that most people share her split mind, and that fear of ghosts is needless once the facts are faced. Nine chapters cover ghosts and their meaning, telepathy, clairvoyance and crystal-gazing, automatic speaking and writing, and poltergeists and mediums. Later chapters turn inward, to the subconscious, to split personality and disease, and to a singular case he calls BCA. He warns that rats, jokes, and drink make plenty of false ghosts, so each claim needs sharp scrutiny. Readers get a calm brief for psychical research from its early years.
40909-anthony-trent-master-criminal:
Anthony Trent, Master Criminal, by Wyndham Martyn, was published in New York in 1918. Martyn gives the book to his friends Lily and Ernest Carr. Thirty one chapters trace Trent's career in crime. The first chapter is called The First Step. It opens in a police room, where Austin the butler gives his evidence. Inspector McWalsh grills him again, hoping to startle a slip. Austin stays cool, neat, and bored, to the inspector's dislike.

Later heads promise diamonds, rubies, an emerald, and a Sinn Fein plot. A countess, a baron, and a German spy merchant enter the game. Trent saves a piano in one chapter and takes a holiday in another. Murder and a thief set to catch a thief close the run.
41005-the-great-court-scandal:
William Le Queux wrote this novel of a court scandal. He was London-born and left a post on the Globe in 1893 to write fiction full time. The book opens with a preface life of the author, then a tight spot in Paris.

The prologue finds Harry Kinder and a friend trapped at the Grand with a hotel bill of two thousand seven hundred francs to pay. Their hope, a woman called the Ladybird, sends them from London a postal order for twenty-seven shillings and sixpence, all she has. The talk hints at a plot that touches a woman's honour and a secret worth forcing help for. Le Queux built his name on tales of spies and courts, and this opening shows his pace: debt, blackmail pressure, and a hinted scandal in the first pages.
41008-the-great-american-canals-volume-2:
Archer Butler Hulbert wrote a history of the Erie Canal in his highway series. Volume two came out in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1904. It is book fourteen in the Historic Highways of America set. Maps and plates go with the text. A front plate shows the old canal basin at Buffalo.

Parts trace the Mohawk River and its first works. Early backers, Clinton's plea, and the build take the mid part. Hulbert then shows how the canal changed towns on its line. A last part deals with canal funds and growth works. Maps from an 1834 French book aid the eye. Road and trade fans get a full tale.
411-the-king-s-jackal:
Richard Harding Davis sets this Tangier tale among exiled kings, guards, and plotters on a hotel terrace. The King of Messina, in hiding under a false name, waits for a boat from Gibraltar while his majordomo scans the sea. Soldiers of the Sultan guard his door, and a colonel frets over each delay.

Davis writes bright, swift scenes of Mediterranean color, court intrigue, and comic suspense. The jackal of the title serves a greater beast, a schemer who feeds on royal hopes. The book reads as a light adventure of old Morocco, full of sun, sea, and whispered plots.
41150-italy-with-sketches-of-spain-and-p:
Italy, with sketches of Spain and Portugal, is a book of travel letters by the author of Vathek. Richard Bentley printed the third edition at London in 1835, in two volumes. The writer's advertisement says the letters slept for many years. Admired authors had gleaned stray thoughts from them, which emboldened him to publish.

Most letters were written in the bloom of youth. That was when the old order still stood, with Venice's dungeons and the Inquisition in the Peninsula. Yet the pages are not crowded with such records. They dwell on landscape and the effects of nature, which no revolution can alter. The travels show three countries as a young man of taste saw them.
41250-mearing-stones-leaves-from-my-note:
Joseph Campbell wrote Mearing Stones, leaves from his note-book on tramp in Donegal, printed at Dublin in 1911. Campbell, who also wrote as Seosamh Mac Cathmhaoil, drew its sixteen pencil pictures himself. A plate shows the wall of Slieve League.

Short notes fill the book, most of them a page or two. Titles run from The Wander-Lust and A Rainbow to Turf-Cutting, A Ballad-Singer, and A Party of Tinkers. Places recur: Glen-Columcille, Carrick, the Rosses, Errigal, and Lochros. Campbell watches peasants, funerals, fiddlers, and the sea, in a prose that stays close to the road and the weather.
41405-the-accumulation-of-capital:
Rosa Luxemburg wrote The Accumulation of Capital, translated from the German by Agnes Schwarzschild and published by Yale University Press in 1951. Joan Robinson wrote the introduction. Luxemburg, the Polish-German socialist thinker, first published the work in German long before this English edition. It is her major book of economic theory.

The first section states the problem of reproduction: how a capitalist economy replaces and enlarges its stock. Luxemburg works through Quesnay and Adam Smith, then takes up Marx's schemes of simple and enlarged reproduction. She criticizes Smith's analysis and tests Marx's attempt to resolve the difficulty. A second section gives the history of the debate, from Sismondi and Malthus against Say and Ricardo onward. The book asks where the buyers for a growing surplus can come from.
41432-the-tale-of-a-field-hospital:
The Tale of a Field Hospital is an account of war surgery by Sir Frederick Treves, surgeon. Treves served as consulting surgeon with the troops in South Africa in the Boer War. A new edition of nineteen twelve reprints a book first published in nineteen hundred. Thirty short chapters tell the story of one hospital through the campaign.

The hospital was Number Four Stationary Field Hospital, moving with headquarters camp. Its officers were majors of the Royal Army Medical Corps and a lieutenant. The unit grew after the move to Spearman's Farm with eight civil surgeons. After the battle of Spion Kop it held about eight hundred wounded men. Chapters treat the hospital dog, the nurses, the trains, and the burials. A tale tells how a surgeon won the Victoria Cross in the field.
41606-comets-and-meteors-their-phenomena:
Daniel Kirkwood, professor of mathematics at Indiana University, wrote Comets and Meteors, published in Philadelphia in 1873. Kirkwood had already written Meteoric Astronomy. His preface dates the science from the great star shower of 1833. After that display, scholars found that similar showers had returned at nearly regular intervals for centuries. The meteor clouds, it turned out, circle the sun in paths that cross the earth's orbit.

Kirkwood then explains the newer theory. Meteor clouds are the scattered fragments of broken-up comets. The shower of November 1872, falling from the debris of Biela's comet, confirmed the idea in striking fashion. The book surveys cometary astronomy, stones that fall from the sky, and the most brilliant star showers of all ages. Kirkwood wrote for an interested public, turning fresh discoveries into a clear account of where shooting stars come from and what they are.
41767-the-hero-of-panama-a-tale-of-the-g:
Captain F S Brereton wrote this boys' tale of the Panama Canal, printed by Blackie and Son of London, Glasgow, and Bombay in 1912. William Rainey drew the plates, one showing Jim rescuing Phineas Barton. Brereton had written Under the Chinese Dragon and Tom Stapleton, the Boy Scout. A post of responsibility opens the tale, and the road to New York follows.

Jim Partington shows his mettle in chapter three. The ways of the steam digger, a shot in the dark, and the lair of the robbers fill the middle. Jim becomes a mechanic, runs the gauntlet, and barely escapes. An American undertaking and hustle as the order of the day close the list shown. The tale opens on a roasting Caribbean day of oily sea and fierce sun.
42007-sir-christopher-wren-his-family-an:
Lucy Phillimore wrote this life of Sir Christopher Wren, the great builder of St Paul's and of London after the Fire. Her title promises his family and his times as well, with first-hand letters in the text. Wren's name stands first among English masters of building.

Phillimore works from house papers and letters that had not seen print before her. Such stores let a life be told in the man's own words and his kin's. The old house motto heads one section, in the book's close way with its stuff. Readers get the dome builder as son, father, and courtier, set in the rich, torn years of Charles the Second and his heirs.
4206-the-letters-of-franklin-k-lane-pers:
The letters of Franklin K. Lane, personal and political, show a public man writing to friends, officials, and reformers. One letter praises self-respecting Gaelic-speaking Scots from the northern islands, crofters driven from Highland homes to make place for sheep and fine estates.

Another calls the express job the biggest one yet, claiming a real service to country and express companies alike, which must improve service and rates or face government action. The collection suits readers who like American progressivism in its own voice, frank and practical. Crofters, express rates, and government power share his letters.
42077-the-boy-scouts-at-the-panama-canal:
Lieutenant Howard Payson wrote a Boy Scout tale printed in New York in 1913. Payson had written of the Eagle Patrol, the range, and the army airship. Boy Scouts to the rescue opens the tale. Angry farmer Hiram Applegate has just finished breakfast and feels exceptionally good humored, in spite of news in his morning paper of the day before.

An angry farmer, a mission, modern advertising, and baseball fill the home chapters. Fire makes a scout hero and tests the Eagles, skill against muscle. Then the boys sail off for the isthmus. Something about the canal, old Panama, the Gatun Dam, and a dynamite volcano teach and thrill in turn. A run for your lives chapter tops the adventure.
42238-the-articles-of-faith-a-series-of-:
James Talmage, one of the Twelve Apostles of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, wrote lectures on the principal doctrines of the church. They were prepared by appointment and published by the church. The greater number of the lectures were given before the theology class of the Church University, the preface notes. After the class sessions closed, the lectures were continued before other church bodies.

Article by article, the faith is set out with scripture proofs at every step. A heated idol with burning arms, Beelzebub the prince of devils, and Malachi the last of the prophets appear in the dense notes. Mexican tradition concerning the Savior is treated in one section. The book reached an eleventh edition in English. Saints and students get the church's own teaching in ordered form here.
42277-the-grizzly-our-greatest-wild-anim:
Enos Mills honours a great beast in The Grizzly, Our Greatest Wild Animal, printed at Boston and New York in 1919. Houghton Mifflin made the book. A flashlight photograph of a wild grizzly fronts the volume. The catalog year 1902 is that photograph's copyright, not the book's.

Fifteen chapters treat the bear in the wild. Grizzly sagacity leads, then cubs and mother, and his exclusive territory. Making a bear living and the long winter sleep follow. Trailing without a gun and matching wits with the grizzly show Mills's own field craft. When the grizzly plays and where curiosity wins keep the fond tone. A description, history, and classing close the text, with a last chapter on whether the grizzly will be wiped out.
42603-san-francisco-and-the-nicaragua-ca:
An American diplomat at San Jose, Costa Rica, wrote this letter on the Nicaragua Canal, dated September 15, 1900. He addresses Senator George Perkins of California at San Francisco, by name and office. Perkins had asked him to answer a mutual friend's argument against building the canal.

The friend admits, the writer notes, that his argument does not run on broad lines. The canal is a national undertaking, the reply insists, not to be judged from a narrow standpoint. Yet the writer promises to meet the objections first on that narrow ground, then on a broader and more patriotic basis in brief compass.
42719-a-treatise-on-wood-engraving-histo:
A Treatise on Wood Engraving, Historical and Practical, pairs John Jackson's account of the craft with a historical portion by W A Chatto. Over three hundred pictures engraved on wood fill the book. This is the second edition, with a new chapter on the artists of the present day by Henry G Bohn. Bohn published it at London in 1861, with one hundred forty five added engravings.

The publisher's notice says the first edition had grown scarce and dear. He bought the copyright and the wood blocks from the author's son to reprint it. Two prefaces from the first edition are kept, since they show a split between the joint makers of the book. Jackson speaks as a working engraver; Chatto traces the art from its roots.
43395-the-washer-of-the-ford-legendary-m:
The Washer of the Ford is a set of Celt tales by Fiona Macleod, out in eighteen ninety six. A New York house, Stone and Kimball, brought the book out that year. Its full name adds old time morals and wild tales to the ford name. Saint Bride of the Isles and a fisher of men stand in the scheme. Last supper and dark name one tales give the set a grave cast.

Three feats of Hy split into bird feast, fish sabbath, and moon child parts. Seer tales split in four parts of sight, dark hour, and white heat. Sword song, Culdee flight, and queen laugh parts close the scheme. A front talk calls the tales dreams yet grave chose with care. Magic lives where man wins power over the world, that talk claims.
43417-a-conchological-manual:
Sowerby made this conchological manual, a guide to shells, in a second edition much enlarged and printed in London in 1842. Upwards of six hundred and sixty figures illustrate it. His preface says the book is strictly about shells, and built for two kinds of users at once.

Beginners who want a first grasp of the subject get plain help, with hard words explained and pointed to the figures. Students who wish to go further get a book of reference, with the main facts arranged in alphabetical order. Tables set out the systems of Lamarck and of De Blainville side by side, so readers can follow either scheme or compare them as they work.
43680-the-russian-turmoil-memoirs-milita:
General A I Denikin, once chief of staff at Russian headquarters, recounts the revolution in The Russian Turmoil, his memoirs published at London by Hutchinson and Company. Twenty-seven illustrations, diagrams and maps accompany the text. Early chapters treat the foundations of the old power, the army and the Emperor, before turning to the revolution in Petrograd and its effect on the imperial family.

A long central sequence follows the Provisional Government, the Soviet, the democratisation of the army, soldiers' committees and commissars, and the July advance. The contents show Denikin moving from the Stavka through dismissal from the high command toward the book's later struggles.
43841-scientific-studies-or-practical-in:
Henry Dircks gave the two popular lectures printed as Scientific Studies, issued in London in 1879. The subtitle sets practical work against chimerical pursuits. Dircks had written a life of the Marquis of Worcester before this book. Diagrams run through the lectures to aid the hearer.

The first lecture gives the life of Edward Somerset, second Marquis of Worcester, named here as inventor of the steam engine. The second treats the chimeras of science in a list. Astrology, alchemy, squaring the circle, and the perpetual motion machine stand in that list. In his opening Dircks says a popular lecture needs breadth with brevity, like a view from a high tower.
43844-claret-and-olives-from-the-garonne:
Angus Reach wrote these travel notes from the Garonne to the Rhone, published in London in 1852. Reach had earlier written 'The Story of a Buccaneer' among his works. He inscribes the pages affectionately to Charles Mackay, his earliest and kindest literary friend, in the dedication.

Chapter one rides the diligence through French country places to Bordeaux in the summary. Old Bordeaux, a landlord and a suburban vintaging with its dinner fill that chapter. Claret against port, the claret soil and vine, and the treading of the vintage follow, in notes social, picturesque and legendary, as the subtitle promises.
43852-the-revolutions-of-portugal:
The Abbot de Vertot wrote this tale of the turns of Portugal in French. It was done into English from the last French shape of the work, and printed at London in 1721. A verse from Addison's Cato stands on the title page. It speaks of the dread span twixt the birth of plots and their last, fateful close. The book is sent forth to Philip, Duke of Wharton.

The leaf of gift is full of the forms of that day. The man who bears the book owns that he lays his head open to blame, in that he sets so rough a work in front of so fine a judge. But the grace of the Duke, which he knows well, gives him heart. He notes that this famed author has come out in English more than once in the past.
43909-sometub-s-cruise-on-the-c-o-canal:
Cowan wrote Sometub's Cruise on the C and O Canal, the narrative of a motorboat vacation in the heart of Maryland, in 1916. The edition was limited to 200 copies. Cowan calls his boat the newest type on America's oldest improved waterway.

The Sometub was built in a kitchen from a knockdown frame sent by a Michigan boatbuilder. Doubters in the kitchen gallery called it some tub, and the name stuck. The cruise ran 347 miles, from Oakmont on the Allegheny to Rock Creek in the shadow of the national capitol. Six waterways were crossed, with a portage of 150 miles between them.
44056-zoological-illustrations-second-se:
Zoological Illustrations, second series volume one, holds figures and descriptions of new, rare, or interesting animals. William Swainson made it, and it was printed at London in 1829. Baldwin and Cradock published it. The animals are chosen chiefly from birds, insects, and shells, and arranged by their apparent likenesses.

Swainson dedicates the volume to Mrs. Corrie of Woodville, near Birmingham. He hopes the work may serve the great end every naturalist should keep in view. That end is the unfolding of the harmonies of Creation and the finding of the natural system. His preface calls the drawings a pleasant rest from severer studies, and the descriptions a popular form of longer research.
44057-zoological-illustrations-second-se:
William Swainson wrote Zoological Illustrations, Second Series, Volume Two, issued at London in 1831 and 1832. The full title calls it original figures and descriptions of new, rare, or interesting animals. Birds, insects, and shells hold the chief place. Forms are arranged by their apparent affinities, the title says.

Swainson held posts with the forces and seats in learned groups in London and Paris. The volume is given to Louis Philippe, King of the French. As a private gentleman exiled from his land he won respect, the note says. As king he holds the love of the wise and good, it holds. He is praised as a true patron of science in public and private. Plates and letterpress treat each animal in turn for naturalists and collectors.
44058-zoological-illustrations-second-se:
William Swainson wrote Zoological Illustrations, original figures and descriptions of new, rare, or interesting animals. Baldwin and Cradock published this third volume of the second series at London in 1832-33. The animals are chosen chiefly from ornithology, entomology, and conchology. They are arranged according to their natural affinities. Swainson dedicated the volume to William John Burchell, the African traveller. Burchell's discoveries had benefited every branch of natural science, he writes.

The preface closes the second series with thanks for its reception at home and abroad. The scientific interest of the subjects and the care of the plates grew as the work neared its end, Swainson says. The whole series now divides into three equal parts. The birds, the insects, and the shells form distinct volumes under one general title.
44415-robber-and-hero-the-story-of-the-r:
Robber and Hero tells the story of the 1876 raid on the First National Bank of Northfield, Minnesota. George Huntington wrote it, and a Northfield company published it in 1895. The James-Younger band made the raid. Huntington's preface argues that the tale is worth retelling. A great crime, he writes, was the occasion of great heroism. Bank clerk Heywood refused to open the safe and was murdered.

The citizens fought the robbers bravely in the street. A two weeks pursuit ended in the bandits' capture. These events were once familiar to the whole nation, the preface notes. A new generation, though, has grown up without knowing them. Huntington aims at a correct account, not a sensational one. Revolting details are omitted, and the facts left to teach their own lesson.
44552-science-and-the-criminal:
Ainsworth Mitchell wrote this study of science in crime work, published by Little, Brown in Boston in 1911. A frontispiece shows the trial of Caroline Rudd as an early case in point. Chapter one takes up evidence itself, and warns against scientific partisanship in the witness box.

Chapter two contrasts the eighteenth, nineteenth and twentieth centuries in catching criminals. Margaret Catchpole, Tawell and Crippen appear as cases, with bloodhounds, police dogs and press portraits in the mix. Personal identification comes next, with an experiment by McKeever on how fallible eye-witnesses can be. Fingerprints, blood and documents belong to the same new toolkit.
45350-anno-domini-2071-translated-from-t:
Anno Domini 2071 is a Dutch tale of the future, translated into English by Bikkers and published in London in 1871. The author hid behind the name Doctor Dioscorides. The translator's preface quotes Artemus Ward's rule: never prophesy unless you know for certain. It then defends a safer kind of foretelling, by inference from things that have come to pass.

The little book had run through three editions in the Netherlands, and a German scholar thought it worth translating. It pictures the world two hundred years ahead, as a Dutch writer of 1871 could reason it out. Such forecasts show the hopes and fears of the steam age looking forward.
45463-letters-of-john-calvin-volume-ii-c:
Letters of John Calvin, volume two, compiles the reformer's correspondence from the original manuscripts. Jules Bonnet edited the letters with historical notes. The Presbyterian Board of Publication issued the translation at Philadelphia in 1858. The letters are rendered from the Latin and French.

The volume opens in 1545 with letters to Viret and to Monsieur and Madame de Falais. Calvin writes on his own unpopularity, on constancy amid poverty and persecution, and on the plague in Geneva. Letters to Farel follow, full of church business at Neuchatel and Geneva. One letter marks the rupture between Calvin and Servetus. Another carries a terrible threat against him and word of a Libertin leader's imprisonment. The collection shows Calvin governing a movement by post, week by week.
45471-the-history-of-the-revolutions-of-:
The Abbé Vertot's history of Portugal's revolutions, continued toward the present by Louis de Boisgelin, was printed in London in eighteen nine. It carries notes, a table of the kings of Portugal, and a description of Brazil. Vertot had long been read in English schools. The preface praises the work as both entertaining and instructive for young readers.

The narrative keeps to events that rose into revolutions. It runs from the war the Portuguese call the Acclamation to the battle of Vimeiro in the Peninsular War. It sketches the characters of kings and of the ministers who defended or attacked royal power. Boisgelin declines to treat the newest crisis, the French invasion that had lately threatened the throne itself, calling it too recent and too well known. The book is an early nineteenth century classroom history.
45581-the-story-of-the-nations-portugal:
Portugal, in the Story of the Nations series, was written by Morse Stephens of Balliol College, Oxford, and printed by Putnam in New York in 1903, from a copyright of 1891. Stephens also wrote a history of the French Revolution. A frontispiece portrays Prince Henry of Portugal from a miniature of 1448.

The preface announces a different plan from most volumes in the series. Instead of an episodic history treating only the most striking events, Stephens attempts a consecutive history, since no English book gives the reader the needed groundwork. He is sharp on Dunham, whose history in Lardner's Cabinet Cyclopaedia still feeds the standard reference books. Dunham's old blunders, he charges, include identifying Portugal with Lusitania, accepting the fictitious Cortes of Lamego of 1143, and calling the victory of Ourique prodigious. The series aims to tell each nation's story in graphic narrative.
45738-dissertations-on-the-english-langu:
Noah Webster printed his Dissertations on the English Language at Boston for himself in 1789. Isaiah Thomas and Company did the press work for the young author. He inscribes the book to Benjamin Franklin with long, warm praise in the dedication. Franklin's plain style and useful labor, Webster says, shame fine spun theory at once.

Notes, historical and critical, fill out the dissertations on tongue and usage in full. An appendix adds an essay on a reformed mode of spelling for English. Franklin's arguments on that subject stand inside the appendix by name in the title. Webster praises facts over speculation in science, rule, and farm alike throughout. A young republic gets a language book with a patriot's stamp.
45859-patran-as-or-spanish-stories-legen:
Patrañas titles a collection of Spanish stories, legendary and traditional. The author of Traditions of Tirol gathered them, and Griffith and Farran published the book at London in 1870, with illustrations by Corbould. An introduction tells how a disappointment in Spain turned to profit, and how the author went rambling into out-of-the-way villages. The stories sort themselves into kinds: popular, legendary, chivalric, Moorish, and from beyond the sea.

The popular tales give Carlo Magno and the Giant, El Conde Sol, Simple Johnny and the spell-bound princesses, and the blood-stain of the Alcázar of Seville. The legendary set brings King Vamba and Count Fernan Gonzalez. Raguel, the Jewess of Toledo, stands among the chivalric pieces. Moorish remnants and a Hernan Cortes story close the book. Doña Josefa Ramirez has adventures in Seville. The collection serves Spain to children as a land of story.
46555-the-library-assistant-s-manual:
Theodore Koch, librarian of the University of Michigan, wrote this provisional manual for the State Board of Library Commissioners. Lansing issued it in 1913 for a state teachers' meeting at Ann Arbor. Ten chapters map a small library from birth to daily use. The library movement, organization, and book buying come first in order.

Classification, cataloging, reference work, and circulation fill the middle chapters at length. Binding and care of books, work with children, and the high school library close the course. Koch opens with Franklin's Library Company of Philadelphia, founded in 1731 as a seed. A Rush bequest of $1,500,000 shows how far library fortunes had grown since then. New librarians get a whole trade in brief, clear lessons.
46921-the-thoughts-of-blaise-pascal:
The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal, rendered from the text of Auguste Molinier by Kegan Paul, was printed in London in 1885. A likeness of Pascal fronts the book. Contents open with a preface and a general introduction, giving Pascal's own statement of faith. The thoughts then fall under two great heads. The first is the misery of man without God. The second is the happiness of man with God.

Under the first head stand man's disproportion, diversion, and the greatness and littleness of man. The false powers of the fancy, justice and custom, and the weakness and unrest of man follow. Under the second stand the need of seeking truth, the philosophers, and thoughts on Mahomet and on China. The Jewish people, the proofs of the Christian religion, and the mystery of Jesus fill its later pages. Thoughts on style close the set, with notes and an index.
47438-elementary-instruction-in-the-art-:
Elementary Instruction in the Art of Illuminating and Missal Painting teaches a lost craft. Patient hands once lit church books with gold and bright paints. Victorian craftsmen took up the old art with new zeal and pride. The front pages list gift books in that same rich style.

Longman, Green and Company sold the finest of those bright books. Henry Noel Humphreys lit the Parables and Miracles of the Lord. His Maxims and Precepts and Book of Ruth glow in like kind. Each bound book cost twenty one shillings in carved covers. Laurent de Lara’s Shaksperian Proverbs sold plain or part coloured. Crosses and texts for home walls fill the trade list here. Gold leaf, bright grounds, and fine scroll work rule the craft. Such lists show how wide the taste for lit pages had grown.
47450-the-gamekeeper-at-home-sketches-of:
A country book fills this volume: The Gamekeeper at Home, sketches of natural history and rural life, printed at London in 1880 with pictures by Whymper. An old ballad of Guy of Gisborne supplies its motto, of merry walking in the fair forest to hear the small birds sing. The preface is signed only with initials.

Those who roam fields and lanes, the preface says, or have stayed in a country house, can hardly have missed the keeper of the woods and covers, often something of a character. Contents follow him in order. The man himself, his house and tools, come first, then his family and caste, and life in the fields. His dominions of woods, meadows, and water follow, with his subjects, from dogs and rabbits to small deer. His enemies close the book: beasts of prey, trespassers, poachers, and black sheep.
47611-the-relief-of-chitral:
Captain G J Younghusband and Colonel Sir Francis Younghusband wrote The Relief of Chitral. The first edition came out in October 1895 and was reprinted at once. A cheap shilling edition followed in 1910.

Chitral is a hill state on the north-west frontier of India. A British force there was besieged, and a relief march drew all eyes. A frontispiece shows Colonel Kelly and his officers, who led the rescue. Maps and plates help the reader follow the hard mountain roads. The book is a first hand tale of a famed frontier campaign. Both writers knew the ground and the men. The shilling issue put the tale in many more hands.
47646-joan-of-the-journal:
Helen Olds wrote this tale of Joan and a newspaper office job. Grosset and Dunlap printed Joan of the Journal in New York. Beebe drew the plates, a charity play story among them. Contents open with Joan gets a job at the Journal.

The Journal family, Joan on the beat, and no more mistakes follow. An annual outing, Tim second warning, and Chub ideas fill early. A mysterious disappearance and Tommy by the day come in middle. Joan rarely minded dishes, watching the Journal office from her sink. Tim makes the front page and a comma tail close the contents of the tale.
47726-the-rivers-of-great-britain-descri:
Cassell and Company gather river essays into a picture book issued at London in 1889. This volume treats the rivers of the east coast. An etching of Bolton Abbey on the Wharfe fronts it, signed artist's proofs at a guinea each.

Francis Watt takes the Highland Dee first. His contents run from the Larig and Garchary burns to Aberdeen. Ben Macdhui and Braeriach guard the source. The Linn of Dee, Byron's narrow escape, and the floods of 1829 follow. Balmoral and the birks of Abergeldie bring royalty and Burns into the tale. John Geddie then takes the Tay. He weighs it against the Tiber. Rannoch Moor, Dunkeld, and Birnam Wood line his road. Such gift books married fine printing to the new love of touring.
48079-opuscula-essays-chiefly-philologic:
Essays on tongues and on the folk of far lands fill a book called Opuscula. Old spell forms of the last age stand as first printed. Tongues from all the world crowd its pages with their marks. Long and short sounds, dots, and hooks mark each strange word. Greek marks for counts show in the text as well.

Each piece takes one tongue ask or one folk ask in turn. Word roots, place names, and old rites all find a place. The writer moves from proof to proof in grave, dry prose. Such books served men who ran a vast realm's far posts. Tongue past fans get a deep store of small facts. Few fields are left out.
48480-montreal-from-1535-to-1914-vol-3-b:
Volume Three of Montreal From 1535 to 1914 came out in 1914 and holds life stories only. The S J Clarke firm issued the three part work at Montreal, Vancouver, and Chicago. The volume opens with the life of Richard Bladworth Angus. A portrait of Angus faces the first page.

Angus was born at Bathgate in Scotland on May 28, 1831. He came to Canada in 1857 to join the Bank of Montreal. He rose to lead work in Chicago and New York for the bank. He then helped build great rail lines in Canada. The sketch praises his gifts to sick care, schools, and art. More lives of like kind fill the volume.
48551-costume-fanciful-historical-and-th:
Costume: Fanciful, Historical and Theatrical, compiled by Aria with drawings by Percy Anderson, was published by Macmillan in 1906. Aria dedicates the book to the dear memory of Sir Henry Irving, who woke her love of beautiful things. The pair agreed that dress is told first by the hair, and then by the sleeves.

Chapters march from classic times through each century to the nineteenth, then turn to peasants at home and abroad and to Eastern dress. Fancy dress, dominoes and masks, corsets and crinolines, and bridal wear close the survey. Stage memories of great players season the last pages.
48807-first-offensive-the-marine-campaig:
Henry Shaw wrote First Offensive, the Marine campaign for Guadalcanal, as one of the Marines in World War II commemorative pamphlets. The contents follow the campaign month by month. The landing and the August battles come first. September brings the fight for the Ridge. October covers the Japanese offensive, and November the continuing buildup. December closes with the final stages of the campaign.

Sidebars fill out the story. Readers meet General Vandegrift, who commanded the First Marine Division, and the coastwatchers who reported Japanese movements. The amtrac landing vehicle, the division patch, and the first utility uniform each get a note. Portraits honour men such as the coastwatcher Vouza and the coast guardsman Munro. Photographs show Marines at the Lunga River and the airfield the Japanese were building when the landing came. The pamphlet gives the official Marine Corps account of America's first offensive of the Pacific war.
48949-the-bird-hospital:
The Bird Hospital, by Caroline Crowninshield Bascom, was published in 1905, illustrated from photographs. Bascom gives the book to a lifelong friend, Hannah Gould Mynverse. A front picture names the cast: Bobbinette, Dick, Dona Marina, Bobby, and Blondell, all birds in her care.

Chapter one is Little Billee. Bascom says she has always been passionately fond of animals, and would like to make pets of them all. In winter she keeps a free lunch counter on her bedroom window sill for English sparrows. Often two dozen feed at once, no two looking alike. Their table manners, she is sorry to say, are not always the best. Later chapters treat Taffy and Tricksey, Dewey, Trinata, Cady, transient patients, and two orphans. Readers get true tales of pet and patient birds, told with love and close watching.
49037-health-service-support-in-a-nuclea:
Army head staff put out a field book on health aid in a foul war zone. The book is Field Manual 4-02.7, dated October 2002. Its full theme is help where atom, germ, or gas arms are used. Free spread of the book was cleared for all hands. Form sheets and blank forms fill some of its pages.

Medics learn how to sort the hurt, guard food and water, and clean gear. Plans deal with mass hurt, taint on skin and ground, and safe move of the sick. Charts and tables fix each step in plain order. Unit medics and chiefs are the key users.
49130-hovey-s-handbook-of-the-mammoth-ca:
Hovey's Handbook of the Mammoth Cave of Kentucky is a practical guide to the set routes of the great cave. It was written by Horace Carter Hovey and published at Louisville in 1909. The guide map at the front was drawn by Hovey himself.

A table gives the lengths of the walks in yards. The Giant's Coffin lies about 875 yards in. The Star Chamber is twice as far. Echo River ends near 3,000 yards, and the Maelstrom near 9,600. Hovey warns that no full measured survey of the cave has ever been made. His map rests on older plans, back to 1814, and on his own notes from twenty-seven years of visits. Names on the route include Ole Bull's Concert Hall and the Black Hole of Calcutta.
49382-the-life-of-nephi-the-son-of-lehi-:
The Life of Nephi is a biography by George Cannon, published at Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1888. Its subject is Nephi, son of Lehi. In the account of the Book of Mormon, Nephi left Jerusalem for a land now known as South America. That journey came some six centuries before the coming of the Saviour.

In his preface Cannon explains his aim. He had long wished to write the life of Nephi, and with time the lives of other great men of that record, as a series of lives for the young. His purpose was to make the children of his church familiar with the events of the Book of Mormon and with its leading men. Nephi, he says, was one of the greatest founders of that mighty people. Pressure of other work delayed the plan for years.
49538-mexico-aztec-spanish-and-republica:
Mexico: Aztec, Spanish and Republican, volume two of two, is a historical and geographical account by Brantz Mayer, formerly secretary of legation to Mexico. It was printed at Hartford in 1853. The work covers the country from the Spanish invasion to the present time, with a view of the ancient Aztec empire and notices of New Mexico and California.

The contents of this volume treat the physical structure of Mexico, its volcanic mountains, and its climates, the warm, temperate, and cold lands. Rivers and lakes are catalogued. A long chapter divides the population into whites, Indians, Africans, and the castes between. It sketches the ranchero, the leperos, and the Indian race, with their habits, superstitions, and the burden of peonage. Tables of population follow. Mayer wrote from his own service in Mexico, for American readers of the years after the Mexican War. His survey joins geography to social portrait.
4963-moral:
Ludwig Thoma's play Moral arrives with an introductory sketch of the author's career, from law practice abandoned in 1899 to humorous verse for Simplicissimus under the pen name Pete Schlemiehl. His poems, later collected as Grobheiten, nearly identified the paper with his name, and his Bavarian dialect prose and boyhood tales won a large audience.

Thoma became editor of Simplicissimus in 1899, and his renown grew from there, with critics ranking him next to Hauptmann in modern German drama. When Moral appeared, reviewers called its author shocking yet casting a long shadow. Readers get a German satirist at his sharpest, introduced by the career that made his mockery matter.
49676-the-boy-scouts-of-the-field-hospit:
Robert Shaler, a scout master, wrote a boys tale held under copyright in 1915 as book twelve in a set of fifteen scout books. The set, sold at twenty five cents a copy, lists signal, pioneer, life saving, and flood tales among its titles. Fourteen chapters carry this tale from a camp to a welcome sight at the close.

Chapter one camps the scouts on a river called the Hurricane, where bad luck seems to dog their leader. A close call in rapids and a good turn for an ill one follow. A frog hunter is trapped, calls to duty are heeded, and a field hospital is set up before a strike tragedy strikes.
49692-an-outline-of-the-phonology-and-mo:
Grandgent, professor of Romance languages at Harvard, wrote this outline of the sounds and forms of Old Provençal for Heath's Modern Language Series. The revised edition appeared at Boston in 1909. The preface tells of twenty years of desultory labor behind the little book. Grandgent's own introduction to the science was Paul Meyer's course at the École des Chartes in the winter of 1884 and 1885. Since then he had gathered material from texts and from the great grammars of Diez and Meyer-Lübke.

He confines himself to the old literary language, the tongue of the troubadours. Modern dialects of southern France enter only where they throw light on the geography of sound changes. Catalan and Franco-Provençal appear incidentally, and word-formation is left to a student's treatise in preparation. The outline served the classroom as a map of a language learned from poems.
49706-smokiana-historical-ethnographical:
Smokiana is an illustrated album of smoking history and ethnography by Robert Pritchett, published in 1890. The original was handwritten, text and captions alike, with drawings throughout. Pritchett dedicates his plebiscite, with a wink, to the memory of King James the First of Counterblaste fame and to the anti-tobacco fraternity of the present day.

His preface follows the goddess Nicotina's triumph from west to east since the sixteenth century, girdling the world with devotees. The plates then tour the pipe family, from churchwardens to Arctic pipes. Ignition gets its own section. The album is a Victorian collector's cabinet of smoking, drawn and lettered by hand in a spirit of cheerful defiance.
49735-from-libau-to-tsushima-a-narrative:
From Libau to Tsushima tells the story of Admiral Rojdestvensky's fleet on its long voyage to the Far East. The writer, Eugène Politovsky, was engineer-in-chief to the squadron. His book rests on letters to his wife, never meant for print. He went down with the battleship Kniaz Suvaroff at Tsushima on May 14th, 1905.

The English edition came out in 1908, turned from the Russian by Major Godfrey. The account gives the Dogger Bank incident in full, when the fleet fired on British fishing boats. Coaling without bases and repairs in the open sea fill the middle chapters. The translator notes the obsolete ships and low hearts that doomed the fleet.
49920-the-mentor-the-contest-for-north-a:
One number of The Mentor, volume one, number thirty five, tells the story of America in pictures. Its subject is the contest for North America. Albert Bushnell Hart, a Harvard professor of government, wrote the text. Pictures name La Salle, the capture of Louisburg, and the Deerfield massacre. The capture of Quebec, Braddock's defeat, and the Pontiac war follow. The whole round world is now open, Hart begins. Gone is the pleasure of finding new lands.

After Everest is climbed and an airship lands on McKinley, he asks, what will be left for the seeker of novelty? The Mentor sold illustrated history lessons by subscription. Hart was among America's leading historians. His serial made the colonial wars a picture story.
50317-scandal:
Scandal is a novel by Cosmo Hamilton, held under a 1917 copyright and printed in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Richard Culter drew the plates. A Browning verse heads the book, on life as our chance of learning love.

A front plate shows Fraser become at once the object of Beatrix whole attention. The tale opens with a man crying out at the sight of Beatrix Vanderdyke in New York out of season. His friend shrugs and claims no interest, yet talk turns on her visits to York studio near midnight. Pelham Franklin laughs that it is her life. The plate list jokes on a charming picture of wedded bliss and warns that scandal will rear its head in days. Society tale fans get love under the eye of gossip.
50457-the-luzumiyat-of-abu-l-ala-selecte:
The Luzumiyat of Abu'l-Ala gathers poems of the blind Syrian poet, chosen from his Luzum ma la Yalzam and his Suct uz-Zand. Ameen Rihani, author of The Book of Khaled, rendered them into English for the first time. James T White and Company of New York issued this second edition in 1920, and Rihani dedicates it to Emir Feisal.

Rihani opens with a long poem of his own to Abu'l-Ala, hailing the thrice-imprisoned thinker whose sight was shut by fate so that light flowed inward. The critics quoted agree on the poems' force: bold and original, with a sombre and earnest tone. Abu'l-Ala, one judge says, was a poet many centuries ahead of his time. The selection made a classic of Arabic doubt and reason speak English.
50546-royal-winchester-wanderings-in-and:
Royal Winchester is the Reverend A G L'Estrange's wanderings in and about the ancient capital of England. Spencer Blackett of London published this second edition, with many illustrations from original sketches by C G Harper. L'Estrange thanks the Dean of Winchester and the Warden of New College among his helpers.

The walk is laid out in days. The first covers the High Street, the castle, King Arthur, and Charles the Second's palace; the second adds the Butter Cross, King Alfred, and the guildhalls. Walls, gates, the College, Wykeham, and Wolvesey fill the third day, and Hyde Abbey the fourth. Two days belong to the cathedral: Saint Swithun, Walkelin, the nave, the crypt, Isaak Walton's monument, and the library. The book is a guided tour on foot, history read off the stones.
50592-selected-letters-of-saint-jane-fra:
Chosen notes of Saint Jane Frances de Chantal came out in English in 1918. Sisters of the Visitation at Harrow turned them from the French. Cardinal Bourne wrote the front words for the set. A plate shows the saint, who found the Order of the Visitation. Church leave to print dates to November 6, 1917.

The notes were drawn from the great French life and works of 1877. That set was made true to her own hand at Annecy. Her notes span years of rule, prayer, and care of souls. Advice to her nuns fills much of the choice in these pages. Church folk get her own voice in plain English.
50676-the-infidel-a-story-of-the-great-r:
Braddon wrote a tale of the great revival, printed at London in 1900. Her Lady Audley's Secret and Vixen are named on the title page. Twenty chapters and a close make up the book. Grub Street scribblers open it, in the days of George the Second.

Father and daughter work the trade of letters side by side. William Thornton writes only what the book sellers want, verse or prose, for pay by the sheet. He can write for or against any cause with equal fire. Heads bring a stage girl of the patent houses, a woman who could say no, and pride that conquers love. Swords and Bibles meet near the end.
50853-ticonderoga-a-story-of-early-front:
James wrote Ticonderoga, a tale of early frontier life in the Mohawk Valley. He was known for romances set in past ages, such as Darnley and Richelieu. This story opens at a neat new house in a lonely clearing.

The master of the house lives there with the two he loves best, in a land where men keep few guards against secret attack. A handsome young stranger rides up at sunset and asks for shelter for the night. From that knock at the door, the tale of love, risk, and war on the frontier begins to unfold.
50934-augusta-tabor-her-side-of-the-scan:
Caroline Bancroft wrote a short Colorado history in 1955, giving Augusta Tabor's side of a famous scandal. Bancroft was a third generation Coloradan who began writing history for the Denver Post in 1928. Her grandfather helped found the Colorado Historical Society and was its first president. She wrote many booklets on Colorado towns and figures.

Augusta Tabor spoke of Baby Doe in a long interview with a Denver Republican reporter. The account appeared on October 31, 1883, under spicy heads. Bancroft uses that interview to let Augusta answer her rival's legend. A fifth edition came out in 1968. The booklet is brief, local, and partisan by design.
51035-up-for-renewal:
Up for Renewal, by Lucius Daniel, ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in November 1954, with drawings by Docktor. The headnote twists a common saying: giving a year off one's life was ghastly reality to Kent. Howard Kent stands with his wife in the Human Rejuvenation Plant.

The long, narrow room, with potted palms and formal chairs, puts Kent in mind of a disposal unit. Leah is young and lovely, and Kent feels his lined face and stooped shoulders beside her. He has a confession to make before the treatment starts. He hid his true age when they wed, fearing she would refuse him. He is sixty-five, not the thirty he seemed, and he has been rejuvenated before. Leah says she suspected as much when he aged so fast last week.
51243-the-life-of-midhat-pasha-a-record-:
The Life of Midhat Pasha, by his son Ali Haydar Midhat Bey, was published by John Murray at London in 1903, with portraits. The subtitle promises a record of his services, political reforms, banishment, and judicial murder, derived from private documents and reminiscences.

The early chapters sweep Ottoman history from the Janissaries to the Crimean War. Midhat's own career follows: success in the Danube provinces, the governorship of Baghdad, and the conquest of Nedjed. Then come the deposition of Abdul Aziz, the new constitution, and Midhat's fall under Abdul Hamid. Later parts track his exile in Europe and his return as governor of Syria.
5128-the-young-carthaginian-a-story-of-t:
G. A. Henty's adventure novel for young readers follows a Carthaginian hero through the age of Hannibal. From a camp in the desert and the streets of Carthage, the story moves to a campaign in Spain, the siege of Saguntum, the crossing of the Rhone. The great battles of the Trebia and Lake Trasimene follow.

Henty wrote for boys who, as his preface notes, often sympathised with Carthage against Rome, and he fills the book with battles, plots, and escapes. The novel doubles as a lively introduction to the Punic Wars, told from the losing side, with history carried along by a hero who is always in the thick of it.
51286-pen-pal:
Milton Lesser match makes in space in Pen Pal, from the July 1951 issue of Galaxy Science Fiction. Don Sibley draws the plates. The head tag states her quest: all she wanted was a mate, and she had the gumption to go out and hunt one down. But that meant poaching in a strictly forbidden territory.

Matilda Penshaws, the seeker at the tale's heart, is thirty three years old and feels time marking her face. She hunts a husband of a rare sort: a prince and a charmer in one, a man who has been everywhere and tasted all the world can give. That no such man may exist does not slow her search at all.
51340-the-mentor-the-metropolitan-museum:
The Mentor, serial number one hundred fifty seven, treats the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Sydney Noe wrote the number, dated June fifteen, nineteen eighteen, for the Mentor Association. It sold for twenty cents and bears the motto Learn One Thing Every Day. The issue belongs to volume six, fine arts number nine of the series.
