An opening essay asks whether art pays, and answers with the shopkeeper and the painter. Painters packed off in youth, like Corot, may end rich and famous in time. The shopkeeper who rose may in turn become a patron of the arts. Beauty, the essay argues, is the life blood of trade in a great city. Polished boots, cotton prints, carpets, and wallpapers all sell because men love beauty. Portraits and museum rooms are pictured through the rest of the number.
51420-license-to-steal:
Louis Newman's License to Steal ran in Galaxy Magazine for August 1959, illustrated by Wood. The story is told as a legal case: Citizens versus Skrrgck, before the Galactic Tribunal. Skrrgck came from Sknnbt, Altair Four, where theft is honorable and sanctioned by law and custom, to Chicago, where it is not. Hearing his landlady say a license to steal, he asked a police desk sergeant for one, and got a joke document.

Relying on it, he stole, and was convicted. The Tribunal held that officials must not misrepresent the law to strangers, and that such misrepresentation, with a law-abiding defendant, amounts to entrapment. Illinois could not prosecute. The fact that he stole a large Chicago building, the Merchandise Mart, was of no significance beside the principle. He owed the building back, though, even if he had to steal where theft was legal.
51435-the-business-as-usual:
The Business, As Usual is a satirical story by Jack Sharkey. It appeared in Galaxy Magazine for August 1960, with illustrations by Trattner. Sharkey sets his scene in 1962. The United States Air Force has gained a radar resistant airplane. Cleared officials rejoice, then face a harder problem: what to do with it. The Secretary of Defense wants a use that warns certain unnamed powers. The President grumbles at the euphemism and asks why they never say the name.

Policy, the Secretary answers: America has always walked softly abroad. Now they hold the big stick at last. It needs only a shake, with no harm intended, unless provoked. Leaflets are proposed and rejected as the talk runs on. Sharkey turns Cold War secrecy and deterrence into office comedy.
51593-essays-literary-critical-and-histo:
Thomas O'Hagan wrote essays printed at Toronto in 1909 in an author's edition. O'Hagan had written Canadian Essays, Studies in Poetry, In Dreamland, and Songs of the Settlement. He gives the volume to his fellow countrymen, the French Canadians and Acadians. Speaking the language of Bossuet and Lamartine, they have added lustre to our Canadian citizenship, he says.

Four of the five essays appeared in past years in the American Catholic Quarterly Review and the Champlain Educator. He owns his debt to Doctor Dawson's admirable work on Tennyson's Princess for his study of that poem. Without Dawson's fine analysis, the first essay could never have been written, he says. The paper on the Italian Renaissance and the popes of Avignon was prepared while sojourning at Louvain in the autumn of 1903. The study and interpretation of literature rests on ideals from post graduate courses at leading American universities.
51680-history-of-the-life-of-gustavus-ad:
History of the Life of Gustavus Adolphus the Second, by Harriet Earhart Monroe, was held under a 1910 copyright and printed at Philadelphia by the Lutheran Publication Society. Monroe calls her hero the hero general of the Reformation. Gustavus was king of Sweden in the Thirty Years War.

In her preface Monroe says she does not try to give a full life, since the tale is hard for young folk to grasp. She picks the lead events of a most eventful life. The sketch first served as a lecture with lantern views and three small plays. One play shows Swedish joy at his crowning, and one shows his farewell to Parliament as he sailed for war. A third treats the women who loved him. Young readers get a hero king in bright scenes.
51693-the-brownie-scouts-in-the-cherry-f:
Mildred Wirt takes girls to a fair in The Brownie Scouts in the Cherry Festival, printed in New York with copyright in 1950. Cupples and Leon made the book. Fifteen chapters follow the troop. A frontispiece shows Connie reading a name aloud at the quilt show.

Crazy quilt leads, then cherry pickers wanted and over the fence. Tail ender and the Brownies lend a hand fill the early run. A missing coverlet and Pa Hooper's trunk bring a small mystery. A duck's foot in the mud, Veve's autograph quilt, and at the cannery work the troop. Trouble afoot, racing the storm, and Washington calling close the book. Chapter one opens at sewing: stitch, stitch, stitch. Six needles nibbled at the gay scraps of cotton cloth, as the Brownies worked in the Williams living room. Veve McGuire, who hated to sew, called the task as silly as the quilt's name.
51731-the-mentor-american-pioneer-prose-:
The Mentor for 1 May 1916 forms this number, the sixth on books in its fourth year. Its theme is the first prose men of America, and its hand is Hamilton W. Mabie. The sheet bears a rule at its head: learn one thing each day. Its price was fifteen cents a copy. The first piece bears the head Fame in Name Only. What do we in truth know of them, it asks: these gods of our shelves?

We know them by name, and their names are words of the house. We know them by fame, and their fame will not die. So we pay them their due by the buy of their books. And too oft, the piece says, we rest content with that. The wealth they give us is in reach of our arm, and we leave it there.
51768-prospector-s-special:
Prospector's Special is a science fiction story by Robert Sheckley, from a magazine called Galaxy dated December nineteen fifty nine. Pictures by Dillon go with it. Its headnote sets its hero lost in the vast Scorpion Desert of Venus. He needed all the courage a man could own, it says. And every bit of credit he could raise, it adds.

Morrison drives a sandcar over rolling dunes in the opening. Its six fat wheels rise and fall like the rumps of elephants, the tale says. A hidden sun beats down from a dead white sky. He talks to himself to stay awake, holding the car to its compass course. It is his twenty first day alone in the desert. Night travel would be easier, but ravines and boulders bar it, he reflects.
52113-fifteen-days-an-extract-from-edwar:
Fifteen Days, printed at Boston in 1866, is an extract from the journal of Edward Colvil. The entries begin on Good-Friday evening, April 5, 1844, after seven silent days. Colvil counts his blessings: farm work that leaves study its zest, books on the way, a mother's love and faithful letters. He thought nothing was wanting to him.

Then a guest crossed his threshold and was taken to his heart at the first handclasp. Keith's visit fills the fifteen days with sunshine, after a week of gray weather. Colvil cannot part the glow of the skies from the glow of his friend's nature. The little book turns a short visit into a study of gratitude.
52354-the-story-of-our-flag-colonial-and:
Addie Guthrie Weaver wrote The Story of Our Flag, a book held by rights from 1898 at Chicago. Weaver drew the flags in color herself for the book. She had long cared for the tale of the first flag and its maker. Kin ties to the Ross line let her learn the family tale at first hand.

The book traces the flag from its first form to the flag of the land in her day. A full part tells of Betsy Ross, the Quaker woman said to have sewn the first flag. Weaver thanks George Canby and Sophia Campion Guthrie, both kin of Ross, for facts. She gives the book to them and to other Ross kin. The work blends flag lore, family tale, and pride in the land.
52840-salvation-universal:
Joseph Fielding Smith wrote a tract on universal salvation, published by the Genealogical Society of Utah in 1920. Smith served as the society's secretary and treasurer. He calls salvation the greatest of all God's gifts to his children. God's greatest work, he adds, is to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.

For that purpose, Smith says, worlds are created and peopled. God gives commandments and grants power to choose whether to obey. Those who obey are promised blessings added upon them in the celestial kingdom. Those who reject the laws become a law to themselves in unrighteousness. Footnotes cite Doctrine and Covenants and the Book of Moses.
53235-the-practical-magician-and-ventril:
Parlor magic and ventriloquism are taught trick by trick in The Practical Magician and Ventriloquist’s Guide, a manual issued at New York by Hurst and Company. The book was entered for copyright in 1876 by Thomas Hurst. Its full title promises a practical manual of fireside magic and conjuring illusions. Full directions for learning ventriloquism come with the magic.

Bound in with the manual are notices for kindred books on the conjuring art. One such book, by Professor Raymond, is praised as the most full work on magic ever issued. It claims to expose all the secrets of the wizard’s art. No trick or illusion of weight is left unnoticed in that work, the notice says. The guide itself serves the home performer who wants clear how to directions, not stage theory.
533-the-song-of-the-cardinal:
Gene Stratton-Porter follows a cardinal bird through a year of song, storm, and love in this nature novel. The cardinal, a yearling of bright crest and black beard, hatches in the Limberlost marsh, then wings south to orange orchards. Five chapters take their names from his cries: good cheer, wet year, come here, so dear, see here.

Stratton-Porter writes the bird's life with close, loving detail, from slugs at breakfast to mates and nests. Men hear his song as a message of cheer. The book charms as a nature romance where a small bird's year mirrors human hope, grief, and joy.
53336-the-public-school-word-book-a-conr:
Public School Word Book, by John Farmer, is a glossary of school speech. It was issued in London in nineteen hundred for subscribers only. Farmer edited works on Americanisms and on slang and its analogues. The book logs words and phrases used at great public schools.

Farmer stresses that the book is not a mere dictionary of school slang. Most items in it do not fall under that class at all, he says. Many words are old forms now lost, and some are modish at universities. Few of the items appear in any other work, he notes with care. Readers get a record of school and college speech of that era.
53371-the-haslemere-museum-gazette-vol-1:
The Haslemere Museum Gazette, Volume One, Number Two, is a museum journal dated June 1906. Its lead piece describes the museum's history room, shown in the frontispiece. The room illustrates human history in a separate division of the main building. Medals, coins, and small models stand with each period.

The room is arranged, as far as can be, on the space-for-time method. Like a diary, it gives every period the same amount of space. The editors admit the method fits ill where dates are unsure. For prehistoric times it can serve only as an open, partly speculative frame. Their first number had ventured such a frame for prehistoric man in Britain. The gazette is the voice of a bold little educational museum, teaching history by walking through it.
53403-old-memories-amusing-and-historica:
Charlotte Holt Gethings Macpherson's recollections of old Quebec, printed for the author at Montreal in 1890, form a sequel to her Reminiscences of Old Quebec. She signs herself an old Quebecer and dedicates the volume to her husband's cousin James Macpherson LeMoine. Her letter to subscribers says five hundred copies of an earlier feuilleton sold within a few weeks, and casts her as Boswell to LeMoine's Johnson.

The contents roam the city she was born in: the old convent, the Saint Louis Hotel, the Quebec Bank, horse boats and ice boats. Other chapters treat Beaumont and Saint Michel, Roberval and Lake Saint John, the Saint Leon Springs, and society in Quebec fifty years before. There are also the subterranean passages of the Citadel, the first Saint Patrick's Society, and New Year's Day in 1840.
53992-peggy-o-neal:
Alfred Henry Lewis published Peggy O'Neal with A J Drexel Biddle in 1902, with pictures by Henry Hutt. An older man who knew camps, caucuses, and war tells the story in the first person. He admits that politics and war made him coarse and hard.

He and the General, he says, toiled and schemed for Peg and broke old friendships for her sake. He holds that the charges laid against her were false. Her beauty, in his view, proved her pure heart. The opening chapter calls her lustrous and sets out to show how one woman's fate shaped acts of state that lasted for years.
54029-historical-record-of-the-twenty-fi:
Richard Cannon wrote the official record of the twenty first regiment, the Royal Scots Fusiliers. It belongs to the set of army records ordered at the Horse Guards on January 1 1836. The king commanded that the service of every regiment be set in print. The adjutant general had charge of the work.

Each account was to give the raising of the corps and each station where it served. Battles, sieges and feats in action were to be named in full. So were colours and prizes taken from the foe. Lists name the officers and men killed or wounded at each place. Men marked out for brave conduct stand by name as well.
54056-in-the-clouds-for-uncle-sam-or-mor:
In the Clouds for Uncle Sam, or Morey Marshall of the Signal Corps, is by Ashton Lamar. The tale is the first volume of The Aeroplane Boys set. Reilly and Britton printed the set in Chicago. Pictures by Riesenberg attend the tale, with a plate showing Morey hitting the mark. The series list shows five more volumes, from The Stolen Aeroplane to Battling the Big Horn.

The publisher's notice calls the stories the newest and most up to date, with all aeroplane details correct. Each volume came fully illustrated with a colored frontispiece, in cloth, at sixty cents. Lamar's opener puts a boy of the Signal Corps in the clouds for his country. The set belongs to the first wave of aviation fiction for boys, when the aeroplane was new enough to carry a series on its own wonder.
54245-bygone-scotland-historical-and-soc: Bygone Scotland, Historical and Social, is a history of Scotland in its older days, as its title states. The hosted text opens with detailed notes on dates tied to its chapters, including the reign of Queen Anne, the execution of Montrose, and a fire at Holyrood Palace. Those notes alone show a book that moves across centuries of Scottish public life, from early kings to festival days and great houses.
54269-a-letter-to-the-rev-william-maskel:
Mayow, vicar of Market Lavington and late student of Christ Church, Oxford, writes to William Maskell in a second edition from Pickering at London in 1850. His question stands on the title page: how far the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council commits the Church of England by its decision, even granting it jurisdiction in points of doctrine.

Mayow says at once that he will not attempt a full answer to Maskell's letter. He feels the difficulties too strongly himself, and he cannot go the whole way with either side. Much as he reveres Keble and those who take Keble's line, he is not persuaded they have proved the court incompetent, and so he offers the points he thinks have been overlooked.
54410-shakespeare-and-the-stage-with-a-c:
Shakespeare and the Stage is a theatre history by Maurice Jonas, in the printed edition of 1918. A transcriber note at the front records that this text is based on that edition. Its full title promises a complete list of theatrical records bearing on the plays. 

Jonas gathers the evidence of the early stage for the plays of Shakespeare in one survey. Playbills, title pages, and the records of the theatres are his matter in the study. The chapters in the original are numbered inconsistently, the note warns its readers in candour. Such lists of performances and editions were the tools of a new kind of Shakespeare study then. Scholars were turning from praise of the poet to the paper trail of his plays in the playhouses, and Jonas book is a storehouse for that work.
54814-miller-s-mind-training-for-childre:
William Miller of Alhambra, California, wrote and published this first book of his mind training course for children, copyrighted in 1920 and 1921. He calls it a practical training for successful living, built on educational games that train the senses.

The contents move sense by sense: touch games like the button bag and rag bag, ear games like whispering and tapping, then sight, taste, and smell. Later sections train the mind's eye, observation, location, attention, and concentration, with games such as detective and quick counting. Miller held that conscious effort improves every faculty. Parents and teachers get a full program of play with a purpose.
54865-madame-gilbert-s-cannibal:
Madame Gilbert's Cannibal, by Bennet Copplestone, was copyright in 1920 in New York. Copplestone had written The Lost Naval Papers and The Silent Watchers. Madame Gilbert ends her war work as Austria falls out of the great war. In Italy she ran sly schemes to foil the foe, and holds that her side won the war there.

Madame speeds home for her first rest since August 1914, past police who clear her way. Chapters then sail for the South Seas with a yawl, the Humming Top. Names point to a pilot, Willatopy, an isle called Tops, and a night in the straits. Marie Lambert and a hedge lawyer add knots. The tale ends in the Straits of Sunda. Sea fans get a sly, swift yarn of a grand dame and her wild charge.
54976-the-molecular-tactics-of-a-crystal:
The Molecular Tactics of a Crystal is a lecture by Lord Kelvin on the inner structure of crystals. He gave it at Oxford in May 1893 as the second Robert Boyle Lecture. The Oxford University Junior Scientific Club heard it. The Clarendon Press printed it in 1894 with twenty pictures.

Kelvin states his scope with care at the very start. His subject is not the powers of crystals, nor even their motion. It is the bare geometry of their build, the placing of their molecules. Every crystal, he says, is a like-bodied gathering of small parts. In a pure gathering each person stands like every other in even rows. Each has a neighbour at the same distance on every side. From that plain picture the lecture builds its account of crystal form.
55006-the-sundial:
The Sundial is a novel by Fred White, author of The Crimson Blind. Dodge published the book at New York in 1908. The contents run to forty eight chapters. Titles promise a blighted life, a photograph, and a jewel casket.

John Charlock, the hero, has fought his way from hunger to fame as a portrait painter. He has slept in open parks and starved in his early days. Now he stands almost without rival at his art. He has also found the one woman who could complete his joy. Yet the taste of success is dry in his mouth, like Dead Sea fruit. White builds a tale of love, family honour, and a plausible scoundrel. A fire, a search, and a hidden place carry the plot to its close.
55022-the-brain-of-an-army-a-popular-acc:
The Brain of an Army is a popular account of the German General Staff by Spenser Wilkinson, issued in a new edition by Archibald Constable of Westminster in 1895. Wilkinson also wrote The Command of the Sea and The Brain of a Navy. This edition prints letters from Count Moltke and Lord Roberts.

Moltke's letter praises Wilkinson for disposing of a legend. No council of war, the old field marshal assures him, was ever called in 1866 or in 1870 and 1871. The commander consulted his authorised adviser and decided. Wilkinson explained the staff system to British readers alarmed and envious after Germany's victories. His book argued that modern war is run by trained brains, not by councils. It became a text in the British campaign for a general staff of their own.
55034-through-portugal:
Martin Hume wrote a travel book on a pleasure trip through Portugal. The book came out in New York in 1907. Forrest made color plates, and photos add to the views. Hume gave the book, by leave, to the King of Portugal. A Byron quote at the front praises the land's fruit and hills.

The road runs from Oporto to Braga and the Bom Jesus shrine. Old towns, Coimbra, and great church houses fill the mid part. Batalha, Alcobaça, Cintra, and Lisbon each take a full part. Hume ends with hints for those who would make the trip. Armchair trips get both charm and use here.
55346-lectures-on-painting-delivered-to-:
Edward Armitage's Lectures on Painting, delivered to the students of the Royal Academy, were published by Putnam at New York in 1883. Armitage held the Academy professorship from 1876 to 1882. Twelve lectures are selected, to keep the book modest in size. Lectures on the great masters of the fifteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth centuries were left out, needing their engravings. The preface, dated February 1883, offers no plea of friends' entreaty for publishing.

His real reason was the large, attentive audiences his teaching drew. The lectures run from ancient costumes through Byzantine and Romanesque art to David and his school. Drawing, color, decorative painting, and finish take the middle lectures. The choice of a subject and composition close the course. Armitage holds that practical drawing is learned only by real work. The professor's duties, he says, are pilotage through the quicksands and feeding the subtle flame of art.
55508-miller-s-mind-training-for-childre:
William Miller of Alhambra, California, wrote and published this second book of his Mind Training for Children. He had earlier written The Natural Method of Memory Training. The book calls itself a working guide for a good life, built on games that train the senses.

Book two drills the memory, the sense the book calls the strongest: sight. Lessons use clear mind pictures, stretched likeness, motion, and odd links to fix facts fast. A code game, errand games, and story games turn drill into play. Miller also treats health habits, the harm of putting things off, and how to speak with no notes. Lists and steps keep each game plain for home use.
55509-miller-s-mind-training-for-childre:
William Miller of Alhambra, California, wrote and published Miller's Mind Training for Children, copyrighted in 1920 and 1921, as a practical training for successful living through educational games that train the senses. Book three is titled Helping Your Children in School. Miller also wrote a natural method of memory training.

Lessons teach children to remember what they read and hear, using visualisation as the greatest aid. Chapters cover verbatim learning, mastering difficult lists, learning the presidents, studying anatomy, and becoming a good speller. Word games and puzzle maps fill the later pages. Readers get a home memory course for schoolchildren from the self-improvement era.
55893-peeps-at-many-lands-portugal:
Agnes Goodall wrote and painted this peep at Portugal for children. Black printed it in London in 1909 with twelve colour plates. Gossip at the fountain fronts the volume as first picture. Contents open with the growth of the kingdom in chapter one.

Decline of the kingdom and Lisbon with a great explorer follow. Portuguese children, country dances, songs, and legends fill mid chapters. Cintra, Obidos, farms and vineyards, and Oporto come in turn. Coimbra monasteries and bull fighting close the country survey here. A sketch map of Portugal stands in the front pages for the young reader.
56040-memoirs-of-mistral:
Memoirs of Mistral is the life of the Provençal poet rendered into English by Constance Elisabeth Maud. Lyrics from the Provençal by Alma Strettell go with the memoirs. The book came out in London in 1907 from Edward Arnold, with pictures. It is given to the translator's friend Therese Roumanille. A line from Goethe stands at its front, in German: I sing as the bird sings that dwells in the branches.

The front pages list the other books of the translator, Constance E. Maud. Among them are An English Girl in Paris, My French Friends, and Felicity in France. Wagner's Heroes and Wagner's Heroines stand in the list as well, one in its sixth impression. A portrait of Mistral from 1907 stands at the front of the volume. The book brings a French poet's account of his own life to English readers.
56145-tribal-custom-in-anglo-saxon-law-b:
Tribal Custom in Anglo-Saxon Law, by Frederic Seebohm, was published by Longmans, Green and Company in London, New York, and Bombay in 1902. The essay is supplemental to two earlier works, The English Village Community and The Tribal System in Wales, and closes a trilogy.

The first essay approached the early evidence from the manorial system, through the open field farming in which it lived. This third essay approaches the Anglo-Saxon laws from tribal custom instead. Welsh custom is restudied first, as a clue: the gwely, or family unit, and the galanas, the death fine paid in place of the blood feud. The currencies of the wergeld are settled in chapter one. The feud rules hidden in Beowulf and Irish custom follow. Then come the Burgundian and Gothic laws, the Salic and Ripuarian Franks, the tribes Charlemagne conquered, and the early Norse laws.
56201-british-bees-an-introduction-into-:
W E Shuckard wrote an introduction to the study of the bees native to the British Isles, published in London in 1866. Shuckard had written on fossorial wasps and British insects and translated Burmeister's manual of entomology. He dedicates the book to William Wilson Saunders, a fellow of the Royal Society. The dedication praises his zeal for entomology and many years of kindness.

In a preface Shuckard explains his citation of authorities. Facts given without a source, he says, come from his own observation or from study so blended over time that he cannot separate them. He holds that animal habits, prompted by instinct, are uniform. Once well observed, he argues, they stand as permanently established.
56420-halloween-a-romaunt-with-lays-medi:
Halloween, a Romaunt, with lays meditative and devotional, is a poem by the author of Christian Ballads. Parsons published the book at Hartford in 1845 for its unnamed author. A preface tells the odd printing history of the poem for the reader.

Halloween had been printed, though never published, before this edition, the preface states. In the winter of 1842 a private edition of fifty copies was struck off for the author. The romaunt is a tale in verse of the Scottish festival night of its title. Its author, a churchman poet of Hartford, wrote in the manner of Scott romance turned to sacred use. The book is a specimen of the religious verse with which American churchmen of the 1840s answered the novel and the stage for the souls of their people.
56732-a-vagabond-journey-around-the-worl:
Harry A Franck wrote this travel narrative, printed by the Century Company of New York in 1910. More than one hundred photographs dress the book. Franck gives it to his alma mater, the University of Michigan, without whose training, he says, the trip had been impossible. A line from Rousseau heads the title: to know a land's true manners, go down among the lower ranks.

Chapters run from the borders of the Mediterranean to beachcombing at Marseilles, the Arab world, and the wilds of Palestine. The land of the Nile, three hoboes in India, and the ways of the Hindu follow. Franck travelled as a vagabond, working and loafing his way round the world, and his book made the low road respectable.
57179-the-flowing-bowl-a-treatise-on-dri:
Flowing Bowl is a treatise on drinks of all kinds by Edward Spencer. Spencer had written Cakes and Ale, a memory of many meals, before this book. Page numbers of the print original are kept in braces in this text. The subtitle promises drinks of all kinds and of all periods in the survey.

Punch, toddy, cocktails, cups, and old English ales pass under his lively review. Spencer writes as a clubman antiquary of the bowl, with recipes and anecdotes mixed. Temperance England read such books with the same thirst as drinking England. Social history gains a witty cellar book from the height of the drink trade.
57374-annals-and-antiquities-of-rajastha:
Volume one of Tod's Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan came from Humphrey Milford at Oxford in 1920, in three volumes with William Crooke as editor. James Tod, once political agent to the Western Rajput States, first published the work in the 1820s and dedicated it to George the Fourth.

Crooke's edition keeps the old pagination in brackets and gathers more than 1,500 notes at the ends of chapters. A transcriber warns that the map waits at the end of the third volume. The frontispiece shows Tod himself, from the bust made of him in 1837, and the preface sets out Crooke's plan for mending the text and its spelling of Indian names.
57375-annals-and-antiquities-of-rajastha:
James Tod, once the British agent to the western Rajput states, wrote a grand survey of Rajasthan in the 1820s. The work treats the central and western Rajput states of India in three volumes. William Crooke later edited the text, with a preface, rich notes, and care for how Hindi words are spelled in print.

More than 1500 notes crowd this second volume alone, set at the end of each chapter in a clear scheme. Page marks from the first print run are kept in the text so old cites still hold. A map of the land, bound with the third volume, helps readers place the forts and towns.
57376-annals-and-antiquities-of-rajastha:
Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, volume three, completes James Tod's account of the central and western Rajput states of India. Tod was late political agent to the western Rajput states; William Crooke edited this edition with introduction and notes. The original was published in the 1820s, and its pagination is preserved here.

The frontispiece shows Colonel Tod with his Jain guru, from a painting by his native artist Ghasi. More than 900 notes crowd this volume alone, the author's and the editor's together, gathered at each chapter's end. A genealogical chart spanning three pages appears mid-text. The matter turns west and north into the desert tracts: the Ghaggar absorbed in sand, the Luni or salt-river, and the Rann. The towns of the thal country follow, Jalor, Bhinmal, and Barmer among them. It is the closing volume of the great Rajput survey.
575-the-essays-or-counsels-civil-and-mor:
Francis Bacon gathers his famous essays on life, rule, and conduct in this volume, dedicated to the Duke of Buckingham. Topics run from truth, death, and revenge to love, envy, travel, friendship, riches, and studies. Bacon enlarged the essays in number and weight, calling them a new work.

His style is terse, sententious, and full of maxims meant for men of business and courts. Each essay weighs a subject from several sides in a few pages. The book endures as a founding text of the English essay, where wisdom arrives in short, sharp sentences.
57514-index-for-works-of-bill-nye-hyperl:
David Widger compiled this index to the works of Bill Nye, the humorist Edgar W Nye, giving hyperlinks to all the chapters of his books. The volumes covered are Remarks, Baled Hay, Bill Nye and Boomerang, and Bill Nye's Chestnuts Old and New. Bill Nye's Sparks and Bill Nye's Red Book follow, with his Comic History of England and History of the United States.

Under Remarks alone the index lists dozens of sketches, from My School Days and Recollections of Noah Webster to Mr Sweeney's Cat, The Opium Habit, Broncho Sam, and On Cyclones. Each volume gets its table of contents in turn, so a reader can pass straight from the index to any single piece.
57803-medi-val-london-volume-1-historica:
Walter Besant wrote a survey of old London, volume one, issued in London in 1906. The front pages first praise three sister books on London under the Tudors, the Stuarts, and the age that followed. Besant's own first volume treats the city in its early, middle age.

Part one marches through the kings, from Henry the Second to Edward the Fourth and past him. Each reign gets its own chapter, with maps and pictures drawn from old books and records. The work aims to join hard fact with a clear tale, so that both the student and the plain reader can follow the growth of the city reign by reign.
57817-the-doctor-s-secret-journal:
Doctor's Secret Journal is a frontier journal by Daniel Morison, surgeon's mate. Morison served the second battalion of the 60th Regiment at Michilimackinac. His pages run from 1769 to 1772 at that Great Lakes fort. May edited the journal for Mackinac State Historic Parks in Michigan. Plates show pages from the original manuscript in Morison's own hand.

One quoted entry swears a man vowed by bloody oath against him. That man would come with a hatchet and pull down his house. Dirk Cringhuis drew the illustrations for the printed journal here. Printings ran from 1960 onward through seven editions by 2001. Garrison sickness, fur trade quarrels, and cold winters fill the record.
57829-or-the-art-of-embalming-wherein-is:
The Art of Embalming is a treatise by Thomas Greenhill, a surgeon, whose engraved portrait is dated 1705. Its Greek title, Nekrokedeia, heads a long English one. The book shews the right of burial and the funeral ceremonies of most nations.

Ways of preserving dead bodies across the world fill the survey. Opinions, experiments, and inventions of modern physicians are gathered. Surgeons, chymists, and anatomists all contribute their art. Greenhill also proposes new matter: a better method of embalming than any yet discovered. The frontispiece is explained in a long poem. Mortal man, it says, seeks immortality through monuments and balm. Pyramids lift their heads to keep bodies in immortal sleep. Aromatic spice denies death its dissipation of the form. Greenhill wrote for surgeons and for the curious trade of burial alike.
57852-ideals-in-art-papers-theoretical-p:
Ideals in Art, subtitled Papers Theoretical, Practical, Critical, collects essays by Walter Crane, the artist and designer. George Bell and Sons published the volume in London in 1905. Crane's other books are advertised in front: The Bases of Design, Line and Form, and The Decorative Illustration of Books.

The papers open with the Arts and Crafts movement, its general tendency and possible outcome. Crane then treats the teaching of art and its methods, and adds a note on Tolstoi's What Is Art. Other essays ask how modern social and economic conditions bear on the sense of beauty, and what art owes to society and ethics. Later papers take up ornament and its meaning, thoughts on house decoration, and the progress of taste in dress. Book covers, gilding, raised work in gesso, and the easel picture's place in decorative art close the volume.
57996-grace-harlowe-s-overland-riders-in:
Jessie Graham Flower wrote a girls adventure printed at Akron and New York in 1923. Get back, ye hound, a picture cries. The Overlanders get a shock opens the chapters: the arrival at Cinnabar, and it takes more than a sign to make a hotel. The guide is missing, and Stacy goes to look for Jake Coville and meets with a distressing experience. The stock car yields an amazing surprise.

Those are not our ponies, cries Nora. The wires bring bad news next: the mystery of the missing ponies, with the Overland Riders left without a guide or a horse. Hippy makes the telegraph wires sing. Lieutenant Wingate, in his bare feet, chases a telegraph messenger from camp. On the road to wonderland follows, with Emma Dean declining to kiss a horse. Grace Harlowe's party rides the Yellowstone the hard way.
58452-fences-gates-and-bridges-a-practic:
Fences, Gates and Bridges is a hands on manual shaped by George A Martin, printed in New York in 1892 by Orange Judd Company. Three hundred plates fill the book. The work was first entered in 1887.

The preface says farm fences in the United States have cost more than the farm buildings themselves. Yet few books had treated fences alone, while many treated rural building. Martin traces the fence from log, brush, and sod barriers to the latest barbed wire. Plates show fences, gates, and bridges in real use on real farms. A chapter treats fence law in brief, since court rulings alone would fill a large book. Farm readers got a full craft guide in one place.
58614-medi-val-london-volume-2-ecclesias:
Medieval London, volume two, was issued in London in 1906. Black published Besant's ecclesiastical volume that year. The book stands in the Survey of London. Its sister volumes are priced at thirty shillings net each. Tudor London, with Agas's map of 1560, is one of them. Stuart London carries Ogilby's map of 1677. The eighteenth century volume uses Rocque's map of 1741. A first medieval volume treats the city historical and social. Its 108 illustrations come mostly from old prints. Review lines at the front praise the set warmly. Exact and lively, one paper calls the writing. Another finds the grouping admirable throughout.

This second volume turns from streets to churches. Besant traces the city's religious houses, parishes, and rites. The church, in the medieval city, ordered much of daily life.
5883-the-flying-saucers-are-real:
Donald Keyhoe investigates flying saucers in The Flying Saucers Are Real, dedicating the book to Helen with love. Keyhoe, who relates his investigation in these pages, writes with the urgency of a reporter convinced the subject deserves serious attention. Twenty chapters follow sightings, official statements, and the arguments for and against unexplained craft in American skies.

The volume offers a landmark of early UFO literature, written before saucers became pop culture shorthand. Keyhoe gathers cases, questions secrecy, and presses for open inquiry, in plain, earnest prose. The book suits readers of UFO history, Cold War culture, and popular science debates, offering the founding argument that something real flies unexplained overhead.
590-robert-louis-stevenson-a-record-an-e:
Alexander Japp gathers memories, letters, and criticism of Robert Louis Stevenson in this 1905 tribute. Chapters treat Treasure Island, travels, the Vailima letters, and Stevenson's genius, methods, and gloom, with facsimile letters and a Samoan memorial. Friends such as Henley, Gosse, and Stedman add estimates, some fond, some sharp.

Japp writes as a friend who read Stevenson's proofs in Davos while author and wife lay ill. His record stresses Stevenson's cheer, craft, and moral seriousness. The book serves as a rich early life-and-letters volume, where those who knew Stevenson best speak in their own words.
59245-the-nautilus-vol-xxxi-no-2-october:
The Nautilus volume thirty one number two is a shell study sheet of October nineteen seventeen. Pilsbry of Philadelphia and Johnson of Boston led and ran the sheet. Two dollars a year was its price, with two score cents more for far lands. Half a dollar bought one sheet of the four in a year run. Its scheme lists brief notes on shell kinds and shell hunts of the age.

A note on shape shifts in a chiton kind opens the page scheme. Mussel finds in the Potomac and Cuba bay hunts fill next notes. New kinds from mid America and a South Africa snail stand in the list. Growth pace of pond mussels and flood tie of snails get notes too. A death note and a new books list close the sheet scheme.
59484-st-augustine-florida-s-colonial-ca:
St Augustine: Florida's Colonial Capital is a history by J T Van Campen, published by the St Augustine Historical Society with copyright in 1959. The Castillo de San Marcos, the old stone fort, fronts the book. Van Campen tells the story of the oldest city in the United States.

It begins in September 1565, when Don Pedro Menéndez landed with a Spanish fleet. His men took the French Fort Caroline and founded the town. Chapters follow the English threat, the building of the stone fort, and Oglethorpe's failed siege. British rule, the New Smyrna colony, and a return to Spain come next. Under the United States the town endured the Seminole War and a deep freeze. Henry Flagler's hotels then made it a resort. The book ends with the city of today.
59843-the-palace-and-park-its-natural-hi:
A guide to the Crystal Palace at Sydenham, published by the Crystal Palace Library in 1859. Samuel Phillips wrote the original guide, and Shenton newly arranged and revised this edition, with new plans, illustrations, and an index of principal objects. The Palace had risen again in south London after the Great Exhibition, bigger than before. The guide leads the visitor through the building and its park in order, so that every portion can be explored with advantage.

Five guides are bound in this volume's plan: the palace and park, the portrait gallery, ethnology and natural history, the extinct animals, and the Pompeian Court. The splendid botanical collection, thoroughly acclimatised, gets full description. Official announcements and even the refreshment tariff are printed at the front. For the price of the book, a Victorian family got the whole wonder systematized: courts, statues, gardens, and the great glass roof itself.
60538-the-trial-of-captain-john-kimber-f:
A shorthand report of a trial at the Admiralty Sessions was printed at London and sold for one shilling. It was taken by a student of the Temple. The trial sat at the Old Bailey on June 7, 1792. Captain John Kimber stood charged with the murder of two female negro slaves. The killings were said to happen on board the Recovery, an African slave ship. Sir James Marriot presided.

Observations on the trial are added at the end. The trial became a noted test of whether a slave ship captain could be tried for murder at all. Abolitionists used the case in their campaign. Kimber was acquitted, but the pamphlet kept the evidence before the public.
6070-the-unwilling-vestal:
Edward Lucas White tells a tale of Rome under the Caesars. As the jacket claims, it gives for the first time in fiction a correct account of the Vestal Virgins, their powers and privileges, and many strange Roman customs and beliefs. First published in 1918, the book went through sixteen printings.

White pairs a rattling good story with full knowledge of Roman life, bringing to imperial Rome the picturesqueness that marked his South American novel El Supremo. The unwilling vestal at the center must serve a sacred office she did not choose. The result is a vivid pageant of priests, power, and private will.
61420-and-so-ad-infinitum-the-life-of-th:
And So Ad Infinitum, or The Life of the Insects, is a play by the brothers Capek. Paul Selver translated it from the Czech. Playfair and Bax freely adapted it for the English stage. Oxford University Press published the text in 1923. A prologue in the woods and an epilogue frame the acts. A verse from Swift about fleas upon fleas stands as motto.

Act one belongs to the butterflies, all courtship and display. Creepers and crawlers — beetles, crickets, an ichneumon fly — fill act two. The ants take act three, with engineers, journalists, and a commander in chief. Moths, snails, a woodcutter, and school children people the epilogue. A tramp and a butterfly collector open the prologue. The Capeks turn insect life into a mirror of human folly. War, greed, and vanity all find their insect doubles.
61471-ivories-ancient-and-medi-val:
Ivories Ancient and Mediaeval is number two of the South Kensington Museum Art Handbooks, edited by William Maskell. The handbook reprints, in portable form, the dissertation placed before the great catalogue of ivories at the museum in South Kensington. A preface dated August 1875 explains the plan of the series.

The Lords of the Committee of Council on Education ordered the handbooks so that the public could understand the history and character of each art at trifling cost. A carved ivory pastoral staff showing the Nativity, German work of the twelfth century, illustrates the text. The essay traces ivory carving from ancient times through the middle ages: its materials, its uses in church and court, and its styles. Collectors, as well as museum visitors, were the intended readers.
61473-is-a-ship-canal-practicable-notes-:
Abert wrote Is a Ship Canal Practicable, with maps, at Cincinnati in 1870. His notes are historical and statistical, the title page says. They treat the projected routes for an interoceanic ship canal. The canal would join the Atlantic and Pacific oceans across the isthmus. A short account of the Suez Canal stands inside the same covers.

Its character and influence, and the probable effects of both canals, are weighed. The two might stand as rivals, or as parts of one system of navigation. The notes were collected in intervals of a busy professional life. They were laid before Secretary Seward and a former treasury head for reading. Both men commended the work, the front pages record. The paper was prepared before the Suez Canal was finished. Additions bring it down past the last Darien expedition's sailing.
61645-new-york-confidential:
New York Confidential is an expose of the city by Jack Lait and Lee Mortimer. Crown Publishers issued it first in 1948, with a revised edition in 1951. Front matter lists sister volumes on Chicago and Washington in the same series. Lait solo books on Broadway, gangsters, and Will Rogers stand behind the byline.

Mortimer had written New York Behind the Scenes before this joint best seller. Sixth printing by February 1951 shows how fast the scandal guide sold. Night life, crime, graft, and show folk form the stock of such confidential tours. Readers of the day bought a keyhole view of the city after dark.
61778-lafayette-in-america-in-1824-and-1:
A Levasseur wrote Lafayette in America in 1824 and 1825, or Journal of a Voyage to the United States, Volume Two, issued at Philadelphia in 1829 by Carey and Lea. Levasseur was secretary to General Lafayette during his journey. John D Godman made the English text, as the copyright entry states. That entry was filed on November 6, 1829.

Chapter One treats a Maryland cattle show and a Native deputation brought to the General. Lafayette's farewell tour of America fills the two volumes. Crowds, feasts, and visits in each state are set down day by day as the party saw them. The journal gives a French eye on American life fifty years after independence. Its value lies in close notes by a man at Lafayette's side throughout.
61812-from-midshipman-to-field-marshal:
From Midshipman to Field Marshal, by Evelyn Wood, was first published in London in October 1906, in two volumes. A fifth and cheaper edition in one volume followed in November 1907. Wood gives the story of his life to his comrades, past and present, of all ranks in both services.

A record of appointments and war services is printed at the front. Chapter two puts him in 1852 aboard a ship of a hundred and sixteen guns. Life on a man of war, the invasion of Crimea, and the siege of Sevastopol follow. A naked and starving army, and the assault of the Redan, fill the war chapters. Central India, the Mutiny, Ashanti, and staff college come later. Twenty nine pictures and maps go with the text. Readers get a Victorian soldier full career, from sea cadet to the top.
61922-on-the-lady-chapel-in-chester-cath:
On the Lady Chapel in Chester Cathedral is a paper by Canon Blomfield, read to the Chester archaeological society. The Courant Office printed the pamphlet at Chester in 1859. Blomfield treats the chapel as a prized sample of the Early English style. The chapel was then under repair and new painted decoration.

Rickman had praised the chapel's proportions, Blomfield notes. Yet its first windows were lost and side aisles marred it in the fifteenth century. Few close students had ever examined it in detail. New colour work by an artist famed at Salisbury drew fresh eyes to the fabric. Blomfield offers what history he could find of lady chapels in general. He warns that his matter may prove meagre, and gives it anyway.
61924-on-the-architectural-history-of-ch:
Thomas Rickman wrote a report on the building history of Chester Cathedral, read to a Chester society and printed in 1864. Canon Blomfield wrote a life sketch to go before it. The report sheet had been held in private hands for years and had never been in print before this issue.

Rickman was famed, the sketch says, for the clearest school book on Gothic building and for fixing the names of its styles. He took Early English and Decorated from earlier writers, yet gave each name real marks to rest on. The word Perpendicular was his own coinage, made for a style he was first to set out plainly.
62144-letter-to-the-friends-and-subscrib:
Letter to the Friends and Subscribers of the Church Pastoral-Aid Society, by Caleb Whitefoord, was printed in London in 1841 and sold for sixpence. Whitefoord was chaplain to the Infirmary of Saint James, Westminster, and domestic chaplain to the Duke of Roxburghe and the Marquess of Bute. A letter from Molesworth to the Bishop of Chester, alleging faults in the society, called forth the reply.

A synopsis of the society heads the pamphlet. Its object is the salvation of souls, by grants that help parish incumbents keep faithful assistants in their pastoral work. Its principles hold that a Christian land should fund the church's teaching for all. If the legislature fails in that duty, Christians must join to supply the lack. The letter defends the society's men and money against its critic.
62296-the-fly-leaf-no-1-vol-1-december-1:
Walter Blackburn Harte ran The Fly Leaf, a small monthly sheet of new thought from Boston. The copy here is part one of book one, dated December 1895. A single copy cost ten cents, and a year cost one dollar. Harte sought short, sharp pieces of not more than a short span of words.

The sheet bills itself as a place for the new man, the new woman, and new ideas. Harte vows to weigh all work with a fair eye. He says new writers with skill will find a warm welcome. The first piece, on the stir in books, mocks the dull sameness of most print of the day. It claims there is room for a bold, pert voice that dares to think. The issue is a small sign of a loud age in print.
62452-the-fly-leaf-no-3-vol-1-february-1:
The Fly Leaf, number three of volume one, for February 1896, is a small monthly paper of Boston. It calls itself a pamphlet periodical of the new: the new man, new woman, new ideas, whimsies and things. Walter Blackburn Harte conducts it, with picture notes by Russell. The price is a dollar a year, ten cents a number. Pages of praise from the press head this issue.

Footlights of Philadelphia calls the paper distinctive among all the little books of its kind. The Echo of Chicago calls it a keen little fighter. A Philadelphia daily holds it the only one of the lot that knows what it is driving at. The San Francisco Examiner bids anyone who would keep up with the writing world read it. The New York Commercial Advertiser calls it a bright little bundle of tales, talk, verse, and story.
62512-asneha-the-legend-of-the-opal:
Carlo de Fornaro made Asneha, the Legend of the Opal, writing both text and pictures, and it was published at New York in 1902 by Marcus and Company, jewelers of Fifth Avenue. A jeweler's book is a rare thing: a legend told to give a gem its soul. Verses from Baudelaire and a line from the Rig Veda stand at the front as mottoes.

In the land of Kasi there lived a poor musician and poet who had lost his flute in a village brawl. In the jungle a golden bird with emerald eyes sang to him and named him Asneha, bidding him cut a reed that would repeat its songs. The bird warns him to stay pure and shun the love of woman, and so conquer the world.
62548-no-xiii-or-the-story-of-the-lost-v:
Emma Marshall wrote No. XIII, or The Story of the Lost Vestal, issued at Leipzig in 1886 in the Tauchnitz collection of British authors. Her introduction explains the seed of the tale: diggers in the Roman Forum had lately found statues of the chief Vestal virgins, with inscriptions praising their virtues. On one pedestal alone the name was carefully erased. That woman is known only as Number Thirteen.

Marshall supposes the rest. She takes up the guess that the lost Vestal became a Christian and that her conversion was found out. Someone in power, she supposes, chose to wipe her name from memory while her virtues stayed in stone. The story ties her fate to the persecution and martyrdom of the early church, first in Britain and then in Rome. Marshall wrote the tale for young readers. Readers get historical fiction built on a real puzzle of stone.
62590-guarding-his-goal:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote Guarding His Goal, a school story novel printed in 1917 and tied to his Yardley Hall books. The hero is Toby Tucker, a boy at a boarding school who runs a small clothes cleaning and pressing trade from his room in Whitson Hall. A front plate shows Toby pale and crouched, watching, and hints at the goal he guards.

The contents list points to school terms, a capture, Christmas days, first practice, and scholarship awards. Later chapters bring a marked coin, a gray card, a pair of gloves, and talks with the captain and coach. Sports, school honor, and a boy's small business carry the plot.
62655-recipes-from-american-national:
Recipes from American National is a cookbook of cakes, pies, icings, and pastries, many of them heirloom pieces handed down through generations, as its short preface says. It opens with an Orange Nut Cake of butter, buttermilk, raisins, pecans, and orange, iced with orange and lemon icing. Next comes a pie that is different, a date nut puddin'-pie that makes its own crust.

Annabel's Prune Cake follows, with its sour cream prune filling, and an Apple Nut Pita, also called Pita Sa Orasima, built on a rich yolk dough with a walnut filling. The measures are plain cups and teaspoons, the ovens mostly 350 degrees, and the manner friendly and unpolished. The charm of the book is its trust that the reader cooks already and needs only the bones of each dish.
62994-craters-of-the-moon-a-guide-to-cra:
Craters of the Moon is the National Park Service guide to Craters of the Moon National Monument in Idaho, issued at Washington in 1991 as handbook 139. The Park Service's publications office made it. A page on using the book lays out its plan in three parts.

Part one presents the park and tells of its early exploration. Part two treats how life has fitted itself to the volcanic ground, and how people have seen that strange land. Part three gives plain travel and reference matter for touring and camping. The handbook series, with over one hundred titles in print, serves the more than 350 sites of the park system and is sold at parks and by mail.
63006-by-ways-on-service-notes-from-an-a:
Hector Dinning wrote these war sketches, printed by Constable of London in 1918 as notes from an Australian journal. Dinning gives the book to Australia. A note warns that the pieces were not written as a book. Most first ran in daily papers or other journals, and friends, not the writer, pushed for collecting them.

He calls the set rough and broken, no full picture of an Australian's war. It holds what struck one limited outlook, written first for a small circle of friends. Egypt and the Canal Zone sit beside Gallipoli and the fighting of 1917 in France. Dinning fears the early pieces may seem light beside Picardy, but he prints them as the record of what one Anzac saw.
63469-washington-confidential:
Washington Confidential is an exposé of the American capital by Jack Lait and Lee Mortimer, authors of New York Confidential and Chicago Confidential, published by Crown in 1951. The book promises a behind-the-scenes tour of Washington in two parts, the places and the people, written in the breathless slang of the scandal sheet.

The contents tour the tenderloin, three flophouses, Chinatown, and the government as landlord. The people chapters promise government girls, company girls, and the little red herrings of the political world. The book's period slang is now as much evidence about 1951 as its facts.
63663-survival:
Basil Wells wrote the tale Survival for Planet Stories. The magazine ran it in spring 1946. Mindless things mewled in Ohio streets, the blurb says. Men woke in Venus's swampy hell instead. An ego-moving experiment opens the catastrophe. Doctor Brixson built a machine to transplant souls.

Circuits shorted in a blast of power at the test. Brixson and his aide Elmer Morgus died there. The blast ring spread a mile from Crayton College. Egos tore free and rode the wave to Venus. Mindless bodies grovelled in Crayton's streets at home. The ship Malcolm reached Venus in later years. Rubbery Venusians aboard her told the full truth. Earth minds in alien bodies fight to live there. Body-swap pulp at its wildest strands midwestern minds in swamp beasts under a strange sun.
6404-more-pages-from-a-journal:
Mark Rutherford, in a 1910 Oxford volume, offers more pages from a journal with other papers, dedicated to Horace and Susan E. P. Smith as an inadequate acknowledgement of a great debt. A bad dream, Esther, Kate Radcliffe, and Mr. Whittaker's retirement open the contents, with confessions of a self tormentor, letters to the Rambler and from the authoress of Judith Crowhurst, and a clearing up after a January storm.

The end of the north wind, Romney Marsh, Axmouth, and the preacher and the sea follow. Conversion, July, a Sunday morning in November, Beachy Head in December, dreaming, ourselves, and the riddle come next. A later paper tells of a manager who was the pivot of his firm, until illness and a wife's death let junior partners divide his work. Rutherford writes quiet, inward prose, where a dream or a marsh walk carries a life's moral weight.
64175-distress-signal:
Ross Rocklynne's Distress Signal ran in Planet Stories for spring 1947. The headnote states the choice: marooned on the cold satellite of a dying sun, for Rex there was only one escape, but Carl called it murder. Carl Wyant and Rex Oberling ran away from home as boys, stealing a ride in an interstellar ship from the Space Council. A month's jaunt stretched past Centauri, four and a half light-years out, as star after star beckoned.

The alarm went throughout the known universe for two boys on the loose, and Carl, expert at Morse code, read the wild signals. Years passed on Worta, circling its dying red star, the boys living in the tunnels the Wortans drove beneath the crust. Sol is thirty-five light-years away. Rocklynne's tale is a Robinsonade of runaways grown old in exile, facing one terrible way home.
6452-right-royal:
John Masefield's Right Royal is a poem whose persons, horses, and events are imaginary, with no reference to any living person or horse. An hour before the race, lovers Charles Cothill and the golden lady Em talk in mild March weather. He is from Sleins, a manor up the Lithe, made stalwart, springy, and swift by riding the Downs, with dark honest eyes, a fine firm mouth, and wind tan on his skin.

He is to ride Right Royal, his own horse, in the English Chaser's Cup on Compton Course, colours under a pale coat reaching to his spurs. A mid passage shows Em cheering him, proud to see him followed by all the crowd, picking Right Royal, Soyland, and Peterkin first, second, and third. Masefield writes racing as romance, where a horse, a rider, and a lover's faith carry a whole spring afternoon.
65136-the-cathedral:
James Russell Lowell published this long poem at Boston with Fields, Osgood, and Company in 1870. He dedicated it to his publisher and friend Fields in a letter from Cambridge dated November 29, 1869. A motto from the Bacchae of Euripides stands at its head in Greek. The front pages list Lowell's other writings, from the complete poems to The Biglow Papers and The Vision of Sir Launfal.

The poem opens far through memory, on a happy day cloudless of care that seems farther off than Homer's time, before the child had loudened to the boy. Lowell recalls how a recluse child, kept perforce from playmates, found companionship in things that neither denied nor granted themselves wholly, as is nature's wont. Those first sweet frauds upon the senses, blending the sensual with its imaged world, lead the poem toward the cathedral and the thoughts it raises.
65286-prairie-farmer-vol-56-no-5-februar:
Prairie Farmer, volume 56, number 5, for Saturday, February 2, 1884, is one issue of the Chicago weekly journal for the farm, orchard, and fireside. The paper was founded in 1841. One year cost two dollars in advance.

The contents list farm pieces on fresh meat for the farm, a farmers talk society, botany for farm boys, and the use of salt. Woven paling fences, the Illinois State Fair, and a letter from central Kansas follow. Garden pieces treat the farmer garden, future orchards, and the basket willow. Poultry notes ask what ails the pullets and tell of a duck farm. Bee notes treat corn silk protection and feeding back. Poems, humor, live stock notes, and household pages fill the rest. Farm history fans get one full week of prairie print.
65370-the-mannion-court-martial:
The Mannion Court-Martial, a science fiction tale by Randall Garrett, ran in Imagination in 1957. A blurb asks why a space officer would lead an android rebellion at all. Even Mannion believed he was guilty as they gave him the supreme penalty. Lieutenant Dan Mannion of the Earth Space Patrol stands in the prisoner dock.

He grips the rail of his cubicle so hard his fingers hurt in the scene. Commander Harkness, presiding, glares at him sternly from the bench of the court. The charges are severe, and total memory erasure waits if he is found guilty. Is there anything to say in his own defence before the trial, he is asked. His wife Virginia pale and tense face watches from the military courtroom. Guilt, androids, and a rigged memory drive this Garrett courtroom tale.
65511-this-then-is-upland-pastures-being:
Adeline Knapp wrote This Then Is Upland Pastures, a book of outdoor essays. The Roycroft Printing Shop in East Aurora, New York, printed it in 1897. Only six hundred copies were made, each signed and numbered. The essays treat the fair things that spring and summer bring.

The opening essay greets the first warm rains. Young grass mantles the meadows with tender green. The woods stand cool, dripping, dim, and delicious. Knapp says spring growth is frank and confiding early on. Roots, bulbs, leaves, and buds show their secrets freely. A few weeks later all will be too busy for visits. The season's swift march will claim them. Hope, she writes, comes with spring without fail, and stirs our purest impulses.
65538-the-13th-immortal:
The Thirteenth Immortal is a science tale by Robert Silverberg, put out as a cheap paper book at New York in the late nineteen fifties. A note at the front tells that a long hunt found no proof its rights were made new in law. The book is made out to a named friend of the author.

Its back frame, set at the head, gives the hook. A strange man asks a youth who his father was. The youth can not recall: his past is a blank wall. He knows one thing, that the key to his life lies in Antarctica. That lost land, once ice, is now a warm Eden ringed by a wall no man can pass. To reach it is death on the roads of the Americas.
65540-youth-vol-i-no-6-august-1902-an-il:
Youth, a monthly journal for boys and girls, issued its August 1902 number in Philadelphia. Single copies cost ten cents and a year costs one dollar. Ida Waugh drew the frontispiece, Polly's Letter. Frank Coleburn leads with A Battle with a Windmill, drawn from winery life.

A serial on Washington at Valley Forge and a serial called Little Polly Prentiss run side by side. Mary Lane's higher education, a daughter of the forest, and how plants live fill the mid pages. Puzzles in an old trunk, parlor magic, wood folk talk, and notes on the oldest colleges close the number. The journal mixes tales, facts, and indoor and outdoor fun for its young readers.
65775-the-cry-for-justice-an-anthology-o:
An anthology of social protest edited by Upton Sinclair, published in 1915. Jack London wrote the introduction. Selections come from twenty-five languages across five thousand years. Philosophers, poets, novelists, and reformers all contribute. Reproductions of protest art illustrate the pages. Sinclair published this edition himself at New York and Pasadena.

A Los Angeles doctor bought the plates to make the edition possible. His requested dedication honours the poor and obscure. Their dimes and quarters, he wrote, keep the movement going. Publisher lists in front credit borrowed pieces house by house. Frank Norris, Helen Keller, and Vachel Lindsay appear among hundreds. Sinclair had shaken America with The Jungle a decade earlier. This anthology gave the protest tradition a single shelf.
6597-perpetual-light-a-memorial:
William Rose Benét writes a memorial in verse for a woman now gone, whose face, he says, is no longer of this world. The epigraph speaks of a man without wings who rejoiced in a companion God gave him, and who heard her sigh with her head on his shoulder. Grief here is bitter as myrrh, yet lit by faith in a festival of perpetual light.

Dedicated to Kathleen and Margaret, the poems ask readers to think not of verse, but of her alone, and of the light she left on stone. Benét keeps the language tender and high, with day and night made bright by her memory. Perpetual Light is a short, moving book of mourning, where love outlasts loss.
66258-raw-material:
Dorothy Canfield wrote Raw Material, a book of stories published by Harcourt, Brace and Company at New York in 1923. Her earlier books are listed at the front: The Squirrel-Cage, The Bent Twig, Understood Betsy, and The Brimming Cup among them. Twenty stories fill the volume. The title story opens it, and Uncle Giles follows. Old Man Warner, Fairfax Hunter, and Professor Paul Meyer stand in the early run.

Scylla and Charybdis, Art Atmosphere, and Colonel Shays come midway. A Great Love, Supply and Demand, and Uncle Ellis follow. God's Country, Inheritance, and October 1918 close toward the end. A Breton Among Hsu Hsi stands last but one. The title story opens with a family tale: her clergyman grandfather preached his best sermons silently to himself, sitting under another man's pulpit.
66791-the-city-of-the-saints-and-across-:
Richard F Burton wrote The City of the Saints and Across the Rocky Mountains to California, issued at New York in 1862 by Harper and Brothers. Burton had writ The Lake Regions of Central Africa. A front print shows Great Salt Lake City from the north. Two quotes on cant and on fanaticism head the book.

Burton crossed the plains to the Mormon city and went on to California. The head quote from Montesinos warns that America is in danger from religious fanaticism. New states give no faith teaching, it says. Wild superstition may grow in that gap, it warns. A new prophet might carve a kingdom with faith as his weapon, it holds. Burton's own eye is sharp and dry as he tests such fears on the road. Pictures aid the travel tale.
66890-a-square-deal:
A Square Deal, by Theodore Roosevelt, was compiled in 1906. The Allendale Press issued it at Allendale, New Jersey. Markley held the copyright and shaped the book. Its matter is drawn from the President's many addresses. Passages are sorted under heads, one idea to a section. A new photogravure portrait fronts the volume. Ideals of citizenship open the list. The dignity of labour and the workingman follow. Labour unions, the business man, and success in life come next. Education and the school teacher stand midway. Parenthood, great riches, and the farmer take their turns.

The trusts, the South, and lynch law close one group. Immigration, corruption, and the Monroe Doctrine end the list. Ware's poem on the lasting book is printed at the front.
66901-ancient-rome-and-modern-america-a-:
Ancient Rome and Modern America is a comparative study of morals and manners by Guglielmo Ferrero. Putnam published it in New York and London in 1914. Ferrero also wrote The Greatness and Decline of Rome. This copy is the third impression. A publisher's note explains its place beside his next book, Between the Old World and the New.

The two works came out in reverse order for English readers, at the author's wish. Part one opens with the question: what is progress? Ferrero, an Italian historian, measures American wealth, family life, and manners against the Roman world he knew best. The book reads America through the lens of Rome's rise and fall.
67164-the-crime-of-henry-vane-a-study-wi:
The Crime of Henry Vane, a study with a moral, was published by Scribner's Sons in New York in 1884 under a pen name. Its author had earlier written Guerndale. The story opens in a smoking-room of the Columbian Club in New York, after a dinner for a friend about to marry.

The talk turns to Henry Vane, and every man present damns him without a dissenting voice. Yet when John asks who knows Vane personally, no one does. Each has heard the story at second hand for ten years, from a brother, a friend, or a lady of their set. John undertakes to give the correct and only version. The frame raises the book's moral at once: how a crowd can condemn a man on gossip alone.
67298-stormy-misty-s-foal:
Stormy, Misty Foal, by Marguerite Henry, was printed by Rand McNally in 1963, with plates by Wesley Dennis. Henry gives the book to the boys and girls whose coins helped restore the wild herds on Assateague Island. Their love gave courage to the folk of Chincoteague after a storm.

Early chapters build the storm, with a duck in the horse trough and ninety head of wild ponies at risk. The sea takes over the low island, and Paul goes to the rescue. Later heads name refugees, a backyard landing by helicopter, and Misty trip to Pocomoke. The close stands within the foaling box, then home at last. Horse fans get a true storm tale of the famed Chincoteague ponies.
67455-rebuttal:
Rebuttal is a science fiction story by Betsy Curtis, printed in Infinity magazine in June nineteen fifty six. The editors frame it as an answer to Arthur Clarke's famed story The Star. Clarke's tale, they say, was the hit of their first issue and much argued over. Curtis offers the other side of that question, plus one fresh idea.

A strange sickness strikes the crew of the Phoenix Nebula expedition on their return. Father Phillip Burt, a priest among them, is its worst sufferer by far. He lies at Saint Luke's hospital in pain no drug can calm for long. Father Molina, the hospital's head pathologist, runs cultures and cuts tissue samples. What he finds in the priest's flesh sends him hurrying up to the ward. Quarantine seals the wing while the two priests face each other.
67597-bantu-folk-lore-medical-and-genera:
Bantu Folk Lore (Medical and General), published at Cape Town, is Matthew Hewat's record of the healing customs of the Bantu peoples. Hewat worked for some time in the border districts of the Cape Colony. He saw that the old native ways were fading fast under colonial rule. Teachers, civil servants and missionaries helped him gather what remained.

Chapters describe the Bantu tribes, their doctors and their daily practice. Surgery, midwifery and the care of children each get a full treatment. Hammond Tooke wrote the chapter on the Bantu nation. Herb treatment of disease gets close attention, since plant cures formed the core of the old medicine.
67650-tales-of-the-samurai-stories-illus:
Asataro Miyamori told tales of the samurai to show bushido, the moral code of Japanese knights. The Kyo-Bun-Kwan issued the book at Tokyo in 1920. Miyamori taught English at Toyo University in Tokyo. Eight colored pictures by a Japanese artist grace the set.

Eight tales run from Ungo-Zenji to Honest Kyusuke, with revenge and loyalty at their heart. The first tale finds Date Masamune gazing at snow from a castle pavilion. A sandal bearer waits in the cold while his lord muses on rich harvests. Readers gain brave, grave tales that teach honor, duty, and calm in death.
67704-doctors-an-address-delivered-to-th:
Doctors, an address by Rudyard Kipling, was delivered to the students of the medical school of the Middlesex Hospital on October 1, 1908. Macmillan published it the same year in London and New York. The book was sold for the benefit of the hospital. A photograph of Kipling and a view of a hospital ward go with the text.

A preface from the hospital tells of its cancer wing and its rules: treatment only by staff, all remedies disclosed, and the patient's consent first. It recalls past trials of cures, one man exposed as a fraud at once, another's compression treatment praised by patients yet found to hasten the end. Against that ground Kipling speaks to the young doctors on their calling.
67734-landmarks-medical-and-surgical:
Luther Holden wrote Landmarks, Medical and Surgical, a guide to points on the live body that guide a surgeon’s hand. J and A Churchill issued the third edition in London in eighteen hundred eighty one. Holden had led the Royal College of Surgeons. James Shuter helped him with the text.

Holden chose to use no drawings at all. He wants the eye and hand to learn touch on a sound body. Needles through flesh fixed the marks for chest and belly, he says. Chapters move from head and face down to foot and hand. Two short parts treat checks made through the body’s lower paths. Students at Saint Bartholomew’s Hospital first used the notes in its reports.
68008-venus-equilateral:
Venus Equilateral gathers the science fiction stories of George Smith, first printed in Astounding between 1942 and 1945. The Prime Press issued the book at Philadelphia in 1947 and reprinted it in 1949. John Campbell, the magazine's editor, wrote the introduction. Smith dedicates the book to James Clerk Maxwell, whose equations founded electronics, and to his own son, who may some day work at the station.

The tales centre on Venus Equilateral, a relay station in space. Engineers there keep the interplanetary beams clear, fight pirates of the beam, and solve problems of power and signalling. Story titles include QRM Interplanetary, where QRM is the code for man made interference. Calling the Empress, Recoil, Off the Beam, and Beam Pirate follow. Smith wrote as an engineer, and his heroes fix the future with slide rules and circuits. The book is a landmark of hard science fiction.
6817-chaitanya-and-the-vaishnava-poets-o:
John Beames studies Chaitanya and the Vaishnava poets of Bengal in a paper from the Indian Antiquary of 1873, on Bengali poetry of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The Padkalpataru, or wish-granting tree of song, may be taken as the scriptures of the Vaishnava sect in Bengal, he explains. It is a collection of songs by many poets in many ages. They are arranged to show the sect's views in full.

Put together in recent times, the collection spans devotion, love, and theology in lyric form. Beames writes as a scholar of language and faith. Chaitanya and the Vaishnava Poets of Bengal is a learned, early guide to a rich devotional poetry.
68394-the-trouvelot-astronomical-drawing:
Trouvelot published his Astronomical Drawings Manual with Scribner at New York in 1882. He had worked at the Harvard College Observatory and led a government eclipse party in 1878. Fifteen plates reproduce his drawings, made by Armstrong at the Riverside Press. Sun spots observed June 17, 1875 lead the list of plates.

Solar protuberances, the total eclipse at Creston in 1878, and the aurora follow in order. Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn each hold a dated plate from his own watching. The great comet of 1881, November meteors, the Milky Way, and Orion's nebula close the set. Text gives the sun's distance as 92,000,000 miles in plain figures. Art and exact watching share a sky atlas.
68553-the-festival:
The Festival, by H P Lovecraft, author of Dagon and The Rats in the Walls, opens with an epigraph from Lactantius in Latin. The narrator is far from home, with the spell of the eastern sea upon him, hearing it pound on the rocks in twilight.

It is the Yuletide, which men call Christmas, though they know in their hearts it is older than Bethlehem and Babylon, older than Memphis and mankind. His fathers called him to the old town beyond, where his people kept festival in the elder time when festival was forbidden. They commanded their sons to keep festival once every century, so the memory of primal secrets would not be forgotten. He is the only one who came back that night, for only the poor and the lonely remember.
69078-post-mortem-essays-historical-and-:
MacLaurin, lecturer in surgery at the University of Sydney, wrote these post-mortem essays for Doran. Titian's portrait of the Emperor Charles the Fifth fronts the book, whose method is a surgeon's: take the dead, read their records, and diagnose. The case of Anne Boleyn opens the volume. There is something Greek in her tragedy, MacLaurin says, akin to Oedipus and Thyestes.

Henry, Catherine, and Anne, he argues, can all be explained with medical knowledge and insight, once the bowdlerized sketches are set aside. The problem of Jeanne d'Arc follows, then the Empress Theodora and Charles. Don John of Austria comes with Cervantes and Don Quixote, and Philip the Second gets the arterio-sclerosis of statesmen. Pepys and his wife, Gibbon, Marat, Napoleon, and Cellini fill the round. A final essay is Death itself, and retrospective diagnosis, a parlor game with a scalpel, is one MacLaurin plays in earnest.
70076-the-tusayan-ritual:
The Tusayan Ritual, a study of the influence of environment on aboriginal cults by J Walter Fewkes, came from the Smithsonian Report for 1895. The Government Printing Office issued it at Washington in 1896, with four plates. Fewkes first gave the paper as a Saturday lecture at the United States National Museum in May 1896. Tusayan is the old name for the Hopi country.

Fewkes opens with a plea for the wide study of religion. Ethnology, he says, must take in the beliefs of all peoples, low and high in the scale. To build laws of religion from a few gifted races alone must fail, as a law of language built on one tongue would fail. He then reads the rites of the Tusayan people against the dry land that shaped them.
7066-under-the-prophet-in-utah-the-natio:
Frank Cannon, formerly United States senator from Utah, with Harvey O'Higgins, warns of a political priestcraft in Under the Prophet in Utah. Contents run from the days of the raid and a mission to Washington, through without a country, the manifesto, and the road to freedom, to the goal and after. First betrayals, the church and the interests, and the crossways lead to the downward path and the will of the Lord.

The conspiracy completed, the Smoot exposure, treason triumphant, and the struggle for liberty follow, with the price of protest, the new polygamy, and the prophet of Mammon. A note recalls O'Higgins meeting Cannon in Denver in spring 1910, while working with Judge Lindsey on The Beast and the Jungle. The book is a Progressive era charge against church rule in politics.
70690-trial-of-john-jasper-lay-precentor:
Trial of John Jasper for the Murder of Edwin Drood is a verbatim report of a mock trial. Chapman and Hall published it at London in 1914 from shorthand notes. The hearing took place in the King Hall at Covent Garden on 7 January 1914. Justice Gilbert Keith Chesterton sat with a special jury for the case.

The Dickens Fellowship, London branch, put on the event for its members. Jasper, lay precentor of Cloisterham Cathedral, stands charged with the murder of Edwin Drood. Dickens left that murder unsolved when his last novel broke off at his death. Cuming Walters and Matz appear as counsel for the prosecution in the cast list. Dickens fans staged in earnest play the trial the novel never reached.
