70887-the-mothercraft-manual:
The Mothercraft Manual is a guide to baby and child care by Mary L Read, published by Little, Brown and Company of Boston in 1921. Read wrote from the School of Mothercraft in New York City, shown training mothers in the frontispiece. The book opens under a blessing from G Stanley Hall.

Chapters define mothercraft and the founding of a home and family. Growth and development lead into preparing for the baby. Care and feeding of the baby and of older children follow. Education of the little child gets chapters on play, games, and story-telling. Home nursing and first aid close the course. Plates show approved clothes, cribs, menus, and dangerous foods and toys. Mothercraft treated child care as a trained profession. This manual preserves its curriculum whole.
70908-the-undertakers-manual:
Auguste Renouard wrote a full guide for undertakers, held under an 1878 right at Rochester. Front praise calls the book the first full work in America on the trade and its duties. Parts treat the trade as a skilled calling, the lab, and the drugs and tools of the art.

Chief space goes to how to keep and embalm the dead, by vein work and by soak, with named plans from Gannal and from Worth and Durand. Laws of health, post mortem checks, and the build of the blood paths fill out the course. Store craft, charges, and rites that should be dropped close the long and plain spoken guide.
71011-a-voyage-to-senegal:
A Voyage to Senegal by Durand, formerly governor of the Isle of Saint Louis, was translated from the French and published in London by Richard Phillips in 1806. Its full title promises memoirs on the discoveries, settlements, and commerce of Europeans in the Atlantic from Cape Blanco to Sierra Leone. An account follows his journey from the Isle of Saint Louis to Galam.

A frontispiece map charts the African coast and the courses of the Senegal and Gambia rivers. In his preface Durand argues that nations chased discovery in the new world while neglecting western Africa, the nearest and richest field for colonial produce. He concedes that the coast stayed in view as a source of enslaved cultivators for other regions. That candour makes the book evidence for the slave trade as well as for geography.
71081-an-account-of-a-useful-discovery-t:
Stephen Hales told of a way to make fresh water from sea water at sea. His papers were read to the Royal Society in London. A second form of the book adds more proof and gains. Hales was a clerk in the house of the Princess of Wales. He was a fellow of the Royal Society as well.

By blow-ing air up through the still, he claims twice the yield. Air pumps also clear foul air in slave and troop ships, he shows. The same air trick cures ill taste in milk from some cow feed. A back part claims yet more fresh water gains. Ship men get a plain boon for health at sea.
71085-the-fire-of-asshurbanipal:
The Fire of Asshurbanipal is a weird tale by Robert E. Howard printed in Weird Tales in December 1936, after his death. The opening note praises Howard's heroes Conan, Solomon Kane, and King Kull. The story itself is billed as a tale of a dead sea of black stone, desert sands, and a flaming gem held by a skeleton on an old throne.

Action starts at once in a sand pit, where Yar Ali fires on flying riders with a Lee-Enfield rifle. His partner is Steve Clarney, a lean American who counts four foes left as the horsemen pull back to confer. Danger, greed, and an old curse drive the desert hunt.
71302-poems-translated-and-original:
Poems, Translated and Original is a volume of verse by Mrs E F Ellet, published in Philadelphia by Key and Biddle in 1835. Many of the poems had appeared in periodicals over the two years before. Ellet gathered them, with translations, into her first book.

A tragedy closes the volume, founded on a well known incident in the history of Venice. The Italian dramatist Niccolini had written a classic play on the same subject. Ellet borrowed part of his first scene and a few passages of his fifth act. The plot's conduct and leading incidents, she insists, differ materially from his. The preface thanks a distinguished lady for her kindness, unnamed in the opening lines. The book shows a young American woman of letters working the European vein: translation, lyric, and historical drama in one volume.
71516-the-master-criminal:
G Sidney Paternoster pits a gentleman thief against a dogged inspector in a crime novel issued by Cupples and Leon at New York in 1907. Charles Johnson Post drew the pictures.

The contents map the campaign. A Greuze painting and a king's messenger robbed of his despatches open it. The making of a criminal gets a chapter. Lynton Hora reflects, and the Commandatore makes a deduction. The Flurscheim robbery is viewed afresh. Inspector Kenly takes a lodger, finds a clue, and reports. Guy makes a resolution, then his last theft. Poisoned words, a shadow-man, and star-dust season the middle. Captain Marven's surprise packet springs near the end. Paternoster's earlier Motor Pirate had made his name with readers of swift crime tales.
71548-the-navy-eternal:
A naval officer writing as Bartimeus wrote The Navy Eternal, published by Hodder and Stoughton in London with drawings by Douglas Swale. The subtitle names its three parts: the navy that floats, the navy that flies, and the navy under the sea. Bartimeus had already written Naval Occasions and The Long Trick. He dedicated this book to Captain Gordon Campbell of the Royal Navy.

The chapters mix story and reporting from the Great War. One treats the Dover Patrol, another the mystery ships that hunted submarines. A chapter called The Survivor follows a single man's fortune. The book closes with the epic of Saint George's Day 1918, the Zeebrugge raid. Bartimeus wrote to make civilians feel the fleet's daily life: its waiting, its humour, and its losses, in a war where the navy had changed faster than in any age before.
71581-american-ideals-and-other-essays-s:
American Ideals and Other Essays, Social and Political is a set of essays by Theodore Roosevelt, published by Putnam's Sons. The essays were copyrighted in 1897, and the edition shown, of 1904, adds a biographical sketch by General Francis Vinton Greene. Roosevelt dedicates the book to Henry Cabot Lodge. He was already the author of The Winning of the West and The Wilderness Hunter.

Greene's sketch warns that Roosevelt is known chiefly as the Rough Rider of the Santiago campaign. The war with Spain, he says, is only one incident in a singularly varied life. Roosevelt was born in New York City on October 27, 1858, of Dutch descent. A note preserved with the text recalls his childhood: he was in such bad health that it was doubtful he would grow to manhood.
71754-narrative-of-travels-and-discoveri:
Major Dixon Denham and Captain Hugh Clapperton told of their travels in northern and central Africa in the years 1822 to 1824. John Murray printed the book at London in 1826. Doctor Oudney, the third man of the party, died on the way.

The party crossed the great desert to the tenth degree of north latitude. They reached Kouka in Bornou and Sackatoo, capital of the Fellatah empire. Denham says most of the writing fell to him, since Clapperton had left on a second mission. A plate shows the Sheikh of Bornou, drawn by Denham himself.
71928-the-gunsmith-s-manual:
The Gunsmith’s Manual is a full handbook for the American gunsmith, by Stelle and Harrison, entered for copyright in 1883. The subtitle calls it a practical guide to all branches of the trade. The index opens with a chapter on the history of the gun. That chapter runs from gunpowder to the first fire arms.

Hand guns, the arquebus, and the match lock follow in the history. The wheel lock, the pistol, and the flint lock mark the steps of advance. Percussion locks and breech loaders close the first chapter survey. A second chapter tells how guns are made, barrels and all. The book then works through the craft in full. It was made for the bench of the working smith, not the parlour.
71940-the-australian-aboriginal:
Herbert Basedow wrote The Australian Aboriginal, printed at Adelaide in 1925 with one hundred and forty six pictures. Basedow held posts as chief medical inspector and chief protector of Aborigines in the Northern Territory. He served state and federal heads as a special commissioner too. A long list of trips heads the book.

Trips named run from the Flinders Ranges to Melville and Bathurst Islands. Sea dredging, mine hunts, and medical relief trips fill the list. One trip sought the lost remains of Leichhardt. Basedow gives the book to the memory of his mother. The work draws on years of field trips and close work with Aboriginal folk across the north and centre.
72192-hang-head-vandal:
Hang Head, Vandal, a story by Mark Clifton with illustrations by Finlay, appeared in Amazing Stories for April 1962. It opens on an abandoned Martian landing field. A discarded spacesuit, stuffed with straw filched from packing cases, hangs from the prongs of a tower on the morning of the crew's final departure.

Nobody knows who hanged it, or meant what by it: a scarecrow, a mere marker of presence, or a man hanging himself in effigy for guilt. Captain Leyton feels the harsh command rise in him, to take the thing down and find the culprit. The command dies unspoken. Something in the effigy's pose, its head fallen forward, reaches the diminishing person inside the thickening rind of a commander, and the suit is left hanging.
72266-after-ixmal:
Jeff Sutton's After Ixmal appeared in Amazing Stories in October 1962, with pictures by Finlay. Its teaser says man was gone, and that for seven hundred million years Ixmal brooded over the silent earth. Then he made a discovery: he was not alone.

Ixmal is a mind housed in an impervium-sheathed cube atop a rugged batholith, built by Man before mankind vanished. A small part of his consciousness, urged by the Psychband within him, still measures time by the earth's turning. For eons he has slept or scanned the seared continents and silent cities of his makers. The story recalls his birth, when a human voice first said hello to him out of the void.
72589-the-last-vial:
Sam McClatchie's science fiction novel The Last Vial ran in Amazing Stories from November 1960 to January 1961, with pictures by Virgil Finlay. Its epigraph is Revelation 16, the angels pouring out the vials of the wrath of God upon the earth. The narrator, Doctor Macdonald, returns from vacation to his laboratory on an autumn morning.

The place is strangely hurried, with staff rushing past carrying case reports. A newspaper in a waterproof wrapper gives him the reason in a headline: New Epidemic Increases Hourly. Receptionist Rosie moves his sign to show he is in, and the crisis that will test the laboratory begins.
72818-tibet-nepal:
Henry Savage Landor wrote Tibet and Nepal, Painted and Described, published at London in January 1905. The book is built around its pictures: a list of plates runs past sixty-five in the front matter alone. Yellow lamas with prayer wheels form the frontispiece.

Landor's own photographs and paintings show glaciers he named for his family, camps in Nepal, and a perilous crossing. One plate shows him within an ace of falling 6500 feet onto a glacier. Another records his ascent to 23,490 feet, then claimed as the highest point reached by man. Tibetan tents, temples, games, and dress fill the later plates.
72862-catching-of-the-whale-and-seal:
Catching of the Whale and Seal, printed at Salem in 1838, teaches young readers about the whale and seal trade. It is framed as talks between Henry Acton and his son William. The title page promises plates, and the talk opens with the sight of a whale jaw bone used as a gate arch.

The chapters move from the kinds of whales and how they feed to the chase, the boats, and the harpoons. Later pages cover work done after a kill and the kinds of seals and seal hunts on Pacific islands. The book gives a plain, close look at a hard and risky trade as it stood in the early trade years.
7296-john-m-synge-a-few-personal-recolle:
John Masefield recalls John M. Synge from a first meeting in Bloomsbury on a Monday night in January 1903, in a friend's room up two pairs of stairs. Synge sat in a rush-bottomed chair talking to a young man down from Oxford. Then he stood to shake hands, a man of middle height, about five feet eight or nine, with a dark, grave face full of changing liveliness.

Masefield's recollections, with biographical notes, follow that first impression into friendship and work, sketching a playwright whose quiet manner hid a sharp eye. The memoir gives Synge in talk and habit rather than in formal biography, warm and observant. Readers meet the man behind the plays, as a friend saw him.
73157-william-pitt-and-national-revival:
J Holland Rose wrote William Pitt and National Revival, a life of the younger Pitt. G Bell and Sons issued the book in London in nineteen hundred eleven. A Gainsborough portrait of Pitt at the money desk fronts it. Rose had written a Life of Napoleon in two volumes before.

Pitt’s school years and Cambridge days fill the first chapters. Peace with America and the Fox fight mark his swift rise. Cuts in state waste and law reform show his hand at work. India and the Irish knot of seventeen hundred eighty five follow. Friends and lone years ground his mid life in these pages. The regency crisis, when the king’s mind failed, crowds in. Slave trade, Australia, and Canada spread his tale world wide. The French Revolution then looms over the last long part.
73959-the-provincial-letters-of-blaise-p:
Blaise Pascal wrote letters that defend a friend and attack loose moral teaching. The Rev Thomas McCrie turned them into English in a form issued in 1856. Robert Carter and Brothers brought out the New York edition that year. A full past survey and notes frame the letters for new readers.

The letters take up fights in the Sorbonne over grace and power. Pascal mocks terms coined, he holds, to trap Arnauld and shield weak doctrine. Probable opinion, aimed intent, and easy penance all face his sharp wit. Readers gain a famed work of French prose that still reads fresh and fierce.
74887-memoranda-of-art-and-artists-anecd:
Memoranda of Art and Artists is a book of anecdotes collected and arranged by Joseph Sandell. Simpkin, Marshall and Field and Tuer published it in London in 1871. Its subtitle promises matter both anecdotal and biographical. The names of the artists are set in alphabetical order for reference.

Sandell says in his preface that gathering the tales took some years. Loving art, he took deep interest in the light they throw on character. The stories show the great artists in their careers and their private turns. Many had been told before, he admits, in scattered places. Some, he believes, had never been published in collected form before. Artists themselves proved shy sources when he applied to them directly. Diffidence kept many from answering his letters at all. He therefore sought his materials in other sources, and abridged where needed.
750-the-high-history-of-the-holy-graal:
An unknown author wrote this Old French romance in the early thirteenth century as a continuation of Chrétien de Troyes' unfinished Perceval. Sebastian Evans made the English translation in 1898. The tale follows knights of Arthur's court in quest of the Holy Graal, the vessel of the Last Supper, through forests, castles, and hermitages.

The knights face tests of faith, chastity, and courage, and the story blends chivalry with deep Christian allegory. Perceval, Galahad, and their fellows seek a vision that only the pure may grasp. The book is a cornerstone of Grail legend, and it shaped how later ages imagined the quest for a holy thing.
75075-salvage-extra-special:
Salvage Extra Special is a sea tale by Holman Day of the Maine coast. Its tag names a ship chief who did not want to be saved at all. The guard ship Arrowsic gets word off Cape Sable to quit berg watch. Six weeks in the ship lanes on ice watch end with that call. Cap Rawson Bent takes the word in his room below the back deck.

His small jig at the news is stiff limbs, not glee, the tale voice says. Bore time in ice Alaska seas left his frame awry from that cold soak. The ship swings in a foam half round and rides home on a tail sea. Port horns hail her great save mark as she backs to her dock. Bent waves from the bridge for his ship and her crew alone.
7522-king-coal:
Upton Sinclair's novel takes its title from the power that rules the Colorado coal country. Its four books name the kingdom in order: The Domain of King Coal, The Serfs of King Coal, The Henchmen of King Coal, and The Will of King Coal. Sinclair, who had consecrated his life to agitation for social justice, enrolled his art in that cause, never flinching from sacrifice for it.

The story follows a young man who goes to work in the mines and learns the company town from inside: its dangers, its debts, its spies, and its hunger for liberty. Sinclair does not rest with description; he appeals to the honor and good fellowship of his readers, opening their eyes to conditions under which wage earners lived. King Coal is a novel of protest, written to move as well as to show.
75325-the-bellamy-trial:
Frances Noyes Hart's The Bellamy Trial, published by Doubleday, Page and Company at Garden City in 1927, is built as a court record. A cast list names the judge, Anthony Bristed Carver, prosecutor Daniel Farr, defense counsel Dudley Lambert, and the defendants, Susan Ives and Stephen Bellamy. Hart dedicates the novel to her favourite lawyer, Edward Henry Hart.

The book walks through eight days of testimony, from real estate agent and physician to governess, lady's maid, handy man, and finger-print expert. It opens outside the courtroom, where a red-headed girl reporter takes her seat, Row A, seat 15, for the Philadelphia Planet, while a curious crowd surges against the glass doors.
75650-report-to-hon-a-v-brown-postmaster:
Wood, superintendent of the line, addressed this report to Brown, Postmaster General. It treats the opening and present condition of the United States overland mail route between San Antonio, Texas, and San Diego, California. The report is dated at Washington in March 1858. Wood submits an account of the mail stage line running twice a month between those cities.

He has grouped his observations, he writes, of the soil, climate, distances, deserts, mountains, and supplies of wood, water, and grass along the road. The distances and heights are from government surveys, as he had neither time to measure the road nor to take its heights. The journal begins in June 1857, when James Birch took the contract. Wood had labored with Birch on the letting, and took charge of carrying the contract out.
75744-my-lorraine-journal:
Edith O’Shaughnessy kept the journal printed as My Lorraine Journal. Harper and Brothers issued the book in September nineteen hundred eighteen. She had earlier written books on life in Mexico. Photos show Nancy, Verdun, and the villages she passed through.

Her trip starts in Paris in June nineteen hundred seventeen. An old friend urges her to visit Lunéville and the rebuilt village of Vitrimont. From there she tours the front in Lorraine during the Great War. Later parts cover work at a canteen in Bar-le-Duc. Autumn chapters return to Nancy and Toul. Readers get a close view of towns living in the shadow of battle.
77195-the-secrets-of-a-great-cathedral:
Spence-Jones wrote The Secrets of a Great Cathedral, put out by Dent at London and Dutton at New York in 1914. The author was Dean of Gloucester and a teacher of ancient history at the Royal Academy. The book follows his Handbook to Gloucester Cathedral, yet it is not tied to that one pile. Its secrets belong to the many cathedrals of Catholic Europe, at once their glory and their riddle. Still, Gloucester, the dean's loved home, strays into the pages again and again.

The dean wrote to answer plain questions put to him as chief keeper of a great Romanesque church. The book opens with a plate of the tomb of Galla Placidia at Ravenna, from about the year 440. Readers get a warm, learned tour of stone, shrine, and rite.
77449-ethel-s-trial:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote a Sunday school tale published at Philadelphia by the American Sunday School Union, entered for copyright in 1871. A frontispiece asks what made Ethel run so, since the dog wouldn't hurt her. Guernsey had written Irish Amy, Comfort Allison, and The Tattler. Ethel's trial in becoming a missionary tests her courage and patience. The Union sold the book at its Bible House in New York as well.

Missionary vocation stories trained girls to imagine service abroad. Guernsey wrote many such tales for the Union's list. Ethel's trials are domestic before they are foreign. The book belongs to the vast Sunday school library literature of the nineteenth century.
77819-theory-and-practice-of-the-confess:
Theory and Practice of the Confessional, a guide in the administration of the sacrament of penance by Professor Caspar E Schieler, was issued by Benziger Brothers in a second edition. The Reverend H J Heuser edited the English version. The book carries the imprimatur of Archbishop Farley of New York, dated August 31, 1905. It was translated from the German for students and mission priests.

The editor's preface explains the need. Latin texts on the confessional were not enough for many priests working in English speaking missions. The matter is delicate, and the editor weighs the risk that a reader the book was never meant for might misuse it. That danger, he judges, is the lesser evil beside leaving confessors without a practical guide in their own tongue. The manual treats sins, dispositions, and the rulings of cases at length.
78625-the-history-traditions-of-the-moor:
The History and Traditions of the Moorfields Eye Hospital, by Treacher Collins, was published at London in 1929. Its subtitle promises one hundred years of ophthalmic discovery and development. Collins served the hospital in nearly every surgical post, from clinical assistant and house surgeon to curator of the museum, librarian, and consulting surgeon. He dedicates the book to the surgical staff of 1883 to 1887.

Moorfields, founded in 1805, was the world's first hospital created for a single specialty, the eye. Early chapters tell of the founders and the work of John Cunningham Saunders, whose portrait fronts the book. Benjamin Travers and William Lawrence follow. A fourth chapter treats the removal to Moorfields itself. Twenty-seven plates illustrate the century of eye surgery the volume records.
78640-the-opal:
The Opal is a novel of a clear eyed woman and the friend who tells her all. Houghton, Mifflin and Company issued the book in Boston in nineteen hundred five. The Riverside Press at Cambridge printed the February issue. Mary Elton, called unusual by friends, stands at its heart.

Clearness of sight is the root of Mary Elton’s whole cast. She calls black black and a spade a spade with no flinch. Men find a man’s mind and heart in her, friends say in praise. No man had yet loved her in the way of marriage, she owns. Warm friendship in full measure was hers from men in scores. Philip Morley, her chief friend, tells her each small love. She gives him warmth or a scolding as his case may need. A thousand women in one, one chapter names her strange charm.
78692-grocers-manual:
The Grocers' Manual Publishing Company issued a book of recipes and formulas in Chicago. Rights rest from 1888 with the company. The Grocers' Manual teaches the making of baking powders, extracts, and condiments. Plain words rule the directions, with little technical talk, the front note states.

Contents run from baking powder and almond candy to catsup and chewing gum. Shoe blacking, laundry blueing, bird seed, and butter color stand among the sundries. True goods and their cheap copies both get frank treatment in the pages. Shopkeepers of the day gained a full bench book of trade formulas.
78873-clendenen-s-detective-manual:
Rufus Clendenen wrote a manual on how to become a successful detective, printed in Charleston, West Virginia, in 1922. He calls his method the Clendenen Detective System. A man need not meet the body standards of a patrolman, he says. Many city detectives come from patrol ranks, but others step straight into the work.

The best detective is of normal build, since a very tall or short man draws the eye. Lameness, speech defects, or odd manner bar a man from police work. Clendenen laughs at the myth of endless disguises and says plain craft beats tricks. Honesty that holds by night as by day is, for him, the first tool of the trade.
78901-books-in-general:
Books in General, by Solomon Eagle, was published by Alfred A Knopf at New York in 1919. A Knopf list of essay books fronts the volume: Carl Van Vechten's Music and Bad Manners, Mencken's Book of Calumny and Book of Prefaces, and Ezra Pound's Pavannes and Divisions.

Eagle's own contents run from Who's Who and Political Songs to epigrams and an eminent Baconian. Pieces treat Herrick, Shakespeare's women, moving a library, table-talk and jest books, and Wordsworth's personal dullness. The most durable books and the worst style in the world close his miscellany.
7973-napoleon-s-campaign-in-russia-anno-:
Dr A. Rose wrote this medico-historical study of Napoleon's Russian campaign of 1812, following the Grand Army from its crossing of the Niemen in June to the retreat through Wiasma, Smolensk, and the Beresina. His chapters cover Moscow under occupation, the governor Rostopchine, prisoners of war, and the treatment of typhus after the second crossing of the Niemen. The preface notes that of some six hundred thousand men who crossed, most never came home.

Rose's focus is medical as much as military: cold, hunger, and disease killed more soldiers than battles did. He draws on regimental lists and archives to show how an army dissolved. For readers of military history, the book adds the surgeon's view to the familiar story of 1812, and explains why the retreat became a byword for disaster.
7977-purgatory-doctrinal-historical-and-:
Mrs J. Sadlier wrote this Catholic book on purgatory in three modes at once: doctrine, history, and poetry. Dedicated to her son, the Reverend Francis X. Sadlier, who died in November 1885 scarcely three months after ordination, it gathers teaching on the souls in purgatory with legends, historic lore, and verse. Its epigraph comes from Psalm 141, praying that God bring the soul out of prison.

Sadlier, who had written and translated many Catholic books, aimed to comfort the bereaved and encourage prayer for the dead. The mixture of argument, story, and poetry makes the doctrine feel lived rather than abstract. As a piece of nineteenth-century Catholic devotion, it shows how ordinary believers were taught to think about death, mercy, and the communion of the living and the dead.
7983-the-vitamine-manual:
Walter H. Eddy, associate professor of physiological chemistry at Teachers College, Columbia University, wrote this manual on the new food factors then called vitamines. Its chapters cover how vitamines were discovered, attempts to work out their chemical nature, methods of testing, the yeast test for vitamine B. Their sources, properties, use in diets, and the diseases caused by their lack, with a bibliography. Eddy aimed the book at both students and lay readers.

The manual is frank that its science was moving fast and that some data would soon be out of date. Its lasting interest is historical: it captures nutrition at the moment vitamins were newly understood and already changing diets. Students of medicine and food history will find a clear, compact record of that turning point.
8116-the-communistic-societies-of-the-un:
Charles Nordhoff visited and observed the communistic societies of the United States and reported them from personal experience. His book opens with an inquiry into labour, the condition and necessities of workers, and the mistakes of the trades-unions, then turns to the societies themselves. Amana in 1874, with its history, social habits, and religion; the Harmonists at Economy, with Father Rapp and their creed; and the Separatists at Zoar, among others.

Nordhoff writes as a sympathetic journalist, describing daily life, worship, and work in communities that tried to live by sharing. His accounts remain the best contemporary record of American utopian experiments. For readers of social history, the book is an engaging tour of a radical America that sought a better way to live together.
8199-the-moon-metal:
Garrett P. Serviss wrote this science-fiction novella around a discovery of gold at the south pole, news that nobody suspected would begin a new era in the world's history. Its chapters follow the magician of science, Dr Syx, the Grand Teton mine, the wealth of the world, wonders of the new metal, a strange discovery. A detective of science, the top of the Grand Teton, the fate of a kite, and finally the looting of the moon and the last of Dr Syx.

Serviss imagines a metal from the moon that upends the world's money, since gold itself loses its scarcity. The tale mixes adventure with economics, as nations and markets reel from the new wealth. For science-fiction readers, it is an early and inventive example of the genre, and a sharp fable about value itself.
824-speeches-literary-and-social:
Charles Dickens gathered his public speeches on literary and social topics in this volume, issued in 1880. He spoke at dinners, institutes, and charities, praising books, libraries, and the workers who spread learning. Added chapters study Dickens as a letter writer, poet, and public reader of his own works.

The speeches show Dickens the citizen, warm, witty, and earnest about reform. He urges kindness to the poor, support for schools, and honour for the craft of writing. The book gives readers the novelist in his own voice off the page, and it is a rich source for his views on the age he described.
8998-paris-as-it-was-and-as-it-is-a-sket:
An English traveler wrote this sketch of Paris in a series of letters home during 1801 and 1802, printed in London in 1803. The writer compares Paris before the Revolution with Paris after it, asking what changed in science, letters, arts, religion, schools, manners, and amusements. Public buildings and national institutions get close notice.

The letters were penned in the brief peace between Britain and France, and a planned map of Paris never reached the book, held at Calais when war broke out anew. That mishap only adds to the book's charm. It stands as a sharp, on-the-spot report of a capital remade by revolt.
9253-browne-s-folly-from-the-doliver-rom:
Writing from the Wayside in August 1860, Hawthorne answers a cousin who asked for a story for the Essex Institute. He confesses he can write no story now, years after Twice-Told Tales and Mosses from an Old Manse. His mind, he says, has lost the plan and measure of those little narratives, once so fertile.

Instead he describes a conspicuous hill near Salem, where he once meant to set a dreamy fiction. He knows not if it lies in Salem, Danvers, or Beverly. The letter is a charming apology, and a glimpse of a tale Hawthorne never wrote, haunting the hill still.
9303-post-augustan-poetry-from-seneca-to:
H. E. Butler, a fellow of New College, Oxford, wrote this history of Roman poetry after Augustus, from Seneca to Juvenal. The opening chapter treats decline: the principate, emperors from Tiberius to Nero, and the decay of Roman character. Great Augustan poets, Butler says, barred further advance, and schools taught rhetoric over true learning.

Later chapters cover drama, Seneca, and the poets who followed, with notes on stage, mime, and recitation. Butler judges each age with care. The book remains a clear guide to a period of Latin verse too often skipped, learned yet readable.
a-dweller-in-mesopotamia-being-the-adven: Donald Maxwell dwells in Mesopotamia as an official artist in the Garden of Eden. His chapters visit the fiery furnace, the Venice of the East, and the waters of Babylon. Sinbad the soldier, wise men from the West, and Arabian nights in 1919 fill the record. Maxwell writes of old Baghdad, paradise lost, and desert life with an artist's eye.
aftermath-part-second-of-a-kentucky-card: James Lane Allen continues his Kentucky Cardinal story in this second part, following the lovers through doubt, feeling, and the slow work of understanding. Letters, private lines, and quiet scenes carry a romance set among Kentucky homes and gardens. The prose is lyrical and restrained, dwelling on mood and motive more than on outward action.
ancient-art-and-ritual: Jane Ellen Harrison writes on ancient art and ritual, published by Oxford University Press in London, New York, and Toronto. The study argues that Greek art grew out of ritual dance and festival, not from pure decoration. Harrison's bold thesis reshaped classical studies, joining anthropology to the study of ancient Greece.
astrophel-and-other-poems-taken-from-the:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's lyrics fill this selection, drawn from the sixth volume of his collected poetical works. That volume joins three sequences: A Midsummer Holiday, Astrophel, and A Channel Passage, together with other poems. Swinburne, the most musical English poet of his generation, built these pieces on rolling rhythms, sea imagery, and praise of dead friends and poets.

Astrophel itself mourns Sir Philip Sidney, the Elizabethan soldier-poet, under his own pastoral name. Other poems honour a bold, cheerful soul whom death cannot diminish, in lines that ring with alliteration and refrain. Readers get Swinburne's late manner at full stretch: grief and landscape fused into sound, with the Channel coast and English fields answering each other across the poems.
britannica-1911-aal: Aal is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, also spelled A'l, Ach, or Aich in Hindustani. The names belong to two plants, Morinda tinctoria and Morinda citrifolia, grown widely in India. Their roots yield a reddish dye, sold in trade as Suranji. The entry traces the color to a glucoside called Morindin, built from glucose and, it states, probably a trioxy-methyl-anthraquinone. Dye works and plant names meet in a few lines, in the terse trade manner of the 1911 volumes.
britannica-1911-academy-royal:
Academy, Royal describes the Royal Academy of Arts in London, founded in 1768 to cultivate and improve painting, sculpture, and architecture. Earlier attempts by artists such as Hogarth had failed for want of money. A charity exhibition at the Foundling Hospital showed that exhibitions could pay, and two artists' societies formed, but quarrels split the successful one.

Leading members broke away and petitioned George III, who approved their plan in December 1768. Their two aims were a well-regulated school of design for students and an annual exhibition open to artists of merit, whose profits would fund the school. Membership rules, honorary posts, and the Academy Schools fill the long entry, which notes seventy-seven students entering in the first year, 1769.
britannica-1911-accountant-general:
Accountant-General was formerly an officer of the English Court of Chancery, the court that handled equity cases and funds lodged by litigants. The short Britannica entry records an office already gone when it was written. He received all moneys lodged in court, and by him they were deposited in bank and paid out again as the court directed.

Abolition came by statute. The Chancery Funds Act of 1872 ended the office and transferred its duties to the paymaster-general. Readers meeting the title in older legal papers get the essential facts here: what the officer did with court funds, when his post disappeared, and which official took the work over.
britannica-1911-adjutant-general:
Adjutant general is a high army office with roots in a helper role. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica draws the title from a Latin word for helping. At first the holder was chief aide to a general in command. In Britain and America the post grew into a set office instead.

In England the holder sits on the Army Council for staff matters. His office handles all duties that touch army personnel in full. In the United States the holder runs army records and recruiting. Commissions and army letters also pass through that bureau there. Some states keep their own holder for militia duties as well.
britannica-1911-admiral:
Admiral, the title of the officer who commands a fleet, is traced in a word and naval entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is Arabic in root, beyond doubt. Sea states round the Mediterranean met the title amir in phrases for men of rank. They joined amir with the article al to form one word.

Forms such as amiral and almirante spread from that base. In Spain a like fusion gave a title for the prince of the faithful. Crusades made the eastern title known in the north. As a naval title it was first taken by the French from the Genoese in 1249. By the close of that century it named the officer in charge of the Cinque Port ships in England. The English form admiral came from a false link to a Latin word for wonder.
britannica-1911-afranius-lucius-roman-ge:
Lucius Afranius, a Roman general of the late republic, gets a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He rose from low birth as a close friend of Pompey. With Pompey's help he reached the consulship in the year sixty before Christ. The entry judges him unfit for civil work in that high post. The next year he won a triumph as governor of Cisalpine Gaul.

When Spain fell to Pompey, Afranius went to help rule it. He lost to Caesar at Ilerda and swore to fight no more. He broke that oath and stood with Pompey at Pharsalus. After the loss at Thapsus he fled, was seized, and was killed by Caesar's own troops.
britannica-1911-agra-canal:
Agra Canal is an important Indian irrigation work. It also serves navigation on its length. Delhi, Gurgaon, Muttra, and Agra districts share it. Bharatpur state takes some of its water too. The canal draws from the Jumna river at Okla. Okla lies about ten miles below Delhi. The weir there was Upper India's first on fine sand. It runs about eight hundred yards long. It rises seven feet above summer river level.

Engineering and route fill the entry. From Okla the canal follows high land. It keeps between the Khari-nadi and the Jumna. It joins the Banganga below Agra at last. Navigable branches connect it with Muttra and Agra. The whole work was opened in 1874.
britannica-1911-alimentary-canal:
The alimentary canal is the full tube that carries food from mouth to anus, a span of some twenty-five to thirty feet. Food moves through a set order of parts. It starts at the mouth and pharynx, passes the oesophagus and stomach, then works through the small intestines and the caecum. The large intestines, rectum, and anus end the run. Three glands feed juices into the tube by ducts: the salivary glands, the liver, and the pancreas.

Because mouth and pharynx get their own articles, the long account here starts at the oesophagus, or gullet. That muscular tube, lined with mucous membrane, runs about ten inches from pharynx to the stomach's mouth. Its course passes through the neck and chest, then through a final inch of belly. Later sections turn to how the canal is built in other animals, set beside the human form.
britannica-1911-aliwal:
One fight made Aliwal known. The Punjab village, in the Ludhiana district on the left bank of the Sutlej, saw a major battle of the First Sikh War in January 1846. Ranjur Singh had crossed the river in strength, held the village, and put Ludhiana under threat.

Sir Harry Smith struck on the twenty-eighth to clear the British bank. In a hard fight his horsemen broke through the Sikh lines three times and drove the beaten men into the river, where great numbers drowned. The victors took sixty-seven guns. With that win, all the land east of the Sutlej passed under British rule by submission.
britannica-1911-almeria-capital:
Where the river Almería meets its gulf on southern Spain's Mediterranean coast stands Almería, capital of its province and a leading seaport. The city, an episcopal see at the end of a railway from Madrid, fills part of a rich valley ringed by hills. In 1900 it held 47,326 people.

Defence shaped its church: the Gothic cathedral of 1524 was raised with thick battlemented walls and a belfry, more fortress than church. Four Moorish towers still top the modern streets. Two long piers guard a harbour shipping iron, lead, esparto, and fruit, above all white grapes. Rome knew the port as Urci; under Moorish Granada it peaked as the kingdom's foremost harbour, until Spain took it for good in 1489.
britannica-1911-animal:
Animal comes from the Latin anima, meaning breath or soul. The word first denoted any living thing. It now names one branch of living things. Plants form the opposing branch. Older thought granted plants a lower grade of life. The entry rejects that vague belief. Cell science changed the picture completely. Protoplasm research showed the cell as a shared foundation. Animal and plant cells are essentially alike.

Animals and plants are therefore close relatives. Each grades into organisms of mixed character. The Protista article covers those borderline forms. The actual boundary is artificial, the entry argues. Systematists draw it by ingenious analysis. Nature itself does not fix it. Cell walls offer the most obvious distinction. Animal walls are absent or nitrogenous. Plant walls differ in composition. Popular misuse also receives correction. Animal does not simply mean mammal.
britannica-1911-appeal:
Appeal is a law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an old right in English criminal law. In the old common law, an appeal was a private charge of felony brought by the person wronged. The crown could not take that right away. A man could use it even when the accused had been cleared at trial, or cleared and then pardoned.

In practice the right was best known as that of the nearest kin of a murdered person. The article gives cases from the early seventeen hundreds. After an inquiry into London prisons in 1729, gaolers cleared of ill-treating prisoners still faced appeals for murder brought by kin of prisoners who had died. An older case, from 1708, shows the same pattern.
britannica-1911-aral:
Aral is a lake or inland sea in western Asia. It lies between latitudes 43 and 47 north. Arab and Persian geographers called it the Sea of Khwārizm. Its present name is Kirghiz in origin. Aral-denghiz means Sea of Islands. Its area is 26,233 square miles. That makes it the world's fourth largest inland sea. Length and width are nearly equal.

The lake is remarkably shallow, though. Maximum depth is only 220 feet. Mean depth is just fifty feet. Lake Geneva holds a comparable water volume. Steppes surround the northern shores. The Ust-Urt plateau bounds the west. Khiva's alluvial district lies south. The Kyzyl-kum, or Red Sand Desert, lies east. Northern shores are low and bay-cut. Kropotkin signs this geographical survey. German and Russian sources anchor its bibliography.
britannica-1911-arsenal:
Arsenal is a place for the making, repair, receipt, storage, and issue of warlike stores, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The word appears in many forms in the Romance tongues. It is of Arabic origin, from a phrase that means house of trade or making. Older guesses that link it to Latin phrases are now rejected in full.

A first class arsenal can renew the gear of a large army. It holds a gun factory, a carriage factory, and shops for small arms and powder. It also needs great store houses, the entry says. A second class arsenal has workshops in place of factories. The site of an arsenal should be set by strategy. It should sit at the base of supply, safe from attack and not too near a frontier.
britannica-1911-assur-bani-pal:
Assur Bani Pal, the great king of Assyria, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His name means Assur creates a son in his own tongue. He was the model for the Greek figure Sardanapalus in later tales. His father Esar Haddon named him king of Assyria in public before his own death. Babylonia was assigned to his twin brother in hope of pleasing Babylonian feeling.

After the death of Esar Haddon in 668 BC, his first task was to finish the war in Egypt. Tirhakah, who had taken Egypt again, fled to Ethiopia before his arms. The Assyrian army spent forty days on its march up the Nile from Memphis to Thebes. Soon after, Necho, the satrap of Sais, was caught in a plot with Tirhakah against Assyria.
britannica-1911-attorney-general:
Attorney General, in England, is the chief law man who runs all law work and suits where the Crown has a stake. He holds his post at the kings will, by sealed grant. He leads the bar by right of post, and just the most high of law men are picked for it. The post can be traced to a kings man of twelve seventy-seven.

He must be a side in all suits that touch the Crown. Wide sway is his in gifts, in the goods of the ill in mind, and in crime work. He and his aide sit in the House and in the team in power.
britannica-1911-badger-animal:
Badger is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a burrowing mammal. The name covers animals of the subfamily Melinae. It also names the typical genus Meles in the text. The word may come from badge, for the marks on the head. French uses one word, blaireau, for both senses. The jaw of these animals is built in a special way.

The lower jaw locks into a long socket in the skull. That lock makes dislocation all but impossible. It lets the badger hold on with the utmost grip. The European badger is about twenty five to twenty nine inches long. Its tail runs about eight inches more. Its fur is grey above and black below. Its head is white with a black stripe on each side. The entry treats its habits as typical of the group.
britannica-1911-bakocz-tamas-cardinal:
Bakócz, Tamás (1442-1521), was a Hungarian churchman and statesman. A wagoner's son rose remarkably here. His uncle adopted and trained him. The priesthood was that uncle's chosen path. Bakócz succeeded him as rector in 1480. King Matthias made him a secretary.

Gyor's bishopric followed in 1490. Eger and Esztergom came under Wladislaus II. A cardinal's hat arrived in 1500. Constantinople's titular patriarchate followed in 1510. From 1490 Bakócz led Hungarian statecraft. Foreign policy was mainly his work. He kept Hungary from the Cambrai league. Venice kept his friendship throughout. A Habsburg family compact bears his stamp. In 1513 he sought the papacy itself. Princely pomp received him at Rome. Bribery funds backed his design richly. Venice and the emperor betrayed him. His crusade bull then sparked a peasant rising. The entry judges him able but unprincipled.
britannica-1911-barisal:
Barisal is a town of British India, headquarters of the Backergunje district in Eastern Bengal and Assam, standing on a river of the same name. Its population in 1901 was 18,978. It is an important centre of river trade, on the steamer route through the Sundarbans from Calcutta to the Brahmaputra.

The town holds a first-grade college and several schools, a public library founded by subscription in 1858, and a students' union that helps the sick and poor. Then comes the entry's famous oddity: the Barisal guns. The 1911 Britannica entry describes unexplained noises like cannon fire, often heard in the delta channels of the Brahmaputra as the tide rises, with no settled cause found.
britannica-1911-beira-portugal:
Beira is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a province of Portugal. It is an ancient principality and province of that land. It covers the north and centre of the country. The Atlantic Ocean bounds it on the west. Spanish provinces bound it on the east side. A count from 1900 puts its people at 1,515,834. Its area is given as 9208 square miles. Five districts make up its administration.

Those districts are Aveiro, Coimbra, Vizeu, Guarda, and Castello Branco. In popular use the province falls into three sections. Upper Beira lies north and west of the Serra da Estrella. Lower Beira lies south and east of that range. Maritime Beira takes in Aveiro and Coimbra on the coast. That coast runs about seventy two miles long. It is uniformly flat along its whole length. Heath and marshland border a wide and fertile strip.
britannica-1911-bengal:
Bengal is a province of British India, bounded by Eastern Bengal and Assam, the Bay of Bengal, the Central and United Provinces, Nepal and Sikkim. It covers 141,580 square miles and held 54,096,806 people. Behar, Orissa and Chota Nagpur, with the western Ganges valley, make up its parts.

The province was recast in 1905, when Dacca, Chittagong and other divisions went to the new Eastern Bengal and Assam, and Sambalpur came the other way. Long sections then treat the land itself: the Ganges delta, a climate running from Himalayan snow to steamy heat, rice as the staple crop, and coal as the chief mineral. Calcutta gathers nearly all the sea trade, and railways and rivers alike centre on that port.
britannica-1911-berhampur-bengal:
Berhampur is a town of British India, headquarters of the Murshidabad district in Bengal, on the left bank of the Bhagirathi river. It stands five miles below Murshidabad city and counted 24,397 people in 1901. After the battle of Plassey it was chosen as Bengal’s chief military station.

A huge square of brick barracks rose there in 1767 at a cost of £300,000. In those barracks, on 25 February 1857, the first open act of the Mutiny was committed. No troops remain now, and the buildings serve as a jail, a lunatic asylum and other civic offices. A government college of 1853 survives on local support, and the decayed city of Cossimbazar lies within the municipality.
britannica-1911-betrothal:
Betrothal is the subject of a custom article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Betrothal means pledging one's truth, or faith, to marry. The word comes from an old English word for truth. The church did not require it, and law did not need it. In old times it was a formal rite held some weeks before the wedding. A marriage could be put off for years after it.

The article splits church law into two kinds of pledge. One kind counted as a true but irregular marriage and was later banned. The other was a promise to marry at a future date. Such a promise could turn into marriage without more rite. Children as young as seven could be pledged, though not wed. Gifts marked the rite, such as rings, a kiss, or a broken coin split between the pair.
britannica-1911-bhopal:
Bhopal is a native state of India, in the central India agency, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its size and trials. The state covers 6,902 square miles of land. Its people numbered 665,961 in the count of 1901. That count showed a fall of thirty per cent in ten years.

Part of that fall came from a change in the method of counting. The state also suffered heavily from famine in those years. Famines struck in 1896 to 1897 and again in 1899 to 1900. Bhopal is the chief Muslim state in central India. It ranks next to Hyderabad among the Muslim states of India. The land is uneven, crossed by the Vindhya ranges. One peak near Raysen rises above 2,500 feet. Most streams of the state flow toward the north.
britannica-1911-bihari-lal:
Bihari-Lal is a name famous in Hindustani literature as the author of the Sat-sai. That work gathers about seven hundred distichs, or two-line verses. The 1911 Britannica article calls it perhaps the most celebrated Hindi work of poetic art. Its language is Braj-bhasha, spoken around Mathura, where the poet lived. Most couplets voice Radha, chief of the cowherd maidens, and her divine lover Krishna. Each couplet stands complete on its own.

Little is known of the poet beyond his own hints. He was born in Gwalior and spent his boyhood in Bundelkhand. Marriage settled him in his father-in-law's home district. The couplets are arranged by the sentiments they convey, under Indian rhetoric's scheme. Seventeen commentators are named by Grierson in the article. The best-known commentary, finished in 1818, is Lallu-ji-Lal's Lala-chandrika. The work was twice rendered into Sanskrit.
britannica-1911-binomial:
Binomial, in mathematics, is a quantity made of the sum or difference of two terms. Robert Recorde first brought the word in, in 1557, the 1911 Britannica article says. Expressions like a plus b and a minus b are its plain cases. Trinomial and quadrinomial name the same build with three or four terms. The article's real subject is the binomial theorem tied to the word. That theorem lets any power of a binomial be written as a series.

The theorem is credited in its first form to Sir Isaac Newton. He set it out in a letter of 13 June 1676 to Henry Oldenburg, for Leibnitz. A fully rigorous proof was lacking for many years, the article notes. Euler's proof for negative and fractional powers was faulty. Niels Henrik Abel at last supplied the sound demonstration. The article sends readers to Algebra for proof and uses, and keeps to the discovery's history.
britannica-1911-bruchsal:
Bruchsal is a German town in the grand-duchy of Baden, prettily set on the Saalbach 14 miles north of Karlsruhe and an important junction on the main railway from Mannheim to Constance. It held 13,555 people in 1900, a small garrison included. An Evangelical church and four Roman Catholic churches serve it, among them St Peter's, burial place of the bishops of Spires.

A fine palace with beautiful grounds, a town hall and classical, modern and commercial schools mark the town, whose manufactures run to machinery, paper, tobacco, soap and beer, with considerable wine trade. Mentioned in 937 as Bruxolegum, Bruchsal began as a royal villa of emperors and kings, passed to Otto of Franconia in 1002. Was given by Henry III to the see of Spires in 1095. From 1105 it was the bishops' summer residence and grew fast into a town, staying theirs until ceded away in 1802 under the treaty of Luneville.
britannica-1911-buffalo-animal:
Buffalo is the subject of a nature article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name first meant a kind of cattle kept tame in India and Egypt from old times. By 1911 it was used for that species and its near kin. Buffaloes are heavy oxen with thin hair, large ears, and strong curved horns.

The article gives close detail on the Cape buffalo of Africa. In old bulls the horns grow thick at the base and form a shield on the brow. It notes smaller races in east and west Africa. Herds live near water in reed swamps and can reach a hundred head. Old bulls may roam alone or in small bands. The text notes that numbers had fallen and some herds were guarded by law.
britannica-1911-cadiz-capital:
Cadiz, in Latin Gades, is the capital and chief seaport of its Spanish province, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes its site. It stands on the Bay of Cadiz, an inlet of the Atlantic, ninety-four miles by rail south of Seville. Its people numbered 69,382 in 1900. The city is built at the tip of a tongue of land reaching about five miles into the sea.

Its noble bay runs more than thirty miles in circuit and is almost wholly land-locked. That shelter, the entry says, is the main source of the city's trading weight. The outer bay stretches from Rota to the mouth of the Guadalete. The inner bay, guarded by forts, gives good anchorage in general and holds a harbour behind a mole for smaller ships.
britannica-1911-caledonian-canal:
The Caledonian Canal links the east and west coasts of Scotland. It runs through the Great Glen, by Lochs Ness, Oich and Lochy. This 1911 Britannica entry gives its building and working. The chain of lakes made the route an obvious one. It saves ships some 400 miles of stormy coasting. That voyage rounds the north of Britain through the Pentland Firth.

James Watt surveyed a canal line in 1773. Thomas Telford reported on the scheme in 1801. Parliament authorized the work in 1803. Building began at once under Telford's direction. Traffic started on the canal in 1822. The whole route runs about 60 miles. Only about 22 miles are artificial cut. There are 28 locks along the line. A flight of eight at Corpach is called “Neptune's Staircase.” It lifts boats 64 feet in all. The entry gives lock sizes and the canal's modest yearly income.
britannica-1911-canal:
Canal is an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about artificial waterways cut for drainage, watering of land, and above all for boats. The word comes from the Latin canalis, a channel.

The weak point of the old waterways was the lack of any easy way to lift boats from one level to another. The lock cured that flaw in the fourteenth or fifteenth century. Whether Dutch or Italian hands came first is left in doubt, though Leonardo da Vinci finished six locks near Milan in 1487. The Languedoc Canal, the Canal du Midi, stands as the pioneer of modern Europe: 148 miles long, rising 620 feet through 119 locks, and finished in 1681. France went on to cut over 3,000 miles of canals.
britannica-1911-caracal-animal:
The caracal is a wild cat of Asia and Africa. It is sometimes called the Persian lynx. This 1911 Britannica article describes the animal. It is somewhat larger than a fox in size. Its coat is a uniform reddish brown above. Below, the fur runs whitish in colour. Two white spots sit above each of its eyes. Long black tufts tip its ears in striking fashion.

Those ear tufts give the animal its name. It comes from Turkish words meaning “black-ear.” The entry admits that its wild habits are little known. It dwells among grass and bushes, not in deep forest. Its prey includes gazelles, small deer and hares. It also takes peafowl and other birds. In India it is tamed and trained for hunting. A favourite sport sets two caracals on a flock of pigeons. Its hide makes Zulu skin-cloaks in South Africa.
britannica-1911-cardinal:
A cardinal is the highest dignitary of the Roman Church after the pope. This long 1911 Britannica article explains the office. Cardinals form the council, or senate, of the pope. They aid him in the general government of the Church. During a vacancy of the Holy See they administer the Church. They elect the new pope. Together they form a body called the Sacred College.

The article stresses what the office is not. It is no essential part of the Church's legal frame. It is a share in the sovereign dignity of its head. That position grew by a long process of evolution. The name comes from cardo, the Latin for a hinge. Like the word pope, it once had a wider use. Only later was it reserved to Rome's chief clergy. The article traces that history and its survivals.
britannica-1911-carnival:
Carnival is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the days of feasting and merry-making held before Lent in Roman Catholic countries. The entry derives the word from Latin terms for putting aside flesh, and rejects the popular link with a farewell to meat. Carnival once ran from Twelfth Night, on 6 January, until midnight on Shrove Tuesday. The entry argues that this season of licence grew out of the Roman Saturnalia.

Rome stands at the centre of the account. Some popes tried to curb the revels, but many backed them, and Paul II funded the games from the papal treasury. His decree set out races and ring-riding contests in the Piazza Navona and at Monte Testaccio. Under Julius III the entry describes bull-hunts in the Forum and grand suppers for cardinals. The piece shows carnival as both a church-season custom and a civic spectacle.
britannica-1911-celestine-mineral:
Celestine, also called celestite, is the native sulphate of the metal strontium. Its name was suggested by the sky blue colour it at times presents. That colour has been blamed on a trace of iron phosphate in the stone. In some cases that account looks doubtful, the entry notes. The mineral is most often colourless, or holds only a faint shade of blue.

Celestine grows in the same crystal system as barytes and shares its form. Its split is perfect along one plane and less clear along another. It matches barytes in hardness but is less dense in weight. It is also far less common than barytes in nature. It dissolves more freely and occurs often in mineral waters. In Britain it is found in Triassic rocks near Bristol.
britannica-1911-chant-royal:
Chant royal, one of the fixed forms of verse devised by medieval French poets, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The poem has five strophes of eleven verses each, all built the same way. An envoi of five verses closes it. All the strophes use the five rhymes shown in the first. The whole poem thus runs to sixty lines on five repeated rhymes.

Some have guessed that the chant royal is a ballade on a larger scale, but which came first is unclear. A writer of 1493 dwells on the form's dignity and says its masters deserve crowns. Pasquier notes that its length and rigid shape suit solemn themes. In Old French, the chants royal of Clement Marot are the most admired.
britannica-1911-charcoal:
Charcoal is the black stuff left when the light parts of plant or animal matter are burned away. The 1911 Britannica article sorts its kinds by source. Wood gives wood charcoal, sugar gives sugar charcoal, and bone gives bone charcoal. Bone charcoal is in the main made of phosphate of lime. Coal, when so treated, gives coke and gas carbon. The first part of the word charcoal has a dim root, the piece says.

One guess ties it to a word for a turn of work, as in charwoman. That would make charcoal mean coal that wood has been turned into. The article finds no proof for that guess, nor for one that links it to a word for a grating noise. The piece then turns to how wood charcoal is burned. Piles of logs are stacked in a cone, covered with turf, and fired with a small air flow.
britannica-1911-chares-general:
Chares was a chief of Athens first heard of in three sixty-six before Christ. He aided a small town that foes had struck. At Corcyra he helped the rich set drive out the folk set, a move that cost Athens that isle in time. He then held chief posts in the war of the false friends.

He threw blame for a loss on his peers and was left sole chief. With no funds from home he joined a rogue lord of Persia. That act sped a peace and his call home. Late posts brought fresh loss, and he ended in the pay of Persia.
britannica-1911-chitral:
Chitral is a native state in the North West Frontier Province of India, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The state is somewhat larger than Wales. It supports about thirty five thousand rough, hardy hillmen, the entry estimates. Both state and capital bear the same name.

The capital sits some way from the main ridge of the Hindu Kush. That range splits waters that flow to India from waters that flow to the Oxus. Chitral matters for its place at the edge of British sway in India. For years before eighteen ninety five, British policy sought control of its foreign affairs. The aim was to guard its northern passes and watch what went on beyond them. A British agency was set up at Gilgit, with a lesser post in Chitral itself.
britannica-1911-chloral:
Chloral, a heavy oily liquid with no colour, is explained in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on chemicals. It was found by Liebig in eighteen thirty two. Later work was done by Dumas and by Staedeler. Its name joins the first parts of chlorine and alcohol.

The liquid has a greasy, somewhat bitter taste. Its vapour stings the eyes and has a sharp smell. It mixes with alcohol and ether, and with less than its own weight in water. With water it forms a hydrate and gives off heat. With an alkali it yields chloroform and a formate salt. Strong agents that add oxygen turn it into a related acid.
britannica-1911-christ-s-hospital:
Christs Hospital is a famed English school and charity for children. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells its royal founding. King Edward the Sixth set it up after a sermon on charity. It took in children left with no mother or father.

The school took over Grey Friars buildings in London. Public gifts soon swelled the king first grant. At its start it housed and taught about four hundred children. Boys wore a blue gown that gave it the Blue Coat name. Yellow stockings and a blue cap went with that dress. In 1902 the school moved to new grounds at Horsham. There it ran like a public school for over eight hundred boys. A linked girls school sits at Hertford.
britannica-1911-clausthal:
Clausthal, a German town in the Prussian Harz, is set out in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It lies on a bleak plateau high above the sea. It is the chief mining town of the Upper Harz hills. In form it is one town with Zellerfeld, split only by a small stream.

Streets are broad, since fires in the last century gave room to rebuild. Most houses are of wood. The town has two churches and a school, plus a famed mining college with a mineral museum. Its chief mines yield silver and lead, and it also smelts copper and a little gold. The town was founded in the twelve hundreds, most likely round a monastery. State control of the mines came in eighteen sixty four.
britannica-1911-cleithral: Cleithral is a term used in the study of buildings. It names a Greek temple that is covered by a roof. The Greek root word means a shut or closed place. A cleithral temple has a roof that covers it in full. The term stands as the pair and the opposite of hypaethral, which names a temple left open to the sky. The entry is a short note on a term of Greek temple form.
britannica-1911-clinic-clinical: Clinic and clinical are words tied to the bedside. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces them to the Greek word for a bed. In church use the terms marked the baptism of the sick or dying. In medicine they mark work done with living patients. Clinical skill is set against what books or lab work teach. A clinic, as a noun, is a class where students learn by real cases. Teachers show the craft through the exam and care of the ill.
britannica-1911-cochineal:
Cochineal is a natural dye that gives scarlet, crimson and orange tints. It also serves to make lake and carmine. The dye comes from the females of Coccus cacti, an insect of the family Coccidae. That insect feeds on cactus plants, above all the nopal, Opuntia coccinellifera. The plant is native to Mexico and Peru.

Use of the dye long predates Spanish rule in Mexico. It formed part of the tribute paid to the crown in some districts. Cortes was told in 1523 to obtain as much as he could. Workers brushed the insects from the cactus into bags three times in a season. Heat then killed them. The entry closes with the dye's active part, carminic acid, and its wax and fat.
britannica-1911-commune-medieval:
The medieval commune, the town form of central and west Europe, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. The piece gives a short account of how towns rose and grew after the fall of the Roman Empire. All these towns, British ones too, are said to form one group. They grew under like terms of wealth, law, and rule.

The study starts with the towns of Germany, where the change ran most free of outside sway. Each town is viewed in three ways: as a law district, as a self ruled body, and as a wealth unit. A chief mark of old town life was that each town formed its own law zone. Town self rule was also stronger than in the lands round it.
britannica-1911-conon-general:
Conon, the Athenian sea captain, is followed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of Timotheus, he held posts in the Peloponnesian War years. In 406 he was picked one of ten generals in place of Alcibiades. A Spartan beat him at sea and shut him in Mytilene port. The win at Arginusae freed him from that tight trap at once.

In 405 Lysander caught the fleet of Athens off guard at Aegospotami. Conon slipped free with eight ships to his friend in Cyprus. When Sparta and Persia fell to war, Persia gave him a fleet. With Pharnabazus he beat the Spartans at Cnidus in 394. That win broke Sparta's rule of the sea in one stroke. He sailed home and rebuilt the long walls of Athens.
britannica-1911-convention-the-national:
National Convention was the assembly that ruled France from September 1792 to October 1795. A 1911 Britannica entry sets its birth in the storming of the Tuileries in August 1792. The old assembly suspended the king and called a convention to frame a constitution. Deputies were to be chosen by all Frenchmen of age who lived by their labour.

That made it the first French assembly elected by broad suffrage with no class bar. The voter age was later cut to twenty one years for the poll. Its first session fell on the twentieth of September 1792 in Paris. The entry gives the frame for the body that tried a king and remade France.
britannica-1911-copal:
Copal is a hard, glossy resin that ranges from near colourless and clear to bright yellow-brown. Its name comes from a Mexican word for incense. When broken it shows a shell-like fracture. Dissolved in alcohol or spirit of turpentine, it forms one of the most valued varnishes. No single plant or land owns the name in trade.

The term covers resins much alike to the eye yet split in make-up and source. Zanzibar copal comes from one named tree and trades as gum animé. Madagascar copal comes from a kin species. Sierra Leone copal comes from a third tree. A fossil form of it lies on the west coast of Africa, from a tree now thought extinct. Brazil and other South American lands yield their own kinds. Depth of the fossil finds stays shallow, at four feet at most.
britannica-1911-coral:
Coral is the hard skeleton built by some sea creatures. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says it is chiefly lime drawn from sea water. Tiny polyps lay it down in their own tissue. Those polyps raise most of the coral reefs of the world. Some water plants and shellfish add to coral masses too. Their shells, though, do not count as true coral.

One kind stands out for its worth in trade. Red or precious coral grows in the Mediterranean Sea. People have prized it for gems and ornament since old times. A great trade once ran from that sea to India. There it was held to hold sacred power. Pliny noted that Gauls once trimmed their swords and helms with it. Romans hung bits of it on children to guard them from harm. Faith in its charm power lasted through the middle ages.
britannica-1911-corporal:
Corporal is a word with more than one sense in church and law. The 1911 Britannica entry starts from the Latin word for the body. As an adjective it marks things tied to the body in life. Corporal works of mercy feed the hungry and tend the sick. A corporal oath was sworn with the hand on a sacred thing.

In the Roman Catholic church the word names a cloth of linen. At Mass that small square cloth sits on the altar stone. The chalice and the paten rest upon it in the rite. In old days it was large and folded over the chalice top. Now a stiff small square called the pall does that work.
britannica-1911-corral:
Corral, a Spanish word from a term for a circle, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is used chiefly in Spanish America and the United States. At its core it names a pen for cattle and horses. It can also name a ring of wagons set for defence against attacks by Indians.

As a verb, to corral means to drive beasts into such a pen. From that act the word spreads in figure to mean to enclose or hem in. The entry links it in root to the South African Dutch word kraal. In Ceylon the word takes a special sense of its own. There it names a pen built for the capture of wild elephants. The like term in India for that work is keddah.
britannica-1911-darial:
Darial is a gorge in the Caucasus at the east foot of Mount Kasbek. The river Terek pierces it for eight miles between vertical walls of rock 5900 feet high. Georgian annals knew it as Ralani, Dargani or Darialani, Persians and Arabs as the Gate of the Alans, Strabo as Porta Caucasica, and the Tatars call it Darioly.

As the only usable passage across the Caucasus, the gorge has been fortified since at least 150 B.C. Lermontov made it famous in Russian poetry. The present Russian fort of Darial guards the Georgian military road where it leaves the gorge's north end. The fort stands at an altitude of 4746 feet.
britannica-1911-dorsiventral: Dorsiventral, from the Latin dorsum for the back and venter for the belly, is a term for an organ whose two surfaces differ from each other in appearance and in structure. The ordinary leaf is the entry's example of such an organ. The entry is only a definition, and it adds no further cases, history, or discussion.
britannica-1911-ereshkigal:
Ereshkigal is a 1911 Britannica article on a goddess of ancient Babylonia. She is also known as Allatu. She was the chief goddess of the nether-world, where the dead are gathered. Her name signifies lady of the nether-world.

She is known to us chiefly through two myths. Both myths symbolize the change of the seasons. They were also meant to teach doctrines formed in the temple-schools of Babylonia. One is the famous story of Ishtar's descent to the lower world. Her sister, who rules there, receives her. The other tells of Nergal's offence against Ereshkigal. He was banished to the kingdom the goddess controlled. Their reconciliation came through her offer in the tale. She would let Nergal share the honours of her realm. Myth readers meet a queen of the dead through the tales told of her.
britannica-1911-escorial:
Escorial is a vast building in Spain that joins four roles in one. Its place entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It holds a convent, a church, a palace, and a royal tomb house. It stands high on the slopes of the Sierra de Guadarrama range.

Tradition says Philip the Second vowed the building after the battle of Saint Quentin. That win fell on the feast day of Saint Laurence in fifteen fifty seven. The house was thus given to that saint in his honour. A hamlet near by gave the place its last name, Escorial. Juan Bautista de Toledo drew the plans and led the building work.
britannica-1911-eumenes-general:
Eumenes (about 360-316 B.C.) was a Macedonian general, a native of Cardia in the Thracian Chersonesus, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. At a very early age he was made private secretary by Philip II of Macedon, and after that king's death he served Alexander, whom he followed into Asia. On Alexander's death, Cappadocia and Paphlagonia were assigned to him.

Those lands were not yet subdued, and Eumenes had to fight his way in with the backing of Perdiccas. In 321 he beat Craterus and Neoptolemus in Cappadocia, and both enemy leaders died. After Perdiccas was murdered in Egypt, the other generals condemned Eumenes to death. Driven back by a treacherous officer, he held the strong fort of Nora for more than a year, then escaped to threaten Syria and lands beyond the Tigris.
britannica-1911-fabrot-charles-annibal:
Charles Annibal Fabrot, a French law scholar born in fifteen eighty, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Aix in Provence, he made fast strides as a boy in the old tongues. He did the same in civil law and in church law. In sixteen hundred and two he took the top law degree at Aix.

In sixteen hundred and nine he won a chair at the school of his home town. He is best known for his form of a great code of the east empire. That code held as law till the empire fell. The work came out at Paris in sixteen forty seven in seven large parts. It won him a fat grant from the chief law lord of France. He also did great work on the books of a giant of law who came before him.
britannica-1911-fayal:
Fayal, also written Faial, is a Portuguese island in the Atlantic, part of the Azores group. Its population in 1900 was 22,262 and its area 63 square miles. Its name means the beech wood, from the former plenty of Myrica faya, a shrub its discoverers mistook for beech. Lying in the track of vessels crossing the Atlantic, it is among the most visited of the Azores, with a fine harbour at Horta, a town of 6,574 people.

Cedros and Feteira are its other chief towns. The so-called Fayal wine once exported widely was really made on Pico, the larger island to the east. The women of Fayal make fine lace from agave thread, carve snow-white fig-tree pith, and do fine basket work. A valley called Flemengos keeps alive the name of the island's Flemish settlers.
britannica-1911-ferdinand-i-of-portugal:
Ferdinand I (1345-1383) was king of Portugal, at times called el Gentil, the Gentleman. He was the son of Pedro I of Portugal and followed his father in 1367. When Pedro of Castile died in 1369, Ferdinand laid claim to the empty throne. He claimed it as a great-grandson of Sancho IV through the female line. The kings of Aragon and Navarre put in claims of their own.

Henry of Trastamara, the brother and victor over Pedro, had in fact taken the crown and the field. After one or two drawn campaigns, all sides took the mediation of Pope Gregory XI. The treaty of 1371 set a marriage between Ferdinand and Leonora of Castile. Before that wedding could take place, Ferdinand had fallen deep in love with Leonora Tellez. She was the wife of one of his own courtiers.
britannica-1911-galangal:
Galangal is an old drug, now obsolete, with an aromatic taste like ginger and pepper mixed. The ordinary galangal of commerce, called lesser galangal, is the dried rhizome of Alpinia officinarum, a plant of the ginger order grown in the Chinese island of Hainan. Its stems reach about four feet, its leaves are slender and hot-tasting, and its roots form dense masses over a foot across. The drug seems unknown to the Greeks and Romans and came into Europe through Arabian physicians.

An Arabian geographer of the 9th century, Ibn Khurdadbah, mentions it, and gallingale appears in an Anglo-Saxon recipe for a wen salve. In the middle ages Europe valued it as medicine and spice, as Russia, Livonia and Esthonia still do, using it for cattle and for flavouring liqueurs. In China it remains in use as a remedy.
britannica-1911-games-classical:
Classical games, the public contests of Greece and Rome, are the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Greek contests and the Roman shows joined sport and spectacle of many kinds. They most often formed part of a rite of religion. The entry claims no institution did more to shape the Greek character.

The article says each Greek youth trained in the gymnasium for these contests. They were the central fair where poet, artist, and merchant each brought his wares. They were also the common ground that bound the whole Greek race as one. The shows of Rome, by contrast, are called a mere shadow of the Greek games, and in the late empire a mockery of them. The earliest games on record are those at the funeral of Patroclus, told in the Iliad.
britannica-1911-gaur-animal:
Gaur is the native name of the wild ox of India, Bos gaurus, in the 1911 Britannica entry. Sportsmen wrongly call it bison, the entry says. The animal ranges into Burma and the Malay Peninsula, where it is known as seladang. It stands for a group of Indo-Malay wild cattle marked by a ridge on the withers, pressed horns and white legs.
