The gaur itself reaches nearly six feet at the shoulder. Its special mark is the high, forward-curving ridge between the horns. Its general colour is blackish-grey. Hill-forests are its haunt. The entry is a brief natural-history notice: name, range, kin, build and home, in a few lines.
britannica-1911-gem-artificial:
Gem, Artificial, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on gems made by man's craft. The term does not mean a fake or copy of a real gem. It means the true stone itself, formed by art by human hands. Such a stone is the same in make-up and look as the natural one.

The diamond serves as the chief case in the text that follows. A diamond is no more than carbon in crystal form, it says. If black carbon could melt and then set as clear crystal, that would count. That would be a true making of diamond by man's art. Shop window paste, by contrast, lacks the hardness and fire. The entry then tells of real diamonds made of late years.
britannica-1911-gerona-capital:
Gerona is the capital of the province of Gerona in north-east Spain. It stands on the rail line from Barcelona to Perpignan in France. The town lies on the right bank of the river Ter, where the river Oña joins it. Its people numbered 15,787 in 1900. The old town climbs the steep slope of Montjuich, the Hill of the Capuchins. Its old houses look scenic against higher hills.

The new part of Gerona spreads down into the plain and past the Oña, crossed by a bridge of three arches. Old city walls and bastions still stand, though worn. Strong forts once crowned the hill and now serve as a prison. Gerona is the seat of a bishop and has a seminary, a public library, and a theatre. Its trades include paper and cloth goods, and its churches draw note, above all its grand Gothic cathedral.
britannica-1911-gimbal:
Gimbal is the subject of a short device article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A gimbal is a device for hanging an object so it stays level and steady. The body that holds it can move freely without passing that motion on. At sea it is used most for compasses, time keepers, and lamps. In its usual form a ring swings on one axis. The object swings inside that ring on a second axis set across the first.

The article then traces the word itself. It comes from an old French word linked to a Latin word for a twin. The same root gives a term for a ring made of two linked hoops. Such rings could be pulled apart into parts. In the fifteen and sixteen hundreds they served as betrothal and keepsake rings. Some were made of three or more linked hoops.
britannica-1911-glarus-capital:
Glarus is the capital of the Swiss canton of the same name. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on the left bank of the Linth, under the Vorder Glarnisch peak, 1,578 feet above the sea. In 1900 it had 4,877 people, almost all German-speaking, of whom 1,248 were Romanists.

It is a clean, modern little town, and the entry explains why: fire destroyed nearly the whole place on 10-11 May 1861, driven by a violent south wind. The loss ran to about half a million sterling, a fifth of it made up by subscriptions from every side. Broad streets and modern buildings followed. The parish church, used in common by Protestants and Romans, is its stateliest building. Zwingli was parish priest here from 1506 to 1516, before he became a Protestant.
britannica-1911-goral:
The goral, a small rough haired animal from the Himalaya, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is classed with the chamois group and has round, tube shaped horns. Its local name is now used for the whole genus. Gorals differ from serows by lacking a gland below the eye.

Several kinds are known, from the Himalaya to Burma, Tibet, and north China. The two Himalayan kinds most often move in small parties, at times in pairs. They favor grass hills or rocky ground with woods. In fair weather they feed at dawn and dusk. When skies are cloudy, they graze all day long.
britannica-1911-graves-alfred-perceval:
Alfred Perceval Graves, an Irish writer born in Dublin in 1846, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the son of the bishop of Limerick. He was taught at Windermere College and took high honours at Dublin University. In 1869 he entered the Civil Service as a clerk in the Home Office. In 1874 he became an inspector of schools.

Graves wrote prose and verse for journals such as the Spectator, the Athenaeum, and Punch. He took a leading part in the revival of Irish letters and led the Irish Literary Society for years. He is the author of the famous ballad Father O'Flynn and many other songs. With Sir Charles Stanford he published Songs of Old Ireland in 1882 and Irish Songs and Ballads in 1893. Their airs came from the Petrie manuscripts. Later collections, with Charles Wood, kept the same Irish focus.
britannica-1911-hal:
Hal is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town in Belgium. The town lies in Brabant, south west of Brussels. It stands on the river Senne and the Charleroi canal. A count from 1904 gives it 13,541 people. The place is of interest chiefly for its fine church. That church, Notre Dame, was once named for Saint Martin. It is a good case of pure Gothic building.

Work on the church began in 1341. It was finished in the year 1409. Its chief ornament is an alabaster altar by Mone. That altar was completed in 1533. A bronze font in the church dates from 1446. A black marble tomb honours the dauphin Joachim, son of Louis the Eleventh. The church treasury holds many costly gifts. Kings, emperors, and popes are named among the givers. The church is famed most for a miraculous image of the Virgin.
britannica-1911-hasdrubal:
Hasdrubal is a collective life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about Carthaginian generals of that name. The first of them was the son in law of Hamilcar Barca. By shrewd dealing he widened the new empire and founded New Carthage as its capital. A treaty with Rome fixed the Ebro river as the bound between the two powers. An assassin killed him in 221.

The second Hasdrubal, a younger son of Hamilcar and brother of Hannibal, held Spain when Hannibal marched on Italy in 218. He fought the Scipio brothers for six years and routed and killed them both in 212. Called to join Hannibal, he crossed the Pyrenees by the west, passed Gaul and the Alps, and drove deep into Italy in 207. He fell at the Metaurus, and his head was cut off and thrown into the camp of Hannibal.
britannica-1911-hawkins-sir-john-admiral:
Sir John Hawkins (1532–1595) was a British admiral born at Plymouth. His family were Devonshire shipowners and skippers. His father William thrice represented Plymouth in Parliament. Hakluyt called the father a principal sea-captain of the west. John was bred to the sea in family ships. In 1562–1563 he sailed to the Guinea coast. He robbed Portuguese slavers of their captives. He then smuggled those captives into Spanish America.

A second voyage in 1564 repeated the pattern with royal approval. Elizabeth hired one of her own vessels to him. Force backed his trading when Spanish officials objected. His arms bore a chained demi-Moor as crest. The third voyage of 1567 was in effect a national venture. The rivalry with Spain was turning acute. The narrative follows his later naval administration. It ends by ranking him among his age's great seamen.
britannica-1911-heart-burial:
Heart-burial means laying that organ to rest apart from the corpse. The custom is very old. Deep respect for the seat of soul and courage explains it. Men tied it to love, faith and conscience too. In the middle ages Europe used it quite often. Richard I's was sent to Rouen in a casket. Eleanor of Castile's went to Lincoln, Edward I's toward Jerusalem. French kings' were kept at Paris.

Since the 1600s the Habsburgs' rest in Vienna's Loretto chapel. Robert Bruce's case is the most famed of all. Douglas bore it toward the Holy Land in silver. He fell fighting Moors in Spain on the way. It was laid at last in Melrose Abbey. Montrose's had a stranger fate still. It was stolen in India and lost in France. Pope Boniface VIII banned the rite; Benedict XI lifted the ban.
britannica-1911-humane-society-royal:
The Royal Humane Society was founded in England to give first aid in cases of near drowning. Its aim was to bring back to life, by craft means, those who seemed dead from the water. The 1911 Britannica entry traces the seed to an English doctor who strove to prove that such folk could be raised.

For a year that doctor paid a prize from his own purse to any man who brought him a body pulled from the water in good time. A second doctor, who had seen a like group at work in Amsterdam, joined his cause. Each brought a band of friends to a coffee house meet by a great London church. There the society was born, with its chief rooms later set by a famed square.
britannica-1911-ibn-haukal: Ibn Haukal, a tenth century Arabian writer on the lands of the world, is covered in a short 1911 Britannica note. Nothing is known of his life. His work, written in 977, is a rework and growth of a book by al-Istakhri from 951, which itself reworked a still older text from near 921. His book was printed at Leiden in 1873, and a short form of it was made in 1233.
britannica-1911-imphal: Imphal was the capital of the state of Manipur in eastern Bengal and Assam, on the north-east frontier of India. It stood where three rivers meet, and its population in 1901 was 67,903. Rather than a compact town, it was a spread of villages hidden among trees. A clearing in the middle held the palace of the raja, the military cantonments, and the houses of the few European residents. The entry is brief and gives the place, the setting, and the count of people, with no history or trade details.
britannica-1911-john-i-of-portugal:
John the First of Portugal is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a king. Born at Lisbon on the 22nd of April 1357, he was a natural son of Pedro. In 1364 he was made grand-master of the Aviz order. His half-brother Ferdinand died in October 1383 with no male heir.

A plan to give the crown to Beatrice and her Castilian husband was fought. The folk voice cried out against a Spanish-ruled Portugal in that plan. After wild tumults John was named protector and regent that December. In April 1385 the estates picked him as king at Coimbra. The win at Aljubarrota in August made his throne safe for good. In 1415 his sons took Ceuta from the Moors.
britannica-1911-john-ii-of-portugal:
John the Second of Portugal, called the Perfect, is the subject of a short life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He lived from 1455 to 1495 and came after his father Alphonso the Fifth in August 1481. His first task as king was to cut back the swollen power of his nobles.

The article names two grim steps in that fight. In 1483 the duke of Braganza was put to death for secret dealings with Castile. The king also killed the young duke of Viseu with his own hand for plotting. The reign is marked by a great sea feat as well. In 1488 Bartholomeu Diaz found the Cape of Good Hope. A famed treaty with Castile in 1494 split the claims of the two crowns.
britannica-1911-john-iii-of-portugal:
John the Third, king of Portugal who lived from 1502 to 1557, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Lisbon in June 1502, he came to the throne in December 1521 in place of his father Emmanuel the First. In 1524 he married Catherine, sister of the Emperor Charles the Fifth. Charles in turn married John's sister Isabella. John succeeded when Portugal stood at the height of its power.

Lisbon then held a commercial importance never known before. Yet John, the article says, became subservient to the clerical party among his subjects. That turn had disastrous results for the trade and social prosperity of his kingdom. He died of apoplexy in June 1557, on his birthday. His grandson Sebastian, then a child of three, succeeded him. Readers get a brief reign sketch with a clear verdict on its central failure.
britannica-1911-john-iv-of-portugal:
John the Fourth, called the Fortunate, king of Portugal, is the subject of a brief 1911 Britannica article. He lived from 1603 to 1656 and was born at Villaviciosa in March 1603. He gained the dukedom of Braganza in 1630. In 1633 he wed Luisa de Guzman, daughter of a great Spanish duke.

By the voice of the people, John was raised to the throne in December 1640. A revolt that month threw off the rule of Philip of Spain. John was held to be the right heir to the crown. His rise led to a long war with Spain. The piece notes that Portugal's freedom was only granted in the next reign, in 1668. John died in 1656.
britannica-1911-john-v-of-portugal:
John V (1689-1750) was king of Portugal, born at Lisbon on 22 October 1689. He followed his father Pedro II in December 1706 and was proclaimed on 1 January 1707. One of his first acts was to hold to the Grand Alliance his father had joined in 1703. His troops marched into Castile but met defeat at Almanza in April 1707. In 1708 he wed Maria Anna of Austria, which bound his land closer to that power.

The wars that followed went badly, but peace with France in 1713 and with Spain in 1715 ended on fair terms. The rest of his long reign was marked by royal service to the clergy. Churchmen ran the kingdom for church ends to a rare degree. That zeal won him the title Most Faithful King from Pope Benedict XIV in 1748. He died on 31 July 1750.
britannica-1911-john-vi-of-portugal:
John the Sixth, king of Portugal who lived from 1769 to 1826, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Lisbon, he gained the title prince of Brazil in 1788. In 1792 he took up rule in the name of his mother, Queen Mary, who had become insane. He took the title of regent in 1799.

The entry notes that he was raised amid church influence and was ill fitted, by a weak nature, for heavy rule. He was recognised as king in 1816 but stayed in Brazil. Unrest led to a peaceful revolution in 1820 and a pledge to a constitutional government on his return in 1822. He also faced revolts led by his son Dom Miguel.
britannica-1911-journal:
Journal is a word for a daily record of events or business, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. It comes through French from a late Latin word that means daily in sense. A private journal is in the main an expanded diary of its keeper. Applied to a newspaper, the word is strict for one published each day.

In wider use any publication issued at set intervals may be called a journal. That takes in magazines and the printed records of learned societies alike. The word journalist, for one who writes for the public press, is as old as the late 1600s. Journal is in special use for the day by day record of a public body. The journals of the British houses of parliament hold the official record of business done. They do not note speeches, save for hints of them in the earliest volumes.
britannica-1911-kendal:
Kendal is a market town and borough in Westmorland, England, 251 miles north northwest from London on the Windermere branch railway. Its people numbered 14,183 in 1901. Its full name is Kirkby Kendal, or Kirkby in Kendal, and it is the largest town in the county. It stands in a fine setting on the river Kent and is built without a regular plan.

Its white walled houses with blue slated roofs and its many trees give it a pleasing look. To the southwest rises Scout Scar, a steep limestone height with a wide view toward Windermere and the southern fells. The church of the Holy Trinity, whose oldest part dates from about 1200, is a Gothic building of five aisles and a square tower. In it hangs the helmet of Major Robert Philipson. He rode into the church during service hunting one of Cromwell's officers, Colonel Briggs, to take his revenge on him.
britannica-1911-keonthal: Keonthal is a petty hill state in the Punjab, India, with an area of 116 square miles. It held 22,499 people in 1901, with a revenue put at £4400. Its chief, a Rajput, gained the title of raja in 1857. After the Gurkha War in 1815, part of Keonthal, which the Gurkhas had held, was sold to the maharaja of Patiala, and the rest was given back to its hereditary chief. The district of Punar was added to the state in 1823. The raja holds lordship over four petty states near by.
britannica-1911-lagos-portugal:
Lagos is a seaport of southern Portugal, in the district of Faro, the old Algarve, on the Atlantic at the estuary of the small river Lagos, crossed by a stone bridge. Its population in 1900 was 8291. Fortifications of the 17th century defend it, and an aqueduct 800 yds. long supplies its water. The harbour is deep, capacious and sheltered on the north and west. Vines and figs grow around, and Lagos is the centre of important sardine and tunny fisheries; its trade goes by small coasting vessels, since there is no railway.

The town stands on or near the Roman Lacobriga and has held the rank of city since the 15th century. Cape St Vincent lies 22 m. W. Prince Henry the Navigator founded Sagres nearby in 1421. Off Lagos, Jervis beat a larger Spanish squadron in 1797 and Boscawen defeated a French fleet in 1759. The great earthquake of 1755 destroyed much of the city.
britannica-1911-lambert-john-general:
John Lambert (1619–1694), English general in the Great Rebellion, was born at Calton Hall, Kirkby Malham, in the West Riding of Yorkshire. He studied law without making it his profession and married Frances Lister in 1639. At the Civil War's opening he took up arms for Parliament, becoming a captain under Lord Fairfax in September 1642 and a colonel a year later. He distinguished himself at the siege of Hull in 1643 and at Nantwich and Bradford in 1644. At Marston Moor, though his regiment was routed, he cut his way through to Cromwell.

In 1645 he was appointed to succeed Fairfax over the northern forces, though Poyntz soon replaced him, and he was wounded before Pontefract. He helped draw up the Instrument of Government, pressed for alliance with Spain and war with France in 1653, and opposed Cromwell's West Indies expedition. In the 1654 debates he proposed making the protectorate hereditary, but was defeated.
britannica-1911-laval:
Laval is a town in north west France and capital of the Mayenne department on its river. A 1911 Britannica entry gives its people as close to twenty five thousand in 1906. On the right bank stands the old feudal city with its ancient castle. Irregular houses with slate roofs and gables peer from groves on the hill.

On the left bank the new town spreads in straight streets across the plain. The river runs eighty yards broad at the crossing in the town centre. A handsome rail viaduct and a stone bridge called Pont Neuf span the stream. The entry paints a town split in two by water, age, and plan.
britannica-1911-martial:
Martial, full name Marcus Valerius Martialis, was a Latin writer of epigrams. He was born in Spain in one of the years thirty eight to forty one. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Most facts on his career come from his own poems alone.

Martial was born at Bilbilis, a town that was also called Augusta Bilbilis. He calls himself sprung from Celts and Iberians, a man of the Tagus. His parents Fronto and Flaccilla seem to have died in his youth. His home held plain comfort, with hunting and fishing near at hand. Dates of public events help fix when his books of verse came out.
britannica-1911-maxims-legal:
Legal maxims are set rules or sayings that sum up points of law. The 1911 Britannica article notes that the Latin word maxima has no exact twin in Roman law. Still, the rule books of Roman jurists hold stores of such sayings. Early English writers praised maxims without reserve. One old book rates them as strong in law as statutes are. Coke held that a maxim bears the highest rank and surest weight of all.

Bacon set out their use in his preface to a store of maxims. They settle doubt, guide judgment, and grace a plea, he wrote. They curb empty quibbles and drag errors into the open. Scots courts of old settled rights by a straight appeal to maxims. The piece notes that later ages set less store by them. Growth of law and of civic life wore down their sway.
britannica-1911-menial: Menial, a word tied to household service, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It means what belongs to home service, and in particular a domestic servant. Since such service was held in low esteem, the term became one of contempt. The word comes from an old term, meinie, for the company of servants or retainers in a house. Its root lies in an old French word that stems from the Latin for a mansion or house.
britannica-1911-montreal:
Montreal is the subject of a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Montreal is a city in Canada, its leading seat of commerce and chief port of entry. It stands on the southeast of Montreal island, where the Ottawa and Saint Lawrence rivers meet. It lies in the province of Quebec. Its place at the head of ocean navigation, near a thousand miles inland, is called fine.

The article stresses the ship channel below the city. Ocean ships drawing thirty feet can pass at low water. Deepening of the channel began in 1844 and passed through several hands. Depth grew from eleven feet to over twenty seven feet by 1888. The Lachine canal opened the way for ships from the Great Lakes. Digging began in 1821, and the canal was finished four years later. It soon proved too small and was enlarged again and again.
britannica-1911-naini-tal:
Naini Tal is a town and district of British India, in the Kumaon division of the United Provinces, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes both. The town stands 6,400 feet above the sea on a lake ringed by high mountains. Its people numbered 7,609 in 1901. It serves as a health resort for people from the plains and as the summer seat of the provincial government.

The town is prone to landslides, and a grave disaster of that kind struck in September 1880. A railway runs from Bareilly to Kathgodam, twenty-two miles away by cart road. The district takes in the lower hills of Kumaon and the flat strip at their foot. Its hills rise to nearly 9,000 feet, and forests cover vast tracts of them. The entry gives the district's area and its falling population.
britannica-1911-nergal:
Nergal was a sun god of Babylon whose chief seat of worship was at Kutha. That town stood as a great cult and trade hub, so his cult outlived the move to merge all sun cults into one god. Hymns and tales paint him as a god of war and plague. He stands for the noon sun and the high sun of the year, which brings death to men.

From that role he came to rule the land of the dead, a vast cave past the earth. A spouse god stood with him there. He is shown as a lion, and his sign is a mace topped by a lions head. Great lion stone guards at shrines and halls bear his form.
britannica-1911-numeral:
Numeral, a sign used to stand for a number, is defined and traced in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The piece opens with a bold claim, that signs for numbers are older than writing itself. Folk first counted on their fingers, it says, and we still count by tens for that reason.

From fingers, the text moves to hand signs that could show any count below ten thousand, with set bends of the fingers for units, tens and more. It then turns to written signs, from marks piled up in the Roman way to the signs of Babylon and Egypt. Egyptian marks for huge counts are noted, one for a million shown as a man with arms raised. A table sets out how early forms ran together into single signs, which helps a reader see how modern figures grew.
britannica-1911-oecumenical:
Oecumenical is a word that comes through Latin from a Greek term for the whole inhabited world, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a short entry. Its chief use is for what belongs to the universal Christian Church. It is applied above all to the general councils of the early church. 

In the Roman Church, a council counts as oecumenical when it is called from the whole church under the pope or his legates. Its decrees, once confirmed by the pope, bind all. The word has also served for gatherings of other bodies, such as the Oecumenical Methodist Conferences that began in 1881. It has been a title of the patriarch of Constantinople since the five hundreds.
britannica-1911-offal: Offal is waste stuff, the off fall, that which drops off in craft work. The 1911 Britannica entry ties the word to Dutch and German kin terms. Its chief use is for waste parts of a beast slain for food. It can mean flesh gone rotten as well. In fishing it means small fry caught with good fish, thrown back or used as soil feed. In grain work it means grains too small to grind. In milling it means wheat husk with flour on it, sold as beast feed.
britannica-1911-paray-le-monial:
Paray le Monial, a town in east mid France, is drawn in a 1911 Britannica place entry. It lies on a hill slope by the Bourbince River, west of Macon. A port on the Canal du Centre serves its trade by boat. Rail lines meet there for five towns of the land. Its folk count for nineteen oh six was three thousand three hundred eighty two.

Its chief hall is the priory church of Saint Pierre from the twelve hundreds. That church copies the great abbey church of Cluny in its plan. Horse trade leads the work of its district as a whole. Brick, tile, and floor work are made in the town shops. Visions of a nun in sixteen eighty five drew church crowds that still come each year.
britannica-1911-penitential:
A penitential was a hand book for priests on the pain due for sins, set out in a church entry in the 1911 Britannica. Such books held a great place in the early mid ages of the church. Ireland, England, and the Frank lands used them most in that age. They taught rough new folk the path of right and wrong by rule. Their rules came from church meets and from the words of old church sages.

Rules for the strayed reach back to the first age of the church. The book of Cyprian bore the rulings of African meets for lost sheep. A church post grew up whose sole charge was to set pains for sins. Three shifts grew those rules into a full code of church law in time. Hush word of sins, more priests with charge of souls, and need all drove that growth.
britannica-1911-perceval:
Perceval is the hero of a group of Arthurian romances in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His name takes many forms, Parzival in German and Peredur in Welsh among them. The group is small beside the whole cycle, yet of high importance. At root the tale has the character of a folk story.

Perceval is the son of a widow in these romances. His father was slain in tourney, battle, or by treachery. Fearing the boy would share that fate, his mother fled to the woods. There she raised him ignorant of his name, his birth, and all knightly skills. The youth grew strong, swift, and fair, but of very limited wit. He passed his days chasing the beasts of the forest on foot. One day he met a party of knights in full armour. He first took their leader for God himself, the article relates.
britannica-1911-photography-celestial:
Celestial photography is explained in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article by comparison with ordinary photography. In a portrait, artificial light is thrown on the sitter's face, directly or by reflection. On a dull day a longer exposure is needed. In photographing the stars, no such lighting is possible. No searchlight could sensibly affect the heavenly bodies.

The light used for the stars is their own, and its feebleness forces long exposures. The fainter the object, the longer the exposure must be. The invention of the dry plate changed the field. With the wet plate, exposures were limited to the few minutes the film stayed wet. A dry plate can stay in the telescope for days, weeks, or even years if need be. At daylight the camera is capped, and at night the plate goes back, pointed at the same stars. The exposure then resumes with no loss.
britannica-1911-pinto-anibal: Anibal Pinto is the subject of a short life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Santiago, Chile, in 1825, he rose to be president there. He trained for foreign service at the legation in Rome. He learned rule as governor of Concepcion, then served as minister of war and marine from 1871 to 1876. As president, from 1876 to 1881, he faced a money crisis first. Then he led his land through war with Peru and Bolivia. The text praises his calm judgment.
britannica-1911-pitch-musical:
Pitch, in music, is treated at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The pitch of a sound is defined by ear through its absolute place in the scale, and through its place relative to other sounds. It is defined precisely by a vibration number, the count of pulsations of a string, a column of air, or another vibrator in one second of time.

The entry warns that lands reckon the vibration two ways, a full swing to and fro in Britain and America, a single swing elsewhere. The only official standard is the French one, dating from 1859 and kept by a tuning fork. Its number is stated in the decree that set the Diapason Normal. The natural basis for a standard, the entry argues, is the voice, above all the male voice. There is no reason to think the voice has changed in the period for which evidence exists.
britannica-1911-power-transmission-elect:
Power transmission by wire, part four of a wide tech survey, fills a long entry in the 1911 Britannica. Wire ropes, air force, and high water force still serve on a small scale, the text notes. The main load now falls on the power house and the motor linked by a wire line. Turns from shaft force to wire force and back waste so little that few rivals stand. Rail and tram work takes the great bulk of such use in that age.

Steady flows serve tram work at five or six hundred volts in the main. Long range work shuns steady flows, since high force is hard to make and trim. One machine seldoms tops three thousand volts with a strong flow at once. Swap flows rule in American use for long range work by choice. Swiss plants join machines in a row for steady force with fair gain.
britannica-1911-power-transmission-mecha:
Mechanical power transmission, the sending of power by belts, ropes, shafts, gearing, and chains, opens a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Each method can work alone or joined with the rest. The entry starts from a plain mill scene. Power made by an engine must reach the many machines in a factory.

A belt on the fly wheel of the prime mover sends power to the line shaft. Pulleys set along that shaft pass power on by more belts. Small counter shafts with fast and loose pulleys let each machine start or stop at will. From there belts drive the pulleys of each tool in turn. The text then turns to how to measure the power sent through such a train.
britannica-1911-pseudo-peripteral: Pseudo-peripteral is a term of building defined in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Greek parts of the word mean false, round, and a wing. It names a temple where walls were built between the columns that ring the inner hall. The columns thus become part of the wall, as in the great temple at Agrigentum. In Roman temples the same plan let builders enlarge the inner room. The porch alone kept free standing columns.
britannica-1911-rascal: Rascal is a short word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word first meant a rabble, the camp followers and dregs of an army, or the lowest of the folk. Now it names one person, a rogue or a knave. It came into English from an Old French word whose root is in doubt. In the hunt it was also used for the weak, poor male deer of a herd. The piece links it to a French verb for scraping, as the scourings of the herd.
britannica-1911-recital:
Recital is the subject of a brief word entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term meaning to read out, most of all of a public document. It names an account or repetition of the details of an act or fact. That broad sense leads into two more precise uses.

In law a recital is the part of a deed that states certain facts. In a lease, for example, it sets out the purpose for which the deed is made. In music the word names a performance by a single person. It also names a performance made up of the works of a single composer.
britannica-1911-rehearsal: Rehearsal, in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, comes from a word meaning to say over again. Its root picture is raking over the same ground, as with a harrow. A rehearsal is the trial playing of a play, piece of music, or recitation in private, for practice before the public showing. A full rehearsal runs the whole piece with all the players. A dress rehearsal adds scenery, dress, and props, exactly as in public.
britannica-1911-rime-royal:
Rime royal is a stanza form described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is Italian in extraction, the piece holds. Yet it is bound up almost wholly with English poetry. Its great age runs from the thirteen hundreds into the early sixteen hundreds.

The form seems cut down from the eight-line ottava rima. Dropping the fifth line leaves seven lines on three rhymes. Chaucer used the stanza with skill, if he did not invent it outright. His long poem Troilus and Cressida is written in rime royal throughout. The Prioress's Tale in the Canterbury Tales shows the same mastery. Hoccleve and Lydgate used the stanza as a habit in the next century. In the fifteen hundreds it stood as the classical form for heroic verse in England. Scotland had long prized it too, in the King's Quair and the fables of Henryson.
britannica-1911-ring-goal:
Ring goal is a game for two persons, described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It is played on a ground or indoor rink of set length and width. A ring of split cane forms the core gear. That ring is driven through the air by two sticks held inside it, like small billiard cues.

The goals are two uprights with a net stretched on a slope behind the goal line. The aim is to drive the ring into the goal of the other player. Each goal made scores one point. The server drives the ring, and the other player must catch it on one or both sticks and return it. Points are also scored for faults, such as a ring that falls short or goes out of court. Eleven points make a game. The game was devised at Oxford about eighteen eighty five.
britannica-1911-rock-crystal:
Rock-crystal is a clear, colourless kind of quartz used as a gem stone. The 1911 Britannica article says it lines hollows in quartz veins that run through granite and like rocks. Its glassy look and cold feel led the ancients to think it a kind of frozen water. The very word crystal comes from the Greek for ice. In the Swiss Alps a class of hunters, called Strahlers, seek the stones at great risk.

A famed find in the Bernese Oberland in 1719 yielded some twenty tons of crystal. One piece weighed eight hundredweight. The Romans of the empire prized the stone and cut it into vases and cups. Balls of crystal served to kindle sacred fire and to cool the hands of ladies in summer heat. In modern times glass has taken much of its place.
britannica-1911-romsdal:
Romsdal is the valley of the river Rauma in Norway, a stream of the west coast. The Rauma is a torrent that drops from a lake to the Romsdal Fjord. The nearest port is Molde, from which steamers run to the foot of the valley. A good road runs through the valley from end to end. That valley is one of the finest in southern Norway, the entry says.

Steep mountains flank the road, ending in abrupt peaks of great height. Vengetinder, Romsdalshorn, and the witch peaks are named among them in the text. Several waterfalls are seen along the way, one falling near a thousand feet. The lake at the head also drains the other way to the Skagerrack. The Romsdal gives its name to a county of the coast. That county holds ports such as Aalesund, Molde, and Christiansund.
britannica-1911-saetersdal: Saetersdal is a district in the south of Norway, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It comprises the valleys of the Otter river and its tributaries. The river rises in the high fells above the Bukken Fjord and flows south to Christiansund. The entry notes that the people keep old customs and a distinctive costume of their own. A railway follows the valley to Byglands Fjord, fostering the local farm and timber trade, and a driving road runs on from there.
britannica-1911-seal:
Seal is an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the common seal and the wider group of sea mammals that share its name. In the strict sense the word names the common European seal, the lead kind of the suborder Pinnipedia. In wider use it covers all members of that group except the walrus.

The article describes how seals live: they swim and dive with great ease, stay under water a quarter of an hour or more, and eat only live prey caught in the sea. They still come onto beaches, rocks, or ice floes to sleep, bask, and bear their young. A mother bears one pup a year in most cases, first clothed in thick white fur. On land the true seals shuffle and drag themselves along, unlike the eared seals, which walk on all four feet. Most kinds gather in huge herds at the breeding season.
britannica-1911-sign-manual-royal:
Sign-manual, royal, is the sovereign's own signature, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains what it does in British government. By it the sovereign shows his pleasure in an order, a commission, or a warrant. A sign-manual warrant may be an act of rule, such as an appointment to office. It may also be the authority for putting the Great Seal to a document.

Such a warrant must be countersigned by a chief secretary of state or another answerable minister. A royal order under the sign-manual, as apart from a warrant, allows the spending of money. Some posts are filled instead by commission under the great seal, such as an army officer's post or a colonial governor's. The sign-manual also gives power to make and confirm treaties. When George the Fourth grew too weak to sign, an act let a stamp stand in its place.
britannica-1911-signal:
Signal, a word found in near forms across the tongues of Europe, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It comes from a Latin word for a mark or sign. A signal is a means to send word by a set system or code. It serves where a plain spoken or written word is needless, unwise, or out of reach.

The ways used shift with the case and the aim in view. What carries the thought may be things seen, sounds, or motions. In fact it may be anything that can touch the senses at all. The one firm need is a prior deal with the receiver on what each sign means. Any two persons can thus build a private code. Such secret codes, built on voice tones or stress, have grown fine enough to mimic wonders at times.
britannica-1911-spiral:
Spiral, in the science of sums, is the path traced by the tip of a line that grows as it turns round a fixed point. Such curves are best told by sums that link the length of that line to its turn. The entry deals with the chief flat forms of the curve. Plates show four kinds at a glance.

One kind grows in step step as its turn grows in plain step. Its cut line meets the ray at one set slant at all points. Kin forms bear the names of old Greek men of sums. One set comes from the path of a mote drawn to a core.
britannica-1911-states-general:
States General is a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a name used for great assemblies in France and in the Dutch lands. In both lands the name meant a meeting of men sent by the ranks of the realm. Kings called them to gain funds and counsel for the state.

The entry traces why kings found it best to meet the ranks as one body. Feudal power hemmed in royal power as it grew in scope. The first full French meeting of the kind is dated to thirteen hundred and two. Lords, church men, and town men sat in that first assembly. Like bodies in England, Spain, and Germany are set beside it for scale.
britannica-1911-stendal:
Stendal, a town of Germany in Prussian Saxony, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in a scenic spot on the Uchte river, seventy miles west of Berlin. Rail lines to Hanover, Bremen, Magdeburg, and Wittenberge meet there. The entry gives it 23,281 people in 1905.

Relics of its old importance include a cathedral, built in the 1420s on a site founded in 1188. It now houses the finds of the Altmark region. A Gothic church of Saint Mary, a Roland column of 1535, and two fortified gateways also survive. The town has large railway workshops and trades in cloth, tobacco, machinery, and stoves. Stendal was founded in 1151 by Albert the Bear on a Wendish site. It became capital of the Altmark and a frequent imperial residence, and rose to great prosperity.
britannica-1911-suez-canal:
Suez Canal is the subject of a long study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, which opens with the old links between two seas. Before the modern canal, no straight water road joined the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. At sundry past times a link did exist by way of the Nile. Trade with the east first went overland to ports at the head of the Gulf of Suez.

Old writers credit a king called Sesostris with the first canal from the Nile to the Red Sea. Marks on a temple at Karnak hint that such a cut existed under Seti the First. It ran from the Nile along a green valley to a port at the head of the gulf. Pharaoh Necho began a fresh cut that was never done. Darius took up the work and made the channel fit for ships.
britannica-1911-sulphonal:
Sulphonal is a drug once prized as a means to bring on sleep. It is made by a chain of steps from plain goods, as set out by a German hand in past years. It forms in clear prisms that melt at a set heat. It scarce thaws in cold drink but thaws well in hot drink and in strong drink.

It gives long sleep in nerve forms of no rest, and it serves in mad states too. It does not drag the heart or breath down as some drugs do. Its work is unsure, though, and next day drag is oft felt. Long use builds a habit with grave harm, so its use is now held with great care.
browne-s-folly-from-the-doliver-romance-:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote a letter-sketch of a Salem hill, dated at the Wayside on 28 August 1860. Cousin had asked for a tale to aid the Essex Institute. Hawthorne owns he can write none. Years have passed since Twice-Told Tales and Mosses from an Old Manse, and the knack of small tales has left him, he says.

In place of a tale he gives a place: Brown's Folly. The hill, long and low like a whale's back in a calm sea, lay near Salem, in Salem, Danvers, or Beverly — he owns he knows not which. A green lane, seldom trod, ran at its base. On that rise he had once meant to set a dream tale. The piece stands inside The Doliver Romance and Other Pieces, a set of late tales and sketches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostino-bern:
Agostino Bernal, Spanish theologian of Magallon in Aragon, was born in 1587. He died at Saragossa on 13 September 1642. He joined the Jesuits in 1603, aged sixteen. Classically finished, he taught humanities and rhetoric with success. Most of his life, however, went to professing philosophy and theology at Saragossa, ending there.

A man of rare innocence and candour of soul, his love of prayer was so great it would be hard to say whether meditation or study took more of his time. Many looked on him as one of his age's most learned men. His published works are Disputationes de Divini Verbi Incarnatione, Saragossa 1639, and Disputationes de Sacramentis in genere, Eucharistia et Ordine, Lyons 1651, a posthumous work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-vandal:
Albert Vandal was a French writer born at Paris in July 1853 and dead there in August 1910. His father directed the postal service under the Second Empire. Vandal joined the Council of State as auditor, but family tradition and moderate, liberal views cost him his post under the Republic. He became the disciple and friend of Albert Sorel, professor of diplomatic history, and later succeeded him in the chair.

Vandal's first book, a travel account of Sweden and Norway, appeared in 1876. It was followed by works on Louis XV and Elizabeth of Russia and on the French embassy in the East. The book that fixed his reputation was Napoleon and Alexander I, which twice won the Gobert grand prize and opened the French Academy to him in 1897. He later published on the advent of Bonaparte and joined fellow Catholics in writing to the pope after the law separating Church and State.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-frontal:
The altar frontal, or antipendium, covers the altar front, from table to predella and gospel corner to epistle side. It grew from silk or precious curtains veiling the space under the altar, later joined into one drapery hung from the table. A partial frontal is forbidden, and an altar facing the people at the back needs its back covered too.

No material is prescribed. Precious metals with enamels and jewels, painted or gilt wood, cloth of gold, velvet, or silk usually match the vestments. It may bear Christ's image, scenes from his life, or emblems such as lamb, pelican, chalice and host. The altar's patron saint may appear too, but never skulls or cross-bones on a black frontal. Where the altar front is beautifully painted or a reliquary stands beneath a column-borne table, the frontal may be unnecessary, though solemn occasions call for richer ones.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-marec:
Ambrose Maréchal, third Archbishop of Baltimore, was born at Ingres near Orléans in 1764 and died at Baltimore in 1828. Set for law by his parents, he entered Orléans's Sulpician seminary, took tonsure late in 1787, and, fleeing revolutionary chaos, was ordained at Bordeaux in 1792. On ordination day, at life's risk with Abbés Richard, Martignon, and Cicquard, he sailed for America, reaching Baltimore on 24 June 1792 for his first Mass.

He served missions in St. Mary's County and Bohemia, taught theology at St. Mary's in 1799 and Georgetown's staff in 1801. He then taught in France at Saint-Flour, Lyons, Aix, and Marseilles under Napoleon. Back in Baltimore in 1812, he declined Philadelphia in 1816 and became coadjutor to Archbishop Neale in 1817. He was consecrated Archbishop of Baltimore in December 1817 after Neale's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belial:
Belial is a short doctrinal and scriptural entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, untangling a name many readers take for a devil. It explains that in Hebrew the word is not a proper name at all, but a phrase for worthlessness or wickedness. Only in later translation did it harden into a personal name for evil.

The entry walks through Bible passages where translators render the same Hebrew word in different ways, sometimes as Belial and sometimes as the devil. It notes the famous contrast in Paul's second letter to Corinth, where Belial stands for darkness against Christ as light. Milton's separate demon of impurity gets a brief correcting note.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedictional:
The Benedictional, a book of blessings used in the Church, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Its Latin name, Benedictionale, marks it as a collection of benedictions, or formal blessings, drawn largely from ancient sacramentaries, books of prayers for Mass. Some manuscripts scatter the blessings through the book, while others gather them apart.

A famous manuscript in the imperial library at Vienna gave the collection its name when Lambecius edited it, believing his edition the first. The entry corrects him, noting that nearly all its blessings had already appeared in print elsewhere. It is a brief note on a book's name and tangled publishing history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-lo:
Bernardino López de Carvajal, a Spanish cardinal, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Plasencia in 1455, he died at Rome in 1523. Nephew of the famed Cardinal Juan Carvajal, he rose fast at Rome under Sixtus IV, holding Astorga, then Badajoz, then Cartagena, three Spanish sees in turn.

As nuncio to Spain and then Spanish ambassador to Alexander VI, he moved between courts with ease, and Alexander made him cardinal in 1493. Later years brought the troubled Council of Pisa and a fall from favour, followed by restoration. The entry sketches a courtier-prelate of the Renaissance papacy at its most worldly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-betrothal:
Betrothal, the promise of future marriage, receives a full canon-law entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its Latin name is sponsalia, and the Church defines it as a deliberate, free, mutual promise, put into words, between two fit persons. It is a true compact, not a mere intention, and it needs care matching the weight of what it promises.

A one-sided promise, even if accepted, does not make a betrothal, and force, grave fear, or substantial error can void it. A valid betrothal binds the parties in justice to marry, and creates an impediment of public decency toward relatives. The entry maps a promise that law once treated almost like marriage itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-joanna-of-: Blessed Joanna of Portugal, daughter of King Alfonso V, was born at Lisbon in 1452 and died at Aveiro in 1490. From childhood she resolved to be Christ's spouse and enter religion. She resisted with courage every attempt by father and brother to marry her off. As heir in default of male issue, her refusal angered family and country. Princes sought her hand in vain, and she once ruled as regent in her father's absence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blaise-pascal:
Blaise Pascal, the French mathematician, physicist, and religious writer, is the subject of this long 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Clermont-Ferrand in 1623, he died in Paris in 1662. His father taught him grammar, Latin, Spanish, and mathematics by an original method, and at twelve he wrote on sounds, at sixteen on conic sections.

At Rouen he built an arithmetical machine to ease his father's tax calculations. A night of religious conversion, recorded in a paper sewn into his coat, turned him to Port-Royal and Jansenism. His Provincial Letters of 1656 defended the Jansenists with wit, and his Pensées, left unfinished, remain a classic of Christian apology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-pro:
Canonical provision is the regular way a vacant benefice, a church office with income, is filled. The entry breaks it into three steps: choosing the person, granting the title through canonical institution, and installing the holder in possession. People may be chosen by election, presentation, recommendation, resignation in someone's favor, or an approved exchange. A proper superior must still confirm the choice.

Greater offices usually come from the pope and lesser ones from the bishop. The bishop normally fills every office in his own diocese, though the pope's full jurisdiction lets him appoint anywhere. The entry recalls English statutes of 1351 and 1390 that resisted papal appointments. Such extraordinary provisions now occur only in defined cases. Appointment letters, it adds, are normally required.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal:
A cardinal is a dignitary of the Roman Church and counselor of the pope. The word once meant any priest permanently attached to a church. It comes from the Latin cardo, or hinge, and later meant a principal or excellent priest of a central church. The entry follows the office through its origin, growth, and changes across ten sections, from cardinal priests, deacons, and bishops to titles, dioceses, and deaconries.

Later sections weigh the cardinals' ties to bishops and to the pope, their nomination, duties, and rights, and the life of the College of Cardinals itself. Examples range from prominent priests at Constantinople, Milan, Ravenna, and Cologne to the great medieval holders of the office. The result is a full institutional history of a rank that grew from parish attachment into the body that counsels the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cathedral:
A cathedral is the chief church of a diocese, where the bishop has his throne and nearby his residence. In the strict sense it is the bishop's own church, where he presides, teaches, and leads worship for the whole community. The name comes from the Greek and Latin for throne, and in early church writing it always carried the idea of authority.

The article recalls Christ's words about the scribes seated on the chair of Moses. It also recalls the feasts honoring Peter's chair at Antioch and Rome, showing how the throne became the chief symbol of authority. It distinguishes the cathedral from a merely episcopal church. It also sets it apart from the churches of archbishops, metropolitans, primates, and patriarchs, and notes that the East simply calls the bishop's church the great church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceremonial:
A ceremonial is the book that gives the full order for religious ceremony and solemn worship in ecclesiastical functions. At present only two official liturgical books bear the title: the Caeremoniale Romanum and the Caeremoniale Episcoporum. The Missal, Breviary, Ritual, and Pontifical also contain directions for Mass, the Office, the sacraments, and episcopal functions. So in a certain sense they may be counted ceremonials.

But their main purpose is to give the texts of the liturgical prayers. Directions are added only in general terms, so they are not regarded as ceremonials in the accepted sense. The oldest ceremonial books and rituals of the Roman Church go by the name Ordines Romani. Mabillon enumerates fifteen of them. They treat the choice of a Roman pontiff, Mass, Baptism and Holy Orders, and functions for special days of the year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-bur:
A long entry on Christian burial, the interment of the dead with church rites in consecrated ground. Jews and most ancient peoples buried their dead, while Greeks and Romans used both burial and cremation. Early Christians used burial only, as Tertullian attests, resting on the resurrection of the body and its likeness to Christ's rising, and on Jewish custom in Tobit, Sirach, and Maccabees.

Canon law lets every person choose his burial ground, even without a formal will, on any reasonable proof, including a confessor's word. The entry sets out the Church's law and rites and its recent prohibitions of cremation. It links cremation to materialism and opposition to Catholic teaching rather than hygiene. It also covers the Greek Church's burial rite, with notes on absolution crosses and burial law authorities such as Lex and Sagmüller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ciudad-real:
Ciudad Real is a bishopric-priorate of Spain's Military Orders, directly subject to the Holy See. The military orders of Santiago, Alcantara, Calatrava, and Montesa held scattered church lands. Article Six of the Concordat of 1851 ordered a single circumscription, a coto redondo, for them, governed by a prior of episcopal rank.

Pius the Ninth created the bishopric-priorate in 1875 by the bull Ad Apostolicam Beati Petri, giving it the whole province of Ciudad Real, drawn from Toledo, Cuenca, and Cordova. The bishop resides at Ciudad Real, population 15,327 in 1900. Alfonso the Twelfth and his successors, as Grand Masters of the orders, nominate the bishop-prior within three months of a vacancy. He takes the titular title of Bishop of Dora. The Cardinal Archbishop of Toledo executed the bull on 4 June 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Sister St. Euphrosine's entry follows the Congregation of Notre Dame de Montreal through foundress Marguerite Bourgeoys, born at Troyes on 17 April 1620. Third child of merchant Abraham Bourgeois, she answered Paul de Maisonneuve's 1653 invitation to teach at Ville Marie, Montreal. She sailed that June, giving herself to works of mercy. Her first school opened on 30 April 1657. A return to France won four companions, then a boarding school, an industrial school, and sodalities.

In 1670 she sailed again, returning in 1672 with royal letters and six new companions. In 1675 she built Notre Dame de Bon Secours chapel. Seeking freedom of action, she founded an unenclosed community under simple vows, winning Quebec's bishop's approbation and pressing those terms into rule. Sisters taught at Ville Marie and trained young women as Christian teachers. Later missions spread across Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island, with day and boarding schools teaching all fundamental branches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corporal:
Herbert Thurston's entry treats the corporal, from Latin corpus, body. It is a square white linen cloth, now usually somewhat smaller than an altar's breadth, on which the Sacred Host and chalice rest during Mass. Though formal evidence is wanting, something in the corporal's nature may fairly be assumed in use since Christianity's earliest days. Early stages blur the corporal with the altar-cloth.

Saint Optatus, about 375, asks what Christian is unaware that in celebrating the Sacred Mysteries the altar's wood is covered with a linen cloth, leaving doubt which cloth he means. This likely forms the earliest direct testimony. Very probably the early centuries used only one large linen cloth, serving both as altar-cloth and corporal, doubled back to cover the gifts. Existing liturgical rules forbid embroidery on the corporal and require pure white linen throughout, though many exceptions seem to have existed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dungal:
Dungal, an Irish monk who taught, studied the stars, and wrote verse, flourished about 820. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry places him in 811 at Saint-Denis near Paris, an Irish priest and scholar. That year he wrote to Charlemagne explaining an eclipse of the sun thought to have occurred in 810. Alcuin calls him a bishop in one letter, and in 823 a capitulary of Lothair names him. In 825 an imperial decree made him master of the school at Pavia.

That is the last imperial record of him, but in 827 or 828 he wrote against Claudius of Turin in defense of images. Since he left his books to Saint Columbanus at Bobbio, he likely spent his last days in that Irish monastery. The entry gathers a career pieced together from charters and letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-encyclical:
An encyclical is, by its Greek roots, a circular letter, and this entry explains how usage narrowed the word. In modern times it means almost only papal documents. They differ in form from Bulls and Briefs. Their heading addresses the patriarchs, primates, archbishops, and bishops of the universal Church in communion with Rome. By exception, some go to the bishops of one country alone.

Thus Pius X's letter of January 1907 to the bishops of France counts as an encyclical. It was issued in French rather than Latin. Leo XIII's Longinqua Oceani of 1895 to the bishops of the United States does not bear the name, though it keeps the form. Encyclicals to the whole Church usually treat the Church's welfare. They condemn an error, warn of dangers to faith or morals, urge constancy, or prescribe cures. The entry prints the opening and close, using Pascendi on Modernism as its specimen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faro-portugal:
Faro is a Portuguese diocese in the southern Algarve, suffragan of Evora. Its see began at Ossonoba in 306 and lapsed under long Moorish rule. Restored at Silves in 1188, it passed in turn through Braga, Seville, and Lisbon. The episcopal title moved to Faro on 30 March 1577.

Its old cathedral began as a Roman basilica, later altered and rebuilt by Moorish hands. The diocese then counted 66 parishes, 214 churches, 112 priests, and many chapels. Some 228,000 Catholics lived within its wide bounds at the time. The article traces the see through Moorish conquest, transfer, and later revival.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-cab:
Francisco Cabral, born in the castle of Govillou in the diocese of Guarda, Portugal, in 1529 and dead at Goa in 1609, was a Portuguese Jesuit missionary in Japan. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1554 and, after his studies, went to Japan. There he laboured strenuously to spread the Christian religion, winning the friendship of princes and kings, several of whom, with their subjects, were brought to the faith by his zealous work.

He held high posts in his order's government in the East. They were superior of Japan for twelve years, master of novices, rector of the College of San Pablo at Goa, and visitor to India, the inspector of Jesuit missions there. He died at eighty-one with a reputation for prudence and holiness. He was a figure of the first century of the Japan mission, before persecution closed that field to the missionaries who had built it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-de-b:
Francois de Bonal, born in 1734 at the castle of Bonal near Agen and dead at Munich in 1800, was Bishop of Clermont through the French Revolution. As a clerical deputy to the Estates-General of 1789 he stood out for moderation and firmness.

 From prison Louis XVI asked whether he should receive Easter communion. Bonal answered with sympathy yet advised abstaining, since the king had sanctioned decrees destructive of religion, above all the civil constitution of the clergy. Refusing the constitutional oath, he fled through Flanders and Holland, was captured and sentenced to deportation, escaped, and spent his last years in German cities, leaving a Spiritual Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-de-m:
Francois de Montmorency Laval, born at Montigny-sur-Avre on 30 April 1623 and dead at Quebec on 6 May 1708, was the first Bishop of Canada. Scion of an illustrious family whose motto claimed God aid the first Christian baron, he studied under the Jesuits at La Fleche and at Clermont College in Paris. He joined a fervent group directed by Father Bagot that became the seed of the Seminary of Foreign Missions, sister to the future seminary of Quebec. His two elder brothers died in battle, leaving him the family title and estate.

 As bishop at Quebec he built the Canadian Church in hardship. The entry ranks him among the most holy figures of his age for mortification, humility, lively faith, and boundless charity to the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-ludwig-:
Franz Ludwig von Erthal, born at Lohr on the Main on 16 September 1730 and died at Wurzburg on 16 February 1795. He was Prince-Bishop of Wurzburg and Bamberg whose rule was a boon for Church and State. After theology at Mainz, Wurzburg, and Rome and law at Vienna, he became president of Wurzburg's secular government in 1762. Sent to Vienna in 1768 for the investiture of Prince-Bishop Adam Friedrich von Seinsheim, Joseph II made him imperial privy councillor and inspector of the Imperial Chamber at Wetzlar. In 1776 he served as imperial commissioner at the Diet of Ratisbon.

He succeeded Adam Friedrich at Wurzburg on 18 March 1779 and at Bamberg the following 12 April. As temporal ruler he put people's welfare above personal considerations, spending private means on charitable institutions, founding a model hospital at Bamberg and greatly improving and partly rebuilding St. Julius Hospital at Wurzburg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-kar:
Friedrich Karl Joseph von Erthal, the last Elector and Archbishop of Mainz, began as a reformer and ended as a champion of Febronianism. Born at Mainz in 1719, he held cathedral posts, led the university, and served as envoy at Vienna before taking the electorate in July 1774. His first act as bishop was to dismiss his predecessor's free-thinking councilors.

Soon he reversed course, filling Mainz University with Protestants and free-thinkers and shutting monasteries to fund it. With three fellow archbishops he issued the Punctuation of Ems in 1786, cutting papal power to a bare honor. Wars undid him: Campo-Formio in 1797 took his lands west of the Rhine, and the Concordat of 1801 took his rule over them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-funchal:
Funchal, a diocese in the Madeira Islands, takes its name from fennel, the plant that gave the town its Latin name. Madeira, known to Rome as Purpuraria, was claimed for Portugal in 1419, and vines from Crete planted in 1445 made the island famous. Leo X raised Funchal to a see in 1514, and Clement VII briefly made it an archdiocese over Goa, Cape Verde, and other far-flung suffragans.

Set on Madeira's south coast, Funchal became the first stop for ships bound to the New World and a hub of wealth, trade, and missions. The Portuguese ringed it with four forts, though cliffs already guarded it well. By 1909 the city held about 20,000 people, and the diocese counted some 150,000 Catholics served by ninety-three priests in fifty parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaspar-de-car:
Gaspar de Carvajal, a Dominican missionary born in Extremadura around 1500, sailed down the Amazon with Orellana and lived to tell it. He reached Peru in 1533 for Indian missions, then joined Gonzalo Pizarro's 1540 push toward Quixos and the Amazon. Hunger and hostile tribes wore the party down until Pizarro sent Orellana down the Napo for food, with Carvajal aboard.

At the Amazon's meeting with the Napo, Orellana abandoned his comrades to the river's course. Carvajal and Sánchez de Vargas protested the treachery and were set ashore, later found by Pizarro in the wild. Only eighty of four hundred reached Quito in 1542. Carvajal then worked Tucumán for years, ruled his province, and died at Lima in 1584.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gradual:
The Gradual, in English often called the Grail, is the oldest and most important of the four chants of the choir's part of the Proper of the Mass. From the Latin graduale, a step, it represents, with its supplement the Tract or Alleluia, the singing of psalms alternating with Bible readings. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces a custom as old as the readings themselves.

The psalms at this place are an inheritance from the synagogue service. Alternate readings and psalms filled much of the first half of the liturgy everywhere from the beginning. Originally whole psalms were sung, in responsorial form. One reader chanted the text while the people answered each clause with an acclamation. The practice of whole psalms lasted until the fifth century, and singing them was for a time a privilege of deacons at Rome, suppressed by Gregory I in 595.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-fra:
Paris mathematician Guillaume-François-Antoine de l'Hôpital, born in 1661, gave the new differential calculus its first clear textbook. Meant for the army, he served as a cavalry captain until extreme near-sightedness forced him out. He had already solved problems set by Pascal at fifteen and studied mathematics in his tent.

In 1692 he spent four months learning the calculus from Jean Bernoulli at his estate near Vendôme. He then published his Analyse des infiniment petits in 1696, a careful guide to curves that let many readers grasp methods only a handful had known. The rule for fractions whose top and bottom both tend to zero still bears his name. His wife is said to have shared his work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-antoine-:
Jean-Antoine Chaptal, count of Chanteloup, was a French chemist and statesman born in 1756 at Nogaret and dead in Paris in 1832. Trained in medicine at Montpellier, he took the new chemistry chair there in 1781 and built chemical works of wide repute. He stayed in France through the Revolution, refusing posts abroad.

Chaptal improved gunpowder making at the Grenelle saltpetre works in 1793 and later taught at the Paris Polytechnic. Under Napoleon he sat on the Council of State and served as minister of the interior, setting up trade exchanges, chambers of commerce, and loan offices. He also brought the Sisters of Charity into hospital work and ordered the mineral water trade.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-brehal:
Jean Bréhal, a French Dominican theologian who died about 1479, earned his place by clearing Joan of Arc's name. Doctor of theology at Caen in 1443, prior of Saint-Jacques in Paris, and inquisitor-general of France from 1452 to 1474, he stood high in church and university life.

At Charles VII's instance Bréhal reviewed the acts of Joan's trial, and on 7 July 1456 solemnly declared her condemnation unjust and wicked. His full inquiry, later printed by Dominican and Jesuit scholars, remains the backbone of her rehabilitation. He resigned in 1474 and spent his last years at Évreux in study and strict observance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-de-la-ca:
José de la Canal was a Spanish Augustinian friar and church historian who lived from 1768 to 1845. Born poor in Ucieda, in Santander province, he studied in Burgos convents, joined the Augustinian order in 1785, and later taught philosophy and kept the university library at Salamanca. A spell of confinement near Avila followed his liberal newspaper writing after King Ferdinand VII returned to Spain.

Canal is best known for carrying on España Sagrada, the great source collection on Spanish church history begun in 1743. Working with Antolín Merino and then alone, he produced volumes on the churches and monasteries of Gerona, drawing on archives he searched in Barcelona and Gerona. Readers turn to this entry for a clear account of a scholar who dug up unpublished records and checked them with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-mercado-:
José Mercado Rizal was a Filipino doctor, poet, and novelist who became his country's national hero. Born at Calamba in 1861, he studied in Manila and Spain, trained in eye medicine, and published the novel Noli me tangere in Berlin in 1886. The book satirized both friar landlords and Filipino society, and its sequel, El Filibusterismo, appeared in 1891.

Spanish officials linked his writing to rebellion, exiled him to Dapitan in Mindanao, and later tried and shot him in Manila on 30 December 1896. The entry also records his retraction of Freemasonry before death, his marriage on the morning of execution, and the honors that followed, including a national holiday and a province bearing his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-carvajal:
Juan Carvajal was a Spanish cardinal and tireless papal legate of the fifteenth century. Born about 1400 at Trujillo in Extremadura, he rose in canon and civil law to auditor of the Rota and governor of Rome by 1440. His contemporary Ammanati says he was sent twenty-two times as legate to rulers and lands.

Carvajal helped end German neutrality in the Council of Basel's last phase and win the concordats of 1447 and 1448. Sent to Hungary in 1455, he joined St. John Capistran in raising some forty thousand men and lifting the siege of Belgrade in 1456. He kept organizing Hungary's defense until 1461 and died at Rome in 1469.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-mathias:
Louis Mathias, Count de Barral, was Archbishop of Tours, born at Grenoble in 1746 and dead at Paris in 1816. Trained at St. Sulpice, he served as secretary, then coadjutor, to his uncle, Bishop of Troyes, succeeding him in 1790.

Refusing the clergy oath in 1791, he fled to Constance and England, returning in 1801 to govern Meaux under the Concordat, then Tours from 1805. He often carried Napoleon's messages to the captive Pius VII at Savona and Fontainebleau, served as almoner to Empress Josephine, and sat as senator and count. He kept his peerage under Louis XVIII, lost it at the second Restoration, and died a year later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-de-carva:
Luis de Carvajal was a Franciscan theologian of Trent, born about 1500, his death date unknown. Of noble Baetican stock, he showed rare gifts of mind and heart, studied at Paris, joined the Franciscans, and taught theology there.

Sent as legate to the Council of Trent, he spoke in the fifth session, on original sin, for the Immaculate Conception, a cause he had already made famous at Paris. The council's closing words, Declarat tamen, in the fifth canon likely owe their place to him. Last seen at Antwerp in 1548, publishing a third edition of his theological sentences, he also wrote a declamation for the Immaculate Conception and a defence of monastic life against Erasmus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luisa-de-carv:
Luisa de Carvajal was a Spanish lady who gave her life to England's persecuted Catholics, born at Jaraizejo in 1568 and dead at London in 1614. Orphaned at six, she was raised by an uncle and aunt at Pamplona, showed rare holiness, and refused marriage without feeling drawn to convent life.

After her guardians died, she gathered a few household women for twelve years of prayer, then sailed for England in 1605 with her Jesuit confessor's leave. In London she visited prisoners and those in danger, tending Father Roberts and Thomas Somers just before their martyrdoms. Officials said she converted more Protestants than twenty priests, jailed her twice, and sought her removal, until death on her forty-sixth birthday ended the hunt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquis-de-po:
Sebastiao Jose de Carvalho e Mello, Marquis de Pombal, was a Portuguese statesman, born at Lisbon in 1699 and dead in 1782. His father was a country gentleman of modest means; he served in the army and married against her family's wishes. 

Joseph I named him foreign minister in 1750, and his masterful will soon made him first power in the state. He clashed with the Jesuits, blaming them for Indian resistance to the 1750 Treaty of Limits and for other troubles. After dismissing Jesuit court confessors in 1757 and implicating them in the Tavora plot, he seized Society property in January 1759 and deported about a thousand Portuguese fathers that September. His reforms abolished Indian slavery, ended the old and new Christian distinction, reorganised finance, the army, and Coimbra University, and founded the College of Nobles, School of Commerce, and Royal Press.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-de-l-:
Michael de l'Hospital was born at Aigueperse about 1504 and died at Courdimanche on 13 March 1573. He took up law at Padua, then served at Rome as auditor of the Rota. In 1537 he became a councillor of the Parliament of Paris. Henry II sent him in 1547 to the council moved from Trent to Bologna, and sixteen months later he was back in his Parliament seat.

In 1554 Marguerite of France made him chancellor of Berry, and in 1554 he became first president of the court of exchequer. When Francis II came to the throne in 1559, Guise backing brought him into the privy council. Catherine de' Medici made him chancellor in 1560. He had praised the Duke of Guise and the Cardinal of Lorraine in Latin verse. Brantome paints a mixed figure: men took him for a Huguenot though he went to Mass, and courtiers joked, God save us from l'Hospital's Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miraculous-me:
The Miraculous Medal devotion traces back to Zoe Labore, a Daughter of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul who in religion was known as Sister Catherine and was later canonized. The Blessed Virgin Mary showed herself to her three times in 1830 at the community's mother-house in Paris. The first visit fell on 18 July, the second on 27 November, and the third came a short time after that.

Sister Catherine's account of the second visit has the Virgin standing on a globe. The Virgin held a globe in her hands, its rings set with precious stones that sent out rays of light. She told Catherine a medal should be struck after this model, with a promise of great graces for those who wear it. The medal caught on fast across France and the world, and countless cures and conversions were laid to it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missal:
The Missal, from the Latin Missale, from Missa, Mass, is the book containing the prayers said by the priest at the altar. It holds all that is officially read or sung in connection with the offering of the holy Sacrifice of the Mass through the ecclesiastical year. Today's Roman Missal, now in use almost everywhere in the Catholic Church where the Latin Rite holds, falls essentially into two very uneven parts.

The smaller division, containing the portion of the liturgy said in every Mass, is placed near the middle of the book for convenient opening. It holds the Ordo Missae with the prefaces and the Canon. The larger division holds the proper prayers for each feast and season. The article traces the missal's origin and its varieties across rites and centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montreal:
Montreal is the metropolitan see of its church province in Canada, with suffragans at Saint-Hyacinthe, Sherbrooke, Valleyfield and Joliette, counting 470,000 Catholics and 720 clergy against 80,000 Protestants of various sects. Separated from Quebec by Gregory XVI in 1836, the diocese spans sixty miles by fifty-two.

Its story opens with Cartier's 1535 voyage up the Saint Lawrence to Hochelaga, the village where Montreal now stands, and the mountain he named Mont Royal. Champlain founded Quebec in 1608, and the Compagnie de Notre-Dame de Montreal then planted the island colony. The entry follows the church through British cession in 1763, the diocese's birth, and its schools, parishes and orders down to the Eucharistic Congress of 1910.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-natal:
Natal is the Vicariate Apostolic in South Africa, whose Catholic history reaches back to 1660. That year a French bishop and priests survived the wreck of the Marichal near the Cape of Good Hope. They were allowed to land but not to minister to Cape Town's few Catholics. Not until 1803 was a Catholic priest permitted to say Mass in Cape Colony, and Fathers Lansink, Melissen and Prinsen, landing that year, were expelled the next.

Pius VII in 1818 appointed Edward Bede Slater first vicar apostolic of the Cape of Good Hope and neighbouring islands, Mauritius included. Gregory XVI in 1837 set up the Vicariate of the Cape separate from Mauritius. South Africa proved too much for one bishop, so Pius IX in 1847 founded a new vicariate in the east, the seed of Natal. The entry follows its missions, parishes and bishops through the Zulu wars and the growth of Durban.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orval:
Orval, called Aurea Vallis in Latin, was a Cistercian abbey in Belgian Luxembourg in the Diocese of Trier. Benedictines from Calabria founded it in 1071 and left in 1110. Canons Regular followed them, and gave way in 1132 to Cistercians from Tre Fontane. Its first abbot, Constantine, had learned under Bernard of Clairvaux.

Hard work, thrift, and able abbots made Orval very rich. By 1750 it owned three hundred towns, villages, and manors. It drew 1,200,000 livres a year, matched by generous alms to the poor. Discipline held firm except for a lapse around the Reformation. Abbot Bernard de Montgaillard repaired it with new statutes after 1605. Jansenist leanings troubled a few monks in the early eighteenth century, and the abbey was later swept away in the French Revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paray-le-moni:
Paray-le-Monial is a French town of five thousand in Saone-et-Loire, in the Diocese of Autun. Paray surely predates the monks who gave it the surname Le Monial. Count Lambert of Chalon, his wife Adelaide, and Mayeul of Cluny founded its famed Benedictine priory in 973. The borough was already formed, with aldermen and communal rights. An old temple there was dedicated to the Mother of God.
