Polyethylene reflectors complete the stack, all assembled on the Planet general purpose critical assembly machine. Temperature sensors and the room itself get their own sections. Material data for every component follows. It is the record an experimenter needs to model exactly what was built. Measurement can then be compared against calculation, part by part.
doe-osti-3399501-national-laboratories-f:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-26849, issued July 31, 2026, surveys national laboratory capabilities in unmanned aerial systems for environmental management and stewardship. Eight authors are printed, led by James Edward Lee, Damien Michael Milazzo, and Adam Collins. The survey belongs to the National Laboratories for Environmental Management and Stewardship network, whose members run the cleanup and long-term care of former weapons sites.

Drones fit that work naturally: they can map contamination, photograph changing ground, and inspect places people should not walk. The body treats applicability to legacy management sites first, then gives each laboratory its own appendix: Sandia, Los Alamos, Lawrence Livermore, Savannah River, Pacific Northwest, and Lawrence Berkeley. A blank copy of the survey questionnaire closes the volume, so the capability census can be repeated.
doe-osti-3400069-tex-chlorine-for-terrap:
TEX-Chlorine for TerraPower, an experimental execution report by E. Aboud and C. Fitzgerald dated August 2026 from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, documents a critical assembly experiment built around chlorine. TEX experiments assemble fissile material in measured setups. They validate the nuclear data that reactor calculations depend on. Chlorine matters because TerraPower's molten chloride reactor design puts it inside the core.

Two reflected setups were built, and each is described part by part. One uses polyethylene reflectors. The other uses copper reflectors. Both wrap highly enriched uranium plates and sodium chloride plates that supply the chlorine. Long chapters detail the assembly machine in each setup, plus the plates, aluminum inserts, spacers, rings, and shims. An execution report is the experiment's lasting build record. It is written so the setup can be modeled exactly.
doe-osti-3411904-national-laboratories-f:
Revision 1 of an August 2025 survey, by Frederick Day-Lewis and Holly VerMeulen, lists what national labs can do with unmanned aerial systems for environmental work. The survey sits under the NNLEMS group of labs. Drones now survey land, water, and buried hazards at old sites.

One Los Alamos case used a rotary drone for 2.1 square miles over 24 flights in 2 days. A fixed-wing drone covered 1.8 square miles in one 45-minute flight, from higher up. A custom Python package processes magnet survey data. Site managers can match aircraft type to the survey job at hand.
doe-osti-3419329-synthesis-of-lanthanide:
Idaho report INL/RPT-26-94670, dated August 2026, reports Bianca I. Bravo's project on growing lanthanide intermetallic silicide crystals, with Ashini Shamindra Jayasinghe. Clean single crystals let researchers study magnetic and electronic behavior without grain boundary noise. Metal-flux growth can form crystals at lower heat.

Reactions were partly built in an argon glovebox to guard air-sensitive parts. Sealed tubes heated to 1000 degrees Celsius over 12 hours and held there for 24 hours. Cooling to 800 degrees took 72 hours. Careful heat paths aim at new crystal phases that dirty samples would hide. The project seeks novel lanthanide phases that polycrystalline samples cannot reveal cleanly.
doe-osti-3484516-final-technical-report-:
University of California Davis closes award DE-SC0022149 with a final report on whether aerosols speed up or slow down deep storm updrafts. Adele Igel led the project, with Hallie Pimperl in the evidence record. The project ran from August 15, 2021 to May 14, 2026. The hosted report is short, so this note stays at its level.

Storms near the Southern Great Plains site were tracked with GOES satellite data. Each storm was paired with local aerosol and weather readings. Results could not prove the size of the effect, the authors state plainly. The patterns found still matched past hypotheses and model studies.
doe-osti-3505044-tandem-photovoltaics-co:
Report NLR/TP-5900-95272 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated August 2026, sums up the Tandem Photovoltaics Core Program. Emily Warren, Kai Zhu, and Michael Owen-Bellini lead an eighteen-author team. Tandem cells stack two absorbers to catch more sunlight than one layer can.

One fix treats a tin oxide cap layer with ozone before coating. Efficiency improved across three perovskite mixes after the treatment. Spread in efficiency also narrowed for treated samples. All-perovskite tandems gained from the same step. Solar researchers get a simple surface step that lifts and steadies tandem cells.
doe-osti-3685158-developing-a-lightning-:
Savannah River report SRNL-STI-2026-00218, Revision 1, dated July 2026, builds a lightning all-clear signal for the Savannah River Site. Stephen Noble and Stephen W. Weinbeck of Savannah River wrote it with Christopher Kerns of the University of California, Davis. Site notices now fire when three strikes land onsite within fifteen minutes. After that, each contractor judges when outdoor work can resume, often after three quiet hours. 

An electric field mill offers a steadier guide than strike counts alone. The team tested threshold mixes on ninety-eight lightning events holding over a thousand strikes. The best signal used several field limits together. Its average return delay was two hours and thirteen minutes, pulled up by lingering storms and data gaps. Most signals beat the three-hour rule. Only one event in the set cleared less than an hour before fresh lightning.
doe-osti-3705559-power-electronics-grid-:
The final CRADA report for a grid-tied power electronics system is Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4295, dated October 2025. Steven Campbell, Madhu Chinthavali, and Michael Starke are the printed authors, under CRADA NFE-21-05953. Utilities struggle to fold scattered energy resources into one system. Bespoke setups eat time and money, so the project sought a reusable way past that tangle.

The team built a node: a set of smart converters and controllers that act as one dispatchable virtual power plant. The node also carries backup functions for outages. Tests ran in the GRID-C testbed at Building 3114, with solar, storage, grid tie, and load gear linked on a shared direct-current bus. Agent layers handled interface, reasoning, conversion, and the resource itself for both solar and grid sides. A partner utility shaped use cases around cheap dispatch and resilience.
doe-osti-3740270-challenges-for-megawatt:
Oak Ridge letter report ORNL/LTR-2026/4457, dated July 2026, maps the hard problems behind megawatt-scale AI racks. Eight authors are printed, led by Kashif Nawaz and Mostak Mohammad. Rack loads are jumping from the old twenty-to-fifty kilowatt range toward two hundred kilowatts to a full megawatt. At that scale, power, cooling, and machine behaviour lock together. A software surge can spike heat faster than plant controls can react.

Power delivery is shifting toward direct current at eight hundred to fifteen hundred volts. Gaps remain in high-ratio conversion and medium-voltage feeds. Air cooling fades near thirty kilowatts per rack, and AI halls already pass three hundred, so liquid cooling is now standard. Cold plates, manifolds, and coolant units each add their own limits under fast load swings. The team argues the rack must be watched and tested as one coupled system.
doe-osti-3740797-power-electronics-grid-:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4295, dated October 2025, closes CRADA NFE-21-05953 on a grid-tied power electronics system. Steven Campbell, Madhu Chinthavali, and Michael Starke are the printed authors. Utilities face a messy task wiring scattered energy gear into one grid. Differing owners, controls, and device types push each job toward a one-off design. The project set out to show a repeatable fix at low voltage.

Separate resources were grouped into a single node that a utility can dispatch like one plant. The node also keeps key loads alive during outages. Hardware trials ran at the GRID-C testbed in Building 3114. Solar, storage, grid ties, and loads joined on a direct-current bus spanning eight hundred to fifteen hundred volts, tied to one fused box for safety. Layered software agents ran each unit. A utility partner helped shape test cases around cheap dispatch and outage survival.
doe-osti-3816364-canopy-flux-experiment-:
Report DOE/SC-ARM-26-032, dated September 2026, gives an interim account of the Canopy Flux Experiment in Bankhead National Forest, Alabama. Seven authors are printed: Heping Liu of Washington State University leads, with three colleagues and three from the National Center for Atmospheric Research. Towers at the ARM mobile site measure how heat, moisture, and carbon dioxide move from forest floor to open air. Five sensor levels span the canopy and the rough air layer above it. The morning shift draws special focus.

Early results from summer 2025 show turbulent flows keeping a steady vertical order through the day. Wind patterns govern how far gusty sweeps reach into the trees. The team asks to renew the campaign for more field seasons of the same measures. Computer modelling is not part of the renewal ask.
doe-osti-3874675-commercial-industrial-a:
A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report dated September 2026 updates discount rates for commercial energy standards analysis. K. Sydny Fujita is the sole printed author. Federal appliance rules must prove their savings beat their costs over a product's life. That proof leans on the discount rate, which shrinks future energy savings into today's dollars. The report rebuilds those rates from sector financial data spanning 1998 to 2025. It updates earlier editions from 2016 and 2023.

Equity cost comes from the capital asset pricing model. Debt cost starts from long-term Treasury bond rates, with a risk margin added. Rates are given as spreads by business sector, not one flat figure. Small businesses get a separate cut of the data, since their borrowing terms differ. Publicly owned buildings form a special case. Tables in the back map sectors onto federal building types.
doe-osti-3931144-sustainable-chicago-geo:
Blacks in Green, a Chicago community group, leads a broad city coalition in this final technical report on a shared geothermal heating and cooling project, dated August 20, 2026. Naomi Davis is the business contact and Wasiu Adesope the lead engineer. The Energy Department award is DE-EE0010661, and partners span city offices, labor, and the University of Illinois.

The pilot serves West Woodlawn, a neighborhood hit hard by high gas and electric bills. Work from 2023 onward weighed shared ground loops that heat and cool many buildings at once. Design drawings, cost work, and community input fill the report's later parts. The goal is a working model that other city blocks can copy: lower bills, cleaner air, and local jobs, planned with the people who live there.
essays-sthetical:
George Henry Calvert meditates on beauty in Essays Æsthetical, dated 1875. Nine essays ask what the beautiful is, what poetry is, and what style is. Dante and his latest translators, Sainte-Beuve the critic, and Thomas Carlyle get essays of their own. National drama and the usefulness of art close the book.

Calvert calls the beautiful an immortal theme, born the same day with the sun. Nature teems with it, he writes, for whoever has the gift to feel its presence. The Dante essay prints the Italian of the Francesca story from Canto V of the Inferno beside three English versions, Longfellow's among them, to test each translator's measure. Calvert, an American man of letters, writes as a patient amateur of the arts.
fbi-vault-cointel-pro-cointelpro-white-h:
The final part, 14, of the COINTELPRO White Hate Groups file closes the Federal Bureau of Investigation record of its campaign against hate groups. The cover marks this set as sub-file 10 of file 157-9. Airtels in the sampled pages deal with Klan meets and rallies in Ohio.

One grant of power in the part stands out. Headquarters let a field office open a post office box in Dayton, Ohio, under a false name: Harmon Blenerhasset. He was the made-up head of a group called the National Committee for Domestic Tranquility. The bureau backed the group as a low-key voice against Klan policy and Klan feuds. The box was to be set up with no sign of the bureau's hand. The part shows the campaign's covert side in plain words.
first-lessons-in-geography-or-introducti:
Monteith starts the youngest scholars in First Lessons in Geography, printed in 1856. James Monteith made the book as the first of a national series, a primer before his Youth's Manual of Geography. It is written for beginners, and it teaches by question and answer, in the catechism manner of its day.

The lessons march state by state. The sampled pages ask what falls lie between Lakes Erie and Ontario, and answer: Niagara Falls. They ask what the word Pennsylvania means, and answer: Penn's Woods. William Penn enters as a Quaker who was good and just to the Indians. A later lesson counts ten Southern states, names Texas the largest, and calls Florida a peninsula. Short lines, maps, and pictures carry a child from the home state to the wide world.
for-the-admiral:
Marx tells a tale of the French wars of religion, ridden with messages for the Admiral Coligny. The chapters promise a perilous ride, a traitor to the king, the tragedy of Jarnac, and scouting for Coligny. A young cavalier carries the commission at the story's heart.

In battle the Huguenot arquebusiers hold a ditch against repeated cavalry charges. Young Condé then sweeps round and breaks the hostile infantry with a daring charge of his own. W. J. Marx, who also wrote of scouting for Buller, printed this story in 1906. Swords wave and cheers rise as the enemy gives way.
forty-years-in-south-china-the-life-of-r:
Fagg tells the life of John Van Nest Talmage, missionary at Amoy for the Dutch Reformed Church. The missionary's brother, the preacher T. De Witt Talmage, introduces the book and calls John the hero of the family. John had refused a large Brooklyn pulpit to sail for China.

The converts' earnestness fills the quoted letters. Chinese Christians crowded the mission house for explanations of Scripture, and prayer rose from all parts of the house at once. The market-town work owed much to W. C. Burns, the first English Presbyterian missionary to China, who arrived in 1847. John Gerardus Fagg, himself an Amoy missionary, published the life in 1894.
govdocs-archive_org-TheEinsteinHoaxTheDi:
H. E. Retic published The Einstein Hoax in 1997 through his own company in West Caldwell, New Jersey. His target is Albert Einstein's theory of relativity, which he presents as a disastrous intellectual war on common sense.

Retic argues that relativity misled physics and the wider culture, and he presses his case with the certainty of a man correcting a century of error. He writes for general readers rather than physicists, in plain and forceful terms. The book is held as an archive item, without endorsement, as a strong example of popular anti-relativity writing from the 1990s.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAAgentsGenera:
Jeff Gerth of the New York Times reported from Washington, on February 7, on a European figure the CIA had protected. Alfred J. Biihler, a Liechtenstein lawyer and businessman linked to fraud and arms deals, had been shielded by the agency from law-enforcement questioning.

The story is a classic of the post-Church Committee press: an intelligence agency placing its assets beyond the reach of investigators, and a reporter documenting the arrangement. Gerth became known for exactly this kind of digging into the borderland of intelligence and money. The single article is preserved from the Times as part of the era's exposure literature.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CanadaROAdmiral:
Drew Pearson, whose Washington Merry-Go-Round was the most feared column in American politics, turned his column to a book: Jim Bishop's The Day Kennedy Was Shot. Bishop's hour-by-hour reconstruction of November 22, 1963, appeared in 1968 and reached an enormous readership.

A Pearson column on the book put the popular history before the column's own millions, in the syndicated press where most Americans met the assassination's literature. What Pearson praised or disputed sits in the column itself. The piece is preserved as press history: the era's biggest columnist weighing the era's bestselling account of Dallas.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Canale-TNBarAss:
On January 15, 1971, a Tennessee prosecutor named Canale addressed the Tennessee Bar Association, and this transcript preserves the speech. His subject, in the part that survives most clearly, is Memphis geography: the rooming house at 422 and a half South Main Street, near the Illinois Central station.

That rooming house overlooks the Lorraine Motel, and its bathroom window is where the state said James Earl Ray fired the shot that killed Martin Luther King Jr. A prosecutor describing the scene to fellow lawyers, three years on, was still explaining the ground the case stood on. The transcript is legal oratory preserved for researchers of the King prosecution.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClementsManning:
Manning C. Clements was a Dallas FBI agent, a twenty-three-year veteran of the Bureau, and one of the agents who interviewed Lee Harvey Oswald in custody. This statement summarizes his Warren Commission deposition of April 8, 1964.

Oswald was interrogated for hours across the weekend of November 22 to 24, with no recording and no lawyer, and the agents' later testimony is the main record of what he said. Clements' deposition therefore carries weight out of proportion to its length: it is a participant's sworn account of the interrogation room. The summary is preserved for researchers working through the Oswald interviews.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PresidentialPro: nsia-PresidentialProtection Presidential Protection: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PublicityOswald:
An FBI memorandum dated November 24, 1963, two days after the assassination, carries the heading 'Jack Leon Ruby / Lee Harvey Oswald — Victim.' It was written following Mr. Belmont's instructions and kept in file 44-1639. It records Police Chief Jesse Curry's assurance about the case. Curry said the televised Dallas police appearances in the Oswald case were hurting the possibility of prosecution.

That Sunday, Ruby shot Oswald in the police basement, on television. A memo worrying about publicity and prosecution, written the same weekend, shows officials already feared the cameras. Curry's assurance and Belmont's interest mark the bureau tracking a local chief's media problem as it became a national one.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RaidsOfficial_R:
Andrew H. Malcolm reported for the New York Times from Washington on June 24, in a story whose internal dates point to 1973. His subject is violent drug raids against innocent people, found to be widespread. In Miami, residents were handcuffed and held at gunpoint while their homes were ransacked, in raids meant for someone else. Such raids, the story reports, happened once or twice a month.

Wrong-door raids were the drug war's recurring scandal. Malcolm's dispatch counts them, describes the victims' treatment, and names the pattern as policy's cost. The story preserves names, places, and the victims' accounts in a national paper's record. It also shows the early 1970s press beginning to audit drug enforcement itself, not merely to report its seizures.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TattlerNational: Loran Eugene Hall moved through the edges of the Kennedy assassination story for years. The National Tattler article titled The Elusive Mr. Hall follows Hall, who also used the Cuban cover name Lorenzo Eugenio Pascillo, and tracks his movements in 1975. Tabloid coverage kept figures like Hall before the public long after the official investigations ended. The piece shows that fringe of the case as popular papers presented it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WBAL_WBAL: WBAL - a broadcast call sign - titles this declassified US government document at the Internet Archive. The catalog offers no date, no context, no content. Public text not located. A call sign filed among government papers.
govdocs-archive_org-the-papal-origins-of: An article from Historicist.com argues that preterism began with the papacy. Preterism is a school of prophetic reading that treats many Bible prophecies as already fulfilled in the ancient past. The historicist writer behind the piece presents that origin as a Catholic strategy against Protestant teaching. The article serves readers of prophecy debates, where the history of an idea is itself used as a weapon against it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
General Carlos Prats had led Chile's army before General Augusto Pinochet, and he was killed with his wife Sofía Cuthbert in Buenos Aires in 1974. The National Security Archive marked fifty years since that bombing in October 2024. Peter Kornbluh edited the document compilation it posted.

The posting calls the killing the Pinochet regime's first act of international terrorism. It includes CIA intelligence reports and the judicial confession of Michael Townley, the Chilean secret police operative who built and placed the bomb. Together the records trace one murder from the order to the courtroom admission.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
Critical infrastructure means the systems so vital that their loss would debilitate American security, health, or the economy. This Cyber Vault posting, dated October 22, 2020, reviews President Donald Trump's executive orders on protecting those systems. Homeland Security's own definition frames the discussion.

Trump's presidency produced a high volume of executive orders, and they offer a clear view of his approach. The period also saw Congress create the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency by law. Reading the orders together shows how one administration used its direct pen-and-phone powers on power grids, networks, and other vital assets.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_Ira:
For decades the State Department's official history of the 1953 Iran coup whitewashed the American and British roles. Malcolm Byrne edited this briefing book, number 598, published in June 2017, on the long-awaited replacement volume. The department finally released an updated official history.

Formerly secret documents from State and the CIA supply new information on how the covert operation was planned and carried out. Contemporaneous analyses show what officials thought at the time. An official history correcting itself is a notable event: it means the government's own historians now tell a story closer to what the secret files always showed.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p: Presidential transitions are the moments when one American administration hands power to the next, and foreign rivals take the new president's measure. A National Security Archive briefing book page gathers its Russia material under one heading. It covers Putin, Clinton, and the transition years. In those years Bill Clinton left office and Vladimir Putin rose in Moscow. The evidence here is the page capture itself, so the entry works as a signpost to the Archive's wider record on how Washington and Moscow reset their relationship at the century's turn.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
On November 25, 1975, secret police chiefs from across South America's Southern Cone gathered in Santiago, Chile, at the invitation of Pinochet's intelligence service, DINA. A National Security Archive posting on November 26, 2025, fifty years later, returns to that meeting and to the network it created: Operation Condor.

The agenda said the new body should work like Interpol, but aimed at subversion. Delegations from Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Paraguay, and Uruguay spent three days agreeing to hunt each other's enemies across borders. Kidnappings and murders on foreign soil followed for years. Readers get the founding scene in detail, drawn from the confidential record, and a clear view of how state terror became a shared, cross-border system.

Operation Condor, the pact among South America's military regimes to hunt each other's enemies across borders, reached far beyond the region's dissidents. A National Security Archive briefing book page records one of its most chilling targets: officials of Amnesty International, the human rights organization, marked for liquidation in the network's own language. Only the page capture is preserved in this entry's evidence. Even so, the headline documents how a cross-border terror system viewed the world's best-known human rights monitors: not as neutrals, but as enemies to be killed.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Archive_Hist:
On December 1, 2020, four organizations sued President Donald Trump to stop any destruction of presidential records during the transition to the Biden administration. The plaintiffs were the National Security Archive, two national historians' associations, and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, and their suit invoked the Presidential Records Act.

That law makes a president's records public property, not personal property, and sets rules for keeping them. The groups feared that a chaotic transition, and a president already known for tearing up papers, could cost the country part of its own history. Filing suit before any destruction could be proved was the point: records cases are usually lost once the records are gone. The posting explains the claims and why historians went to court alongside lawyers.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_guatemala_Imminen: On May 30, 2019, the National Security Archive warned of an imminent threat to Guatemala's Historical Archive of the National Police, the AHPN. That archive holds millions of police records from the civil war and has supplied evidence for human rights trials; its staff and independence came under government pressure in this period. The posting belongs to a series of Archive alerts about the collection's safety. Readers following the archive's fate will find here the alarm at its sharpest, sounded by the institution that helped bring the records to light.
hemp-hurds-as-paper-making-material:
Lyster H Dewey and Jason L Merrill wrote this United States farm bulletin in 1916. It is Bulletin No. 404 from the Department of Agriculture. The subject is hemp hurds, the woody core left after fiber is stripped. The authors ask if that waste can make good paper.

Dewey covers how hurds are grown, baled, and shipped. Merrill reports mill tests, cooking methods, and the strength of each sheet. Tables compare the test runs with normal mill work. The bulletin gives growers and mill men hard facts on a cheap new raw stock.
history-of-the-mackenzies-with-genealogi:
Alexander Mackenzie, a Scottish historian of the Highlands, compiled this clan history of the Mackenzies with the family lines of its branches. A. and W. Mackenzie published the new, revised, and extended edition at Inverness in 1894. The first edition of 1879 had sold out and drawn clan demand for more. Mackenzie rewrote the whole book and added families the first version missed.

Branch by branch, the history traces chiefs, marriages, landholding, and feuds across the Highlands and the Isle of Skye. Genealogies, meaning lists of descent from father to son, let readers place each principal family of the name. Mackenzie attacks the tale that the clan sprang from an Irish Fitzgerald, arguing instead for native Celtic descent from the stock of the O'Beolan earls of Ross. Dates, charters, and family papers crowd the pages. Genealogists and clan members use the book as a reference first, and a story second.
john-m-synge-a-few-personal-recollection:
John M. Synge: A Few Personal Recollections, with Biographical Notes is John Masefield's memoir of the Irish playwright. Masefield first met Synge in January 1903, in a friend's room in Bloomsbury. They shook hands that night but did not speak again. Masefield spent the evening watching him from across the room and wondering who he was.

He describes a dark, grave face, pale and rather drawn, with smoky, kindling eyes. A humorous mouth kept the face from pure severity. Synge gave an instant sense of a strange personality, a man forever listening to life's case before judging. Masefield, a poet himself, writes of the author of The Playboy of the Western World with personal warmth and close observation.
king-coal:
King Coal is Upton Sinclair's novel of the Colorado coal country, built in four books. Their titles name the system: The Domain, The Serfs, The Henchmen, and The Will of King Coal. Sinclair dedicates the book to Mary Craig Kimbrough. An introduction praises his consecration to the ideal of social justice, carried out through art.

Sinclair follows miners in company camps, where the coal company owns the houses, stores, and law. Strikes and organizing meet spies, guards, and bought officials in his account. He had reported the Colorado strikes himself before turning them into fiction. The novel argues that coal's kingdom runs on the serfdom of its workers.
love-eternal:
Love Eternal is a late romance by H. Rider Haggard. His dedication tells of a woman whose human love led her from darkness into light. The hero is Godfrey, and the woman he loves is Isobel. Early chapters bring a kiss, a garden in a square, and a stern pasteur.

Years intervene, and the lovers meet again across India and France. Chapters named 'Together,' 'For Ever,' and 'Love and Loss' trace their bond. Haggard asks whether true love can outlast death itself. Marriage, orders, and parting test the pair to the end. It is a spiritual love story, told with his usual sweep.
mckinlay-s-journal-of-exploration-in-the:
John McKinlay kept a journal of his search work in Australia's interior. F. F. Bailliere printed it in Melbourne, with three maps. The trip is named in the book as the Burke Relief Expedition.

His diary takes the form of a report to the Chief Commissioner of Crown Lands. He writes from Depot Camp at Buchanan Lake on October 26, 1861. The party left Adelaide on August 16, 1861, with camels and gear. Day by day notes track water, land, and the search for lost men. Charts of the route stand with the text in the book. The search was a state task, and the report keeps that formal air.
military-instructors-manual:
Captain James P. Cole and Major Oliver Schoonmaker compiled this manual at the Plattsburg training camp in New York. Both men taught in the Third Battalion of the Seventeenth Provisional Training Regiment. They dedicate the book to Colonel Wolf, under whom so many candidates trained. Officer candidates helped write and type entire chapters.

The manual gathers the instruction given to America's hastily raised officer corps. Its acknowledgments name the candidates who prepared material and lent their work. The aim was soldiers who would show, in the dedication's words, the true spirit of American manhood. It preserves how the army taught instructing itself during the First World War mobilization.
moral:
Ludwig Thoma's comedy Moral was first produced in Germany in 1908. Its introduction tells Thoma's story: born at Oberammergau in 1867, trained as a lawyer, then lost to literature. He wrote humorous verses for Simplicissimus as Peter Schlemiehl and became its editor in 1899. Critics called him a Bavarian Aristophanes and ranked him next to Hauptmann.

Reviewers shook their heads at Moral's shocks, yet admitted its author cast a long shadow. The play satirizes respectable hypocrisy about morals in a small town. It reached New York in German at the Irving Place Theatre in 1914. Thoma's satire mixes laughter with a serious message about public virtue.
more-pages-from-a-journal:
Mark Rutherford, the pen name of William Hale White, published this sequel volume in 1910. Oxford University Press issued the edition transcribed here. Rutherford dedicates it to Horace and Susan E. P. Smith, calling the book an inadequate acknowledgement of a great debt. The contents mix stories with journal entries.

Pieces include Esther, Kate Radcliffe, and Mr. Whittaker's Retirement. Confessions of a Self-Tormentor stands beside letters and a piece called Conversion. Short entries record Romney Marsh, Axmouth, and a Sunday morning in November. White's quiet pages trace a thoughtful man's wrestling with faith, doubt, and ordinary life in the dissenting tradition.
napoleon-s-campaign-in-russia-anno-1812-:
Dr. Achilles Rose studies Napoleon's Russian campaign of 1812 as a medical historian. The contents march from crossing the Niemen to Moscow. Then come the retreat, Wiasma, Smolensk, and the Beresina. Chapters on prisoners and the treatment of typhus close it.

Rose notes that six hundred thousand men crossed the Niemen in June. Most regiments could only record them as disappeared in the retreat. Survivors came home hollow-eyed, with frozen hands and tales of horror. Cossacks, peasants, cold, and disease did the killing. The book reads the disaster through sickness, wounds, and care, not just strategy.
nasa-tm-19650015747-analysis-of-wind-tun:
Dennis W Camp at Marshall Space Flight Center analyzed wind tunnel data for two makes of anemometer in this May 26, 1965 report. An anemometer measures wind speed. The models tested were the Beckman and Whitley Series 50 and the Climet Model C1-14. Both would be used where accurate wind readings matter.

Camp focuses on how each instrument responds to changing wind. Two measures matter here, the distance constant and the damping ratio. An instrument that reacts too slowly can smooth away real gusts. The analysis gives users a basis for judging each model, rather than trusting a maker's claims alone.
nasa-tm-19650019794-nasa-developments-in:
John C Freche, Richard L Ashbrook, and Gary D Sandrock at Lewis Research Center wrote this article, prepared for Metal Progress in October 1964. It reviews NASA work on cobalt-base superalloys, metals built to stay strong at great heat. Such alloys serve in jet engine stator vanes, turbine buckets, and combustion chamber parts.

The authors note strength plus good resistance to oxidation at high heat. That range runs roughly from fifteen hundred to two thousand degrees Fahrenheit. The article covers chemical, mechanical, and physical properties of these alloys. For engine designers, it gathered NASA's development work on a class of metals that hot sections depend on.
nasa-tm-19660005479-potassium-condensing:
O A Gutierrez, N J Sekas, L W Acker, and D G Fenn at Lewis Research Center tested condensers that turn hot potassium vapor back into liquid. Their paper was offered for a conference in Cleveland in October 1965. The condensers are horizontal banks of many tubes. They work two ways, by moving air convection and by radiating heat away.

Vapor temperatures in the tests ran from about twelve hundred fifty to fifteen hundred degrees Fahrenheit. Potassium was a working fluid for space power systems that run very hot. A condenser is where such a system sheds its waste heat. Measured performance there decided whether the whole power cycle could close.
nasa-tm-19660006558-some-research-relate:
Harry L Runyan at Langley presented this work in Tokyo in late 1965 on the structural dynamics of launch vehicles. His stress falls on the use of dynamic models, small copies that bend and shake like the real thing. Tests of a Saturn I model are discussed in the summary. A one-sixteenth scale Saturn model also appears in the work.

Ground wind effects on a waiting launch vehicle form part of the study. So does the aeroelastic behavior of the whole structure in flight. Runyan reports recent advances in both areas. The paper shows how much of a giant rocket's safety case was built from careful tests on models.
nasa-tm-19660017563-tape-generation-prog:
Richard C Lee at Goddard wrote this users' manual in May 1966 for a tape generation program. The program runs on a UNIVAC 1107 computer. It makes fake satellite telemetry tapes, so ground systems can be tested before a real satellite flies. Simulated tapes let operators practice on lifelike data, with known content, at any time.

A users' manual tells staff how to run the program and read its products. Testing ground systems against real flight data alone is risky and slow. A tape generator gives a safe, repeatable substitute. Lee's manual belongs to the ground software effort that sat behind every Goddard mission of the period.
nasa-tm-19670002066-oso-spacecraft-manua:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued the OSO Spacecraft Manual in July 1966. OSO, the Orbiting Solar Observatory, was a satellite built to study the Sun. A manual like this one served the engineers who built, tested, and operated the spacecraft.

The catalog record lists the systems it covers. They include telemetry, the command system, power supply and distribution, and the antenna system. It also covers the experiment complement and temperature monitoring, plus the launch program. The hosted sample preserves the cover and contents pages, so individual procedures cannot be described.
nasa-tm-19680003405-procedures-and-requi:
The Apollo program office issued these rules for judging the soft goods that fly in a spacecraft. Such goods include plastics, glues, and fabrics, none of them metal. The paper, numbered MSC-A-D-66-3, Revision A, came from the Parts and Materials Program and a test office.

Its contents open with a summary, then set up a review board. That board checked the soft goods used in the Apollo crew bay, where crew safety is at stake. Picking rules and test demands follow. The catalog record calls them specs and test demands for Apollo materials. The rules kept untested goods out of crewed cabins.
nasa-tm-19680014123-a-tropical-cyclone-d:
Guenter Warnecke of Goddard Space Flight Center led a team that traced one tropical storm's birth using satellite data in this 1967 conference paper. Co-authors Lewis J. Allison, Earl R. Kreins, and Larry M. McMillin joined the study. Their case was typhoon Marie of 1966 in the central Pacific Ocean.

Nimbus II infrared readings were combined with ESSA-3 photographs and sparse standard weather reports. Together the records showed the early stages of storm growth in a region with few ground stations. The team checked whether sea surface conditions met the needs usually linked to storm formation. The work shows how satellites can reveal storm development far from land-based observers.
nasa-tm-19690017222-cavitation-performan:
Calvin L. Ball, Phillip R. Meng, and Lonnie Reid of Lewis Research Center report cavitation tests of an eighty-four-degree helical pump inducer in this February 1967 memorandum, TM X-1360. The flat-plate inducer ran in liquid hydrogen at thirty-seven and forty-two degrees Rankine, spinning twenty thousand times per minute. Cavitation, vapor bubbles collapsing inside a pump, can wreck a rocket fuel system's performance.

An improvement in cavitation performance was indicated at the warmer temperature, the summary states. Suction head needed in cold hydrogen ran at least ninety feet below what plain water required. Fluid properties explain the difference, the authors say. The inducer could even pump boiling liquid hydrogen with no appreciable head loss. Photographs of the cavitation are included.
nasa-tm-19690017305-the-electrical-condu:
Norman F. Ness of Goddard Space Flight Center presented this May 1969 paper at COSPAR in Prague. He reads the Moon's electrical conductivity, and from it the Moon's internal temperature, using magnetic measurements from Lunar Explorer 35. That spacecraft had circled the Moon since July 1967, watching the interplanetary magnetic field bend around the lunar body.

The field proved only slightly distorted, with no sign of a bow shock wave, Ness reports. Sudden field changes passing through the Moon revealed very weak induced currents inside it. Such weak conduction means a cool interior for silicate rock. Comparing heat history models, he concludes the Moon is young if its heat sources stay evenly mixed. If those sources rose toward the surface, the Moon can be old.
nasa-tm-19690031539-determination-of-the:
Blair Bradley Gloss determined the shape and inertial properties of an all-flexible parawing in this master's thesis at Virginia Polytechnic Institute. A parawing is a cloth wing that holds its shape from airflow alone, with no rigid frame. Designers need its true flying shape, balance point, and inertia values before they can predict how it handles.

Chapters describe the test model, the facility and equipment, and the test conditions used. Shape data are then reduced into streamwise sections cut along the airflow. A separate chapter judges the accuracy of that shape data carefully. Inertial properties follow, with the center-of-gravity locations determined for the wing. Results and discussion close the thesis.
nasa-tm-19700028229-on-analysis-of-area-:
G. R. Woodcock of the Advanced Systems Office at the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on September 26, 1969. It analyzes how much area orbital photo imaging systems can cover. A camera in orbit sweeps a strip of ground as it moves, and planners must know the true reach of that sweep.

Woodcock describes first steps toward an automated analysis of that coverage from a baseline orbit. The tool was meant to ease mission design for a planetary orbiter. His example is the proposed Voyager 1973 Mars mission, which had already been dropped from planning. The analysis works through the orbit path and the photo coverage it yields, then presents the computer program built for the task.
nasa-tm-19700029481-power-ratio-of-wante:
Edward F. Miller and Royce W. Myhre of the Lewis Research Center ran the tests behind this report. It asks how strong an unwanted television signal can be before viewers notice it. Two systems had to share nearby frequencies, one FM and one AM-VSB.

The team measured the power ratio at which interference stays barely visible. An FM signal inside an AM channel had to sit far below the wanted signal, they found. The reverse case allowed a smaller margin. They then used the results to judge sharing between an FM transmitter in synchronous orbit and AM television on Earth.
nasa-tm-19700030073-neutron-kinetics-of-:
George F. Niederauer of the Lewis Research Center wrote this study of a fast, hot nuclear assembly. The design matches a reactor meant for auxiliary power in space. It uses uranium fuel, a tantalum structure, and a lithium coolant.

Niederauer studies how neutron levels grow while such a reactor starts up. He runs the study with and without the coolant in place. The aim is to find safe ranges for how fast reactivity may be added. He varies the size of two feedback effects across wide ranges. Safe startup rules are the base of any reactor that flies in space.
nasa-tm-19700076084-standard-potting-and:
The John F. Kennedy Space Center issued this standard on November 22, 1965. It governs potting and molding work on electrical cable assembly ends. Potting seals a cable end in a solid compound that keeps out water and strain.

The standard opens by stating its purpose. It then fixes one approved way for shops to seal and mold cable terminations. Launch site cables face salt air, rain, and hard handling every day. A single standard keeps every crew's work alike and testable. Documents of this kind are the quiet base of launch safety, turning craft skill into shared rules.
nasa-tm-19710010849-effect-of-south-atla:
Daniel J Lesco and William C Nieberding of the Lewis Research Center wrote this March 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2232. It explains odd jumps in orbital acceleration readings from the SERT 2 spacecraft. SERT 2 tested electric ion thrusters in Earth orbit. Its sensitive accelerometer kept recording small pushes that flight plans did not predict.

The authors traced those pushes to the South Atlantic magnetic anomaly. That region has a weaker magnetic field, so charged particles dip closer to Earth there. The measured disturbances reached about a tenth of a micro g. Matching them to the anomaly helped separate real thruster effects from magnetic noise in the data.
nasa-tm-19710015150-single-axis-referenc:
Charles E Lee of the Marshall Space Flight Center described this guidance hardware effort in March 1971, as NASA TM X-64586. The Astrionics Laboratory there designed and tested single axis reference strapdown measuring units. A strapdown unit has its sensors fixed to the vehicle frame. It feeds motion data to a computer that tracks position and heading.

Lee explained the theory and operation of the units and their accelerometers. Tests ran in the laboratory, on a sled, and in mobile trials with the computer. Future plans included a twelve sided unit design and new gyroscope ideas. Those ideas were aimed in part at the coming space shuttle.
nasa-tm-19710018388-comparison-of-two-an:
Raymond K Burns of the Lewis Research Center issued this comparison in May 1971, as NASA TM X-67853. It checks two ways of predicting heat inside an isotope heat source. The source was a slight change of the Pioneer design, meant for a Brayton power system. Radioactive fuel heats such a source from within. Exact internal temperatures decide whether the design is safe.

Burns ran both flat two dimensional and full three dimensional heat analyses. He compared them across fuel loads near the standard four hundred watts. Three kinds of reentry insulation sleeves entered the study as well. The simpler flat analyses gave slightly cautious results. That finding told designers when the cheaper method could be trusted.
nasa-tm-19710020434-earth-photography-fr:
Dona L Cauchon, Leonard P Kopia, and Leon A Williams Jr of the Langley Research Center wrote this July 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2208. It evaluates photographs of Earth taken from high altitude balloons. Some flights were coordinated with ground investigations for test purposes. Balloons offered a cheap platform above most of the atmosphere. The team asked how useful their wide area pictures could be.

The report weighs the value of large area photographs and special picture formats. It also lists the strengths and weaknesses of free flight balloons for remote sensing. Two appendixes give the camera system and the camera package design. The work spoke to Earth resources and ocean studies. Both fields needed broad, detailed views of the surface.
nasa-tm-19720010891-hot-salt-stress-corr:
Hugh R Gray, a research metallurgist at the Lewis Research Center, wrote this paper for a May 1972 titanium conference in Cambridge, Massachusetts. It concerns a cracking danger for titanium alloys in jet engines. Laboratory studies had shown titanium can embrittle and crack under stress at high heat. Salt deposits from sea air make the attack worse. Compressor parts face exactly those conditions in service.

Gray's team built special test facilities to copy engine conditions closely. They controlled air speed, pressure, and moisture in the test stream. Salt deposit temperature, salt amount, and surface condition also varied by plan. Each factor's role in the cracking could then be separated. The work linked bench chemistry to real turbine operation.
nasa-tm-19720012221-a-multiple-impulse-f:
James F Kibler and Lawrence H Hoffman of the Langley Research Center wrote this orbital mechanics paper in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2492. Mission planners move spacecraft between orbits with short rocket burns, called impulses. Their function strings several single impulses into one transfer plan. Each single impulse gives the velocity change needed between two orbits. The final orbit may be only partly specified in advance.

The authors derived exact rate formulas for the function. Those derivatives feed optimization methods that search for the cheapest transfer. Exact rates may beat the slower step by step numerical kind. A four impulse transfer is outlined as a worked case. The report runs to twenty three pages. It serves planners of orbital rendezvous and transfer missions.
nasa-tm-19720019044-internal-performance:
Donald L Bresnahan of the Lewis Research Center tested this plug nozzle in June 1972, as NASA TM X-2573. The nozzle had a ten degree conical plug at its heart. Around it sat a primary flow split into many spokes. A sliding outer shroud changed the nozzle's shape in operation. The cold flow test article measured about twenty two centimeters across. Plug nozzles promised good performance across wide speed ranges.

Two spoke designs went through the static test facility. One primary had twelve spokes and the other twenty four. Bresnahan compared their internal performance directly. The catalog record frames the study as experimental throughout. Such spoke patterns break the exhaust into mixing streams. Designers of advanced supersonic engines studied the trade offs closely.
nasa-tm-19720020576-apollo-14-mission-ci:
The Mission Evaluation Team at the Manned Spacecraft Center issued this anomaly report in December 1971. It is report MSC-05814, anomaly report number four for Apollo 14. A circuit breaker aboard the spacecraft had failed to pass current. The breaker was mechanically closed, yet its circuit stayed open. James A McDivitt approved the short five page report. Any power fault on a crewed ship drew careful study.

Investigators traced the fault to a foreign substance on the contact surface. That film blocked the flow of electricity through the closed breaker. The conclusion put the event in reassuring context. It was judged the only failure of its kind. More than thirty four hundred such units had flown by then. The report closed the case without grounding the fleet.
nasa-tm-19720022618-outlet-baffles-effec:
Eugene P Symons of the Lewis Research Center drained tanks in weightlessness for this September 1972 memorandum, NASA TM X-2631. His tanks were cylinders closed by rounded, hemisphere ends. When such a tank drains in orbit, some liquid always clings inside. That leftover fuel is wasted mass on every mission. Baffles at the outlet might guide the last liquid out. Symons tested whether they truly help, and by how much.

The study compared the relative effect of different outlet baffles. Three baffle designs were used in the draining tests. Each run measured the liquid left behind afterward. Weightless conditions came from the center's drop facilities. Results told designers which baffle shape stranded the least fuel. Small savings matter on long missions with tight fuel margins.
old-st-paul-s-cathedral:
William Benham wrote this guide to Old Saint Paul's Cathedral. Seeley published it in London in 1902. Benham was rector of Saint Edmund in Lombard Street. He was also an honorary canon of Canterbury. Old prints and drawings show the lost cathedral.

Wenceslaus Hollar's engravings preserve its look best, Benham says. Hollar was born in Prague in the year 1607. Pictures show bishops, funerals, and pontifical masses. The old cathedral burned in the Great Fire of London. Benham helps readers picture a vanished landmark of faith. The book mixes history, worship, and art.
omnilingual:
H. Beam Piper wrote this science fiction story in 1957. It first appeared in Astounding Science Fiction that February. Martha Dane explores a dead city on Mars. Red dust has buried its streets for fifty thousand years. The breach in one wall opens at the sixth story.

Archaeologists seek a key to read Martian writing. The last Martian writer died long before Earth writing began. Dane weighs the labor of clearing the buried city. People and supplies must cross fifty million miles. The tale asks if science can unlock any language. It remains a classic story about archaeology and translation.
other-things-being-equal:
Emma Wolf set her novel Other Things Being Equal in a San Francisco of hummingbirds, palms, and hazy summer afternoons, where Ruth Levice daydreams by an open window. Her cousin Jennie arrives in silk and jewels with news to discuss. At once she attacks the strange arrangement of Ruth's upbringing. Her father had sole care of her until her twenty-first birthday. Then he handed her over to her mother, like joint property.

Jennie calls the scheme contrary to nature, however sensible it seemed to the parents themselves. Wolf, an early Jewish-American novelist, builds her story on that divided household. Her heroine was raised by her father and delivered at majority to her mother. Now she faces love and choice with her loyalties split at the root.
paris-as-it-was-and-as-it-is-a-sketch-of: Paris as It Was and as It Is is a sketch of the French capital. An English traveller wrote it in letters during 1801 and 1802. The letters went to a friend in London. The subtitle promises the Revolution's effects on many fields. Sciences, literature, arts, religion, and education appear. Manners and amusements appear too. Remarkable national establishments and public buildings are described. The hosted sample shows the first volume's title page only. No letter text appears in the sample.
perpetual-light-a-memorial:
William Rose Benét titled his book Perpetual Light: A Memorial, and a dedication poem tells the reader how to take it. Think of no verse when you read this, he writes, but think of her alone. Day and night were stone until she made them bright, and courage and strength come from her still.

The epigraph, from a play about Mary, is a husband's cry at losing his companion. Benét, brother of Stephen Vincent Benét, wrote these poems for his young wife, who had died. The collection moves between grief and gratitude, keeping her memory as a light that does not go out.
post-augustan-poetry-from-seneca-to-juve:
H. E. Butler, Fellow of New College, Oxford, wrote this literary history of the Latin poetry that followed Augustus, running from Seneca to Juvenal. His first chapter faces the problem head-on: decline. The principate's politics, the characters of Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, and Nero, a rhetorical education without true educational spirit. The sheer greatness of the Augustan poets all barred further advance, leaving cleverness where invention had been.

A chapter on drama finds legitimate comedy nearly extinct, tragedy displaced by dance and recitation, and Seneca's plays holding the stage of the study. Later chapters weigh the epic and satiric heirs of Virgil and Horace one by one. Butler writes as a classicist who loves his authors too much to flatter their age. The book explains how a literature can be brilliant in every line and lesser in every work, a pattern students of other empires will recognize.
purgatory-doctrinal-historical-and-poeti:
Purgatory: Doctrinal, Historical and Poetical, by Mrs. J. Sadlier, is a Catholic work on the souls in purgatory, joining teaching, history, legend, and verse. Sadlier dedicates the book to her son, the Reverend Francis X. Sadlier, a Jesuit who died on November 14, 1885, three months after his ordination, in the month set apart for those souls.

In her introduction she says a lifetime of religious books and translations still lacked one link: a work made for the souls in purgatory alone. Growing older, she writes, draws the mind to the world beyond the grave, and to a doctrine she calls both dread and consoling.
rambles-and-recollections-of-an-indian-o:
Rambles and Recollections of an Indian Official, by Major-General Sir W. H. Sleeman, K.C.B., appears here in the revised, annotated edition by Vincent A. Smith, late of the Indian Civil Service, published by Humphrey Milford for Oxford University Press in 1915, at London, Edinburgh, Glasgow, New York, Toronto, Melbourne, and Bombay.

Sleeman dedicates the book to his sister. Were any man asked, he writes, what gave Englishmen in India their greatest pleasure, nine in ten would name one thing. They would name the letters received from their sisters at home. Those letters link their affections with home. They fill its remembered landscapes with life.
rhetoric-and-poetry-in-the-renaissance-a:
Donald Lemen Clark, assistant professor of English at Columbia University, wrote this study of rhetorical terms in English Renaissance literary criticism in 1922. He dedicates the book to his father and mother. Its first part lays out the general theory of rhetoric and of poetry in the classical world.

Clark treats Aristotle, Longinus, Plutarch, and Horace on poetic, then turns to classical rhetoric and its content. Later chapters trace how the two arts blended, and how false rhetoric in the declamation schools corrupted poetic. The Middle Ages show the tradition decaying into aureate language, before logic and rhetoric meet again in the English Renaissance.
ridgway-of-montana-a-story-of-to-day-in-:
William Macleod Raine calls this Montana story a tale of to-day in which the hero is also the villain. Two Men and a Woman opens the contents, and The Freebooter follows. Fort Salvation, a snow-trail, and the Honorable Thomas B. Pelton carry the plot into range politics.

Virginia intervenes and Aline makes a discovery before First Blood is drawn. A conspiracy, an explosion in the Taurus, and an election fill the middle chapters. One Million Dollars names the stakes in plain figures. A verdict chapter is titled Not Guilty—Guilty, and Aline turns a corner near the close. Friendly enemies and an engagement broken and made end the list.
right-royal:
John Masefield tells this horse-race tale in verse, opening with a note that its persons, horses, and events are imaginary. Part one begins an hour before the race, with a pair of lovers talking in mild March weather. Charles Cothill and the golden lady Em stand together, both fashioned, the poem says, by beautiful England's hands.

Cothill is to ride his horse Right Royal in the great steeplechase at Compton Course, the English Chaser's Cup. His colours are narrow bars of blue and white, and they are also hers. Hard work and waiting have marked his face with trouble and strain. Men would have said something worried him, as the race and the love story start together.
robert-louis-stevenson-a-record-an-estim:
Alexander H. Japp wrote this record, estimate, and memorial of Robert Louis Stevenson, in a second edition from Scribner of New York in 1905. The book prints letters from Stevenson never before published, in facsimile. Japp, who had written on Thoreau and De Quincey, dedicates it to friends at Treviso, with grateful regards, in December 1904.

His preface explains one prize item: the facsimile of the last page of the preface to Familiar Studies of Men and Books. Stevenson was ill at Davos while that book passed through the press, and his wife was ill as well. He begged Japp to read the proofs, and a letter from those days is printed in the book.
speeches-literary-and-social:
Speeches: Literary and Social by Charles Dickens came out in a new edition from Chatto and Windus of London in 1880, with chapters on Dickens as letter writer, poet, and public reader. A first note gives his life from the start. Dickens was born at Landport, Portsmouth, on February 7, 1812. His father, John Dickens, held a post in the Navy Pay Department that kept the family moving among England's chief naval towns.

Peace in 1815 brought cuts, and John Dickens was pensioned off and moved to London when Charles was hardly four. The note argues that the mixed, bustling scenes of those early years fed the boy's taste for watching the ways and quirks of each class at work. His quick sense of the absurd showed even in boyhood. Like Goldsmith's walks and Bulwer's young rambles, such early roving, the note holds, shapes men of thought and fancy for life.
tales-of-bengal:
S. B. Banerjea's Tales of Bengal, edited by Francis Henry Skrine, holds seventeen short tales of Bengali village and small-town life. The contents move from The Pride of Kadampur and The Rival Markets through A Foul Conspiracy and The Biter Bitten to A Brahman's Curse and Gobardhan's Triumph.

Skrine's introduction takes on a famous axiom. East is east and west is west, it runs, and never the twain shall meet. Skrine calls such despair unworthy. Britain bears duty for the happiness of three hundred million Asiatics, he notes. History, he argues, shows civilization growing from the mutual action of Europe and Asia. The tales themselves, of peacemakers, swindles, salt-loyalty, and a tame rabbit, were written to give English readers Bengal from inside its homes and markets.
the-aldine-vol-5-no-1-january-1872-a-typ: The Aldine, a typographic art journal, fills its fifth volume from James Sutton and Company of New York, with the volume dated 1873 and entered in 1872. Its contents list mixes editorial pieces such as A Peep at Abyssinia and The Heart of the Adirondacks with After the Comet by W. L. Alden, Architecture by W. Von Humboldt, and The American Robin by Gilbert Darling.
the-betrayal:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published a novel of intrigue in 1904, opening its contents with a face at a window. Good Samaritans, a cry in the night, and Miss Moyat's promise follow. A duke shows graciousness, and Lady Angela gives the narrator advice.

Colonel Ray's ring, a wonderful offer, and a chapter simply called Treachery deepen the plot. A bribe, two fair callers, and Lady Angela's engagement lead to more treachery and a scene from Miss Moyat. Later headings name a father's letter, a stepmother, a lost post, and a terrible discovery, promising secrets held by the narrator himself.
the-cathedral:
J. K. Huysmans wrote this novel about Chartres, first published in France in 1898. Clara Bell made the English translation, which also came out in 1898. Its hero, Durtal, has come to live near the great church and study it closely.

The first chapter follows Durtal at five in the morning, crossing a wind-swept market square toward the shelter of the building. Nuns and poor women bend against the gusts and gather into lines that split toward different doors. Inside, the air turns mild and still, with a faint scent of oil. The contrast sets the book's tone: a quiet, watchful study of faith, art, and stone, told through one man's daily rounds.
the-christmas-kalends-of-provence-and-so: Thomas A. Janvier, author of In Old New York and In Great Waters, wrote this account of Provencal festivals, published by Harper and Brothers of New York and London in November 1902.The story, if any, begins beyond what is present. The title page also lists his earlier books, among them In Old New York and In Great Waters.
the-cliff-ruins-of-canyon-de-chelly-ariz: Cosmos Mindeleff wrote this report on the cliff ruins of Canyon de Chelly, Arizona, taken from the Sixteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology for 1894-95, printed at Washington in 1897. Only the source note and the start of the contents are present here. The contents promise an introduction, a history and literature section, geography, then classifications and descriptions of the ruins of the pueblo region.The book itself never opens here.
the-communistic-societies-of-the-united-:
Charles Nordhoff wrote this survey of America's communistic societies from personal visit and observation, and dedicated it to Doctor and Mrs. John Davis of Cincinnati. The contents open with the subjects of the inquiry, the condition and necessities of labor, and a charge that trades-unions make a mistake. Labor societies as then managed, one heading argues, are mischievous.

The body of the book walks through the settlements one by one. The Amana Society comes first, with its history, its state in 1874, its social habits, and its religion and literature. The Harmonists at Economy follow, with their creed, their practical life, and particulars of Father Rapp. The Separatists of Zoar get the same treatment: origin, faith, practical life, and present condition. The Shakers and Mother Ann close the list in what is present.
the-creative-process-in-the-individual:
T. Troward published The Creative Process in the Individual in 1915. His contents move from a starting-point through the self-contemplation of spirit, the divine ideal, and the personal factor, ending with the divine offering and our place in it. Lines from Walt Whitman stand before the first chapter.

Chapter I takes up the old saying that order is heaven's first law. Getting things into better order, Troward argues, is the great secret of progress. Men now fly, not because nature's laws changed, but because they learned to arrange things in the right order. What was missing before was a personal factor that could grasp what those laws allow. Flight, for him, proves the triumph of principle over precedent.
the-devil-s-admiral:
Frederick Ferdinand Moore calls The Devil's Admiral an adventure story, dated 1913. Its contents send the reader aboard a steamer called the Kut Sang. They pass through a dead man in the passage, a fight in the dark, and a battle on the bridge. Pirates and gold follow, and a chapter on the art of Thirkle.

Chapter I, Missionary and Red-Headed Beggar, opens on Captain Riggs, who owns a trunk full of old logbooks and says any of them would make a better story than the Kut Sang. Riggs does not want the tale written, fearing print about himself and what happened aboard the old steamer in the China Sea. Folks, he says, care nothing about cargo-boats; they want yarns of floating hotels called liners, with palm gardens, bands at meals, and games from eight bells to the bosun's watch.
the-duty-of-disobedience-to-the-fugitive:
L. Maria Child's The Duty of Disobedience to the Fugitive Slave Act, Anti-Slavery Tract number nine, was printed in Boston in 1860 by the American Anti-Slavery Society. Child appeals straight to the lawmakers of Massachusetts. She needs no pardon for being a woman, she says, since truth gives any tongue the right to speak.

Massachusetts had passed a Personal Liberty Bill granting jury trials to those claimed as slaves, but Child calls that too little. She holds the federal act to be flat wicked and urges that it never be obeyed. Scripture heads her plea.
the-essays-or-counsels-civil-and-moral:
Francis Bacon's The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral runs from Of Truth and Of Death through Of Revenge, Of Envy, Of Love, and Of Great Place. The list goes on: boldness, nobility, atheism, travel, empire, counsel, cunning, friendship, expense, riches, ambition, and plantations all get short, dense chapters. Bacon signs with his titles, Lord Verulam and Viscount St. Albans.

Each essay packs a life's statecraft into a few pages of balanced prose. Kings, courtiers, and climbers have mined them for four centuries. Few books hold so much worldly wisdom in so small a space.
the-flying-saucers-are-real: Donald E. Keyhoe wrote The Flying Saucers Are Real, printed at New York in 1950. Only the front matter is present here: a bare contents list of twenty chapters and a note on the author. That note gives Keyhoe twenty-five years of watching flight, a Naval Academy degree, Marine Corps flying, work with Lindbergh's tour, and a post as chief of information for the Aeronautics Branch. No chapter text can be read in what is present.
the-garden-of-survival:
Algernon Blackwood wrote The Garden of Survival as a tale told in a letter to his twin brother, a confession he feels bound to make. The tale, he warns, is true but unfinished.

The writer says he first thought to tell the thing to a priest, then feared scorn or a charge of dreams from hired believers. He turns to his other half, whose skill as critic and author he teases even as he borrows it. Some strange, sweet experience binds the tale to a garden and to a lost love. Blackwood blends ghost tale and love letter into one hushed, grave piece.
the-high-history-of-the-holy-graal:
The High History of the Holy Graal was first written in Old French. It dates to the early half of the 13th century. It continues Chretien de Troyes' unfinished Perceval. The author is unknown. Sebastian Evans translated the book in 1898. Front pages list the source edition by Ch. Potvin. They also suggest further reading on the Graal.

An introduction describes the Brussels manuscript behind the translation. The manuscript is numbered 11,145. It rests in the library of the Dukes of Burgundy. Evans calls it the most complete known copy. It lacks only part of Branch XXI. Older fragments also survive in part. They amount to nearly one-seventh of the whole.
the-honorable-percival: Alice Hegan Rice wrote The Honorable Percival, published in New York by The Century Co. in 1914. Rice is named as the author of Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch and A Romance of Billy-Goat Hill. The contents list chapters such as A Blighted Being, A Counter-Irritant, Convalescence, Counter-Currents, Stranded, In the Wind-Shelter, and Dragging Anchor. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-infant-system-for-developing-the-int:
Samuel Wilderspin, who bills himself as inventor of the system of infant training, published this manual for developing the intellectual and moral powers of children from one to seven years old. The copy here is the eighth edition, carefully revised, dated 1852, and it opens with scriptural mottoes about receiving little children. His preface thanks God for the favor the infant system has received and reckons what has been accomplished against great difficulties.

Wilderspin insists the system grew from many years of labor and close observation of thousands of children, with provision made for each necessity that arose in their instruction. He claims, apart from one elliptical plan by Dr. Gilchrist, to owe no idea or contrivance to anyone else. Upwards of twenty-five thousand children had passed under his own care across the United Kingdom, none older than six, and the book codifies that experience for other teachers.
the-infidel-a-story-of-the-great-revival: M. E. Braddon wrote this novel. Simpkin, Marshall and Company published it in London in 1900. Her famous books include Lady Audley's Secret. The subtitle calls it a story of the Great Revival. Only the title page and contents start are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. The first headings move through Grub-Street. Scribblers open the tale. Miss Lester of the patent theatres follows. A scene at Mrs. Mandalay's rooms comes next. Hack writers, actresses, and revival religion seem set to collide.
the-inspector-general:
Nicolay Gogol's comedy appears here in Thomas Seltzer's translation. The play runs to five acts. Its introduction insists on a unique standing. The play is a national institution in Russia. No modern work carries such a weight of associations. Germany has Faust for that role. Faust is a cosmic tragedy, though. England needs nearly all of Shakespeare for the same effect. A Russian feels that bigness at the name Revizor.

The introduction explains the place through Russian letters themselves. Literature there is no luxury or diversion. It is bone of the bone of society. It carries collective wrongs, sorrows, and hopes. Before Gogol, Russian writers mostly copied foreign models. The drama followed French patterns. This play and Dead Souls founded a new line. It ran from Dostoyevsky down to Gorky. Seltzer frames a mistaken-identity comedy as a national turning point.
the-king-s-jackal:
Richard Harding Davis opens this tale on a hotel terrace at Tangier. The Hotel Grand Bretagne's private terrace is shaded by a great awning. Red, green, and yellow stripes mark it. Colored mats, potted plants, and wicker chairs strew the floor. Half the hotel is set aside for the King of Messina. He travels incognito by the Sultan of Morocco's orders. Two soldiers of the Bashaw's Guard stand at his door. They answer for his safety with their heads. They speak no language but their own.

Niccolas, the king's majordomo, sweeps the sea with a field-glass. It is his third sweep since sunrise. He hunts the boat from Gibraltar and the yacht's launch. Colonel Erhaupt joins him with brisk questions. The guards nod stiffly at every foreign tongue. Davis sets his light tone there. Diplomacy, exile, and murder plots become drawing-room adventure. Gibraltar's shadow lies across the water.
the-letters-of-franklin-k-lane-personal-: Franklin K. Lane served as Secretary of the Interior under President Wilson, and Anne Wintermute Lane and Louise Herrick Wall edited his personal and political letters. Only a Project Gutenberg header page is present here, giving the book title, its editors, and release details for the electronic text. The letters themselves, covering Lane years in California politics, Washington office, and war era cabinet work, are missing from this record at all.
the-london-prodigal:
The London Prodigal is a city comedy presented as played by the King's Majesty's servants. Its cast centers on the Flowerdale family: a merchant trading at Venice, his prodigal son Matthew, and the merchant's brother. Around them stand Sir Lancelot Spurcock of Kent with his three daughters, suitors, servants, cheating gamesters, and officers, with the scene set in London and the parts adjacent.

Act one opens with old Flowerdale returned from Venice in disguise to test how his son has behaved. The uncle reports grimly that Matthew has spent his allowance and far more, borrowing with oaths and pleas of kinship. The disguised-father device sets up a familiar moral pattern: a wastrel son examined by the parent he thinks absent.
the-makers-of-canada-bishop-laval: A. Leblond de Brumath wrote Bishop Laval for The Makers of Canada series, published in Toronto by Morang and Company in 1912. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the biography does not appear. The eight chapters move from the establishment of the Catholic Church in Canada through the early years of François de Laval, the Sovereign Council, and the seminary. Mgr. de Laval and the Savages, the settlement of the colony, the smaller seminary, and the progress of the colony follow, with page numbers.
the-moon-metal:
Garrett P. Serviss's novel The Moon Metal lists fourteen chapters before Chapter I, South Polar Gold, begins. Headings name Dr. Syx, a magician of science, a Grand Teton mine, wonders of a new metal, and the looting of the moon. The story promises invention, wealth, and mystery in equal parts.

News of gold discovered at the south pole opens the tale, and the narrator insists nobody guessed a new era had begun. Newsboys cried Extra as they had for murders, fires, battles, and Wall Street panics, yet hardly anyone believed the first reports. They sounded too exaggerated and improbable to credit. The chapter continues from that sceptical calm toward the strange metal of the title.
the-mystery-of-orcival:
Emile Gaboriau's The Mystery of Orcival opens before dawn on Thursday, July 9, in a year left as 186-. Jean Bertaud and his son Philippe, known at Orcival for living by poaching and marauding, rise at three in the morning to go fishing. They carry their tackle down an acacia-shaded path from the station at Evry toward the Seine.

Their boat lies moored above a wire bridge, beside a field adjoining Valfeuillu, the estate of the Count de Tremorel. While Jean bails out the boat, he spots an oar-pin about to break and sends Philippe for wood. The young man jumps the wide ditch around the count's park, knife in hand, then stops among the willows and calls urgently for his father.
the-novel-of-the-black-seal:
Arthur Machen wrote The Novel of the Black Seal, first published in 1895. A young lady in Leicester Square tells the tale, and a prologue gives the statement of William Gregg, F.R.S. The lady calls her listener a determined rationalist, setting up a clash between cold reason and strange events.

The title and the use of a learned man of science as witness hint at hidden knowledge behind daily life. Readers who like eerie tales of secret evil, told through statements and testimony, will find Machen's method here. The frame keeps the horror at one remove, which makes it linger.
the-poison-tree-a-tale-of-hindu-life-in-: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's The Poison Tree, a tale of Hindu life in Bengal, was translated by Miriam S. Knight. Edwin Arnold supplied a preface, and T. Fisher Unwin published the book at London in 1884. Knight's name is printed on this record's own title page. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the novel itself is absent. The first chapter is titled Nagendra's Journey by Boat. Later headings include Tara Charan and Oh! Lotus-Eyed, Who Art Thou? Further entries introduce Haridasi Boisnavi and the Babu.
the-poisoned-meal:
Wilkie Collins's The Poisoned Meal takes its readers across the Channel to Normandy. Its subject is Marie-Françoise-Victoire Salmon, a young French girl. Her father was a poor Norman labourer, and her mother died in her childhood. Three mistresses in succession were satisfied with her service. Then she entered Monsieur Dumesnil's household at twenty, the turning point of her career.

A visitor to that house, Monsieur Revel, held a legal post at Caen. He pressed her to better herself by taking service in his town. Marie preferred needlework and tried Bayeux first, but it would not feed her, and she remembered his advice. On August 1, 1781, she reached Caen and was hired the same evening by the Huet Duparc family. Her duties ran from fetching milk for an old man's saltless hasty-pudding to cooking and marketing. They paid two pounds a year.
the-project-gutenberg-rst-manual: The Project Gutenberg RST Manual opens with reStructuredText markup rather than finished pages: container directives, a title page block, and lists of tables and figures. Its first chapter heading is Installing EpubMaker. The leaves provided run only 392 characters, holding the manual's skeleton of contents and lists. The instructions themselves, on formatting texts for the project's EpubMaker tool, are not present in the pages at hand.
the-red-seal:
Natalie Sumner Lincoln opens in a police court. Banker Benjamin Augustus Clymer testifies there as a character witness. The prisoner is John Sylvester, a confidential clerk. His wife has charged him with assault and battery. Clymer corrects the prosecutor at once on a point of fact.

Sylvester was never Clymer's employee, he explains. The clerk served Judge James Hildebrand instead. Clymer shared an apartment with the judge in the winter of 1918. He calls Sylvester honest, sober, and industrious. The man drank little and never quarreled, he says. Sylvester left service only to marry. Precise testimony launches a mystery around a trusted clerk.
the-school-for-scandal: R. B. Sheridan's comedy The School for Scandal is presented here through editorial notes rather than the play itself. Square brackets reproduce the printed book, with one closing bracket added. Footnotes have been consolidated at the end of the play. The editor also says the text follows Fraser Rae's edition, Sheridan's Plays Now Printed As He Wrote Them. Rae used Sheridan's own manuscript, preserved at Frampton Court. That version differs in many respects from the generally known one, Rae claims.
the-shadow-of-the-cathedral:
